items.t: WNBA Finals Scheduling Fumble Puts The Business Of Women’s Basketball In The Spotlight
items.x: The WNBA’s growing popularity is creating new business opportunities, but the Atlanta Dream’s 2026 Finals scheduling controversy highlights the logistical challenges of turning rising fan demand into a larger commercial operation. Game 6 of the WNBA Finals between the Atlanta Dream and Golden State Valkyries was scheduled for October 29 at 12:30 p.m. ET at State Farm Arena in Atlanta. The game was originally scheduled for 8 p.m. at Gateway Center Arena, the Dream’s regular-season home, which holds approximately 3,500 fans. State Farm Arena can accommodate roughly 17,000, which creates more opportunities to sell tickets, attract corporate partners, and generate revenue. It also allows more fans to attend a championship game. However, the change came with a significant compromise: a weekday afternoon tipoff that could make attendance more difficult for fans with traditional work schedules. According to the WNBA’s official announcement , the league coordinated with the Atlanta Dream, Golden State Valkyries, Atlanta Hawks, State Farm Arena, and broadcast partners to make the relocation possible. items.t: North Carolina HBCU Students March Miles To Vote After Campus Polling Sites Removed
items.x: Students at historically Black colleges and universities in North Carolina are marching miles to cast their ballot s after election officials declined to include on-campus early voting locations ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, The Guardian reports. More than 100 students from North Carolina Agricultural and Technical State University, Bennett College, and the University of North Carolina at Greensboro marched to polling stations Oct. 15, the first day of early voting. The demonstration followed decisions excluding campus voting sites previously available during the 2024 presidential election, according to WUNC News . Students at North Carolina A&T, reportedly the nation’s largest historically Black university, walked approximately 45 minutes to reach the nearest early voting location. Some encountered missing sidewalks and obstructed walkways along the route. Election officials cited low voter turnout at previous campus locations to defend the decisions. However, student organizers argue that eliminating convenient polling sites creates additional challenges for young voters, particularly those without reliable transportation. items.t: Renee Montgomery's Atlanta Dream Investment Soars As Team Valuation Hits $280M
items.x: Former WNBA star Renee Montgomery’s investment in the Atlanta Dream has gained significant value, with the franchise’s estimated worth reaching $280 million in 2026 , five years after an ownership group purchased the team for a reported $7 million to $10 million, Afrotech reports. According to the outlet, Montgomery joined an investment group led by real estate executive Larry Gottesdiener in 2021. Suzanne Abair, president of Northland Investment Corp., also participated in the acquisition. The purchase made Montgomery the first former WNBA player to hold both an ownership stake and an executive position with a league franchise . The Dream’s estimated valuation has increased at least 28- fold since the acquisition , according to Sportico . However, Montgomery’s individual ownership percentage and initial investment amount have not been publicly disclosed, making her personal financial gains difficult to determine. “It’s a tremendous investment,” Montgomery told Front Office Sports, reflecting on the franchise’s growth. The two-time WNBA champion, who retired in 2021 after 11 seasons, has also discussed the challenges of transitioning from professional athlete to business executive.

Her entrepreneurial portfolio includes Reframe, a clinical skincare brand developed after two years of research. The venture marks her entry into the beauty industry as she continues expanding her interests beyond her public role as the wife of one of basketball’s most recognizable athletes. Jackson's approach focuses on giving students practical financial knowledge to help them navigate adulthood and avoid costly financial mistakes. items.t: NBA Legend And Entrepreneur Isiah Thomas on Mental Toughness, Building Wealth, And Turning Pain Into Purpose
items.x: Isiah Thomas knows championships are won with more than talent. During a live fireside chat at the 2026 Black Enterprise XCEL Summit for Men , the Hall of Fame athlete, entrepreneur, investor, and philanthropist shared how mental stamina, financial independence, and learning from setbacks have shaped his approach to basketball and business. Moderated by legendary Emmy Award-winning journalist Ed Gordon , the conversation delivered powerful lessons for leaders navigating their own career paths. Staying Focused Under Pressure Thomas explained that he had to sharpen his mindset during his NBA career to compete against iconic players like Magic Johnson, Michael Jordan , and Larry Bird. “I had to be smarter,” he said. He learned to limit his own mistakes, sustain concentration, and recognize the moments when opponents lost focus. He then carried that approach into business, explaining that success also depends on enduring difficult stretches rather than simply enjoying the wins. “Everybody can ride the high times, and everybody gives you good advice in your high times,” he said. “But do you have the mental stamina to ride through the low times and stick it out?” Source: Emmy Award-winni

items.t: Student Loan Borrowers Can Stop Wage Garnishment, Here's How
items.x: Americans with defaulted federal student loans could soon face wage garnishment as the Trump administration reportedly prepares to resume aggressive debt collection efforts. However, borrowers have several legal options to prevent the government from withholding portions of their paychecks, Forbes reports. Federal law allows the government to garnish up to 15% of a defaulted borrower's disposable wages without a court order. Officials can also intercept federal tax refunds and withhold portions of certain federal benefits, including Social Security payments. The U.S. Department of Education is reportedly working with the Treasury Department t o enlist private debt collection agencies, the Washington Sun reports. An Education Department spokesperson has denied reports of the planned collections. Borrowers generally enter default after missing federal student loan payments for at least 270 days. Those who have not defaulted can avoid collection measures by maintaining payments or exploring income-driven repayment plans, deferment, or forbearance. items.t: What dealers say most determines car resale value at point of sale
items.x: Car resale value depends heavily on mileage, service history, accident records, mechanical condition, and how well the vehicle presents at the time of sale. Dealers also look for signs that the owner maintained the car consistently rather than preparing it only when it was time to sell. How much of a car's original value is still there when it is time to sell? A 2026 iSeeCars analysis of more than 950,000 five-year-old vehicles found that the average car had lost 41.8% of its value over five years. Some depreciation is unavoidable. The final offer, however, comes down to the specific car sitting in front of the dealer: how many miles it has covered, what condition it is in, and what its history reveals. How Do Mileage and Age Affect a Car's Resale Value? Dealers usually look at mileage and age early because both give a quick sense of how much use the car has seen. A five-year-old vehicle with 35,000 miles will usually fall into a different value range than the same model with 90,000 miles. items.t: The WNBA Finals Are Playing A Championship Game Thursday Afternoon
items.x: Icon Sportswire / WNBA Finals / Atlanta Dream / Golden State Valkyries There are only so many ways to tell the WNBA you don’t take its audience seriously, and apparently one is scheduling a potential championship-clinching game for 12:30 p.m. on a Thursday. Yes, you read that correctly. Not Thursday night. Not Thursday evening. Thursday at lunchtime, when millions of people are sitting in offices, working from home, pretending to pay attention on Zoom calls, or trying to squeeze a sandwich into a 30-minute lunch break. And these are the people we expect to tune in to Game 6 of the WNBA Finals between the Atlanta Dream and the Golden State Valkyries? The same people who have spent years arguing that women’s basketball deserves the same respect, attention, and investment as the men’s game? Make it make sense. After a weekend of frantic discussions and scheduling negotiations, the WNBA announced that Game 6 would tip off at 12:30 p.m. ET Thursday at Atlanta’s State Farm Arena. The Valkyries lead the series 3-2, meaning a win could give Golden State its first championship. Atlanta, meanwhile, needs to win to force a decisive Game 7 on Saturday in San Francisco. This is a championship.

For some Gary residents, the outages lasted more than two weeks, creating serious hardships for families, senior citizens and people with medical conditions. items.t: Dolores Huerta's Civil Rights Legacy Reaches Across Racial Lines
items.x: Pioneering labor leader dies at 96, leaving a lasting impact on Black and Latino communities and America's fight for equality. Dolores Huerta, the pioneering civil rights activist and labor organizer whose fight for farmworkers' rights helped reshape America's struggle for social and economic justice, died Wednesday, October 28, at her home in Bakersfield, California. She was 96. Her passing marks the loss of one of the nation's most influential voices for equality, whose work connected the struggles of Latino farmworkers with the broader civil rights movement, including the fight for justice and economic opportunity within African American communities. Huerta, who co-founded the United Farm Workers with César Chávez, spent more than seven decades challenging discrimination, organizing workers and advocating for families whose voices were often overlooked. Her commitment to social justice reflected many of the same principles championed by Black civil rights leaders, including Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., Fannie Lou Hamer and Dorothy Height, who understood that political freedom and economic opportunity were closely connected. The initiative includes town hall events in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, on October 26 and Atlanta, Georgia, on October 29. The gatherings are part of the NAACP's continuing efforts to educate voters, expand grassroots participation and ensure that historically underrepresented communities have a voice in decisions affecting their lives. items.t: Illinois medical debt relief program surpasses $1B goal in two years
items.x: The state has erased over $1.4 billion in medical debt for almost 700,000 Illinoisans for pennies on the dollar, two years after launching a new relief program. At its launch, the Illinois Medical Debt Relief Program aimed to eliminate $1 billion in debt. The state has surpassed that goal by $400 million, spending less than $10 million in state dollars to achieve these results. That means that every state dollar invested in the program wiped out over $100 in debt. That was possible due to the state’s partnership with Undue Medical Debt — a nonprofit that works with local governments and healthcare providers to purchase and eliminate qualifying medical debt owed by low-income residents. “Medical debt is a leading cause of bankruptcy,” Gov. JB Pritzker said in a news conference Thursday in Chicago. “It can ruin credit, limit financial opportunities, and cause years of uncertainty long after they leave the hospital. That is a symptom of a truly broken system.” Illinois residents whose household income is at or below 400% of the federal poverty level, or who have medical debt equal to 5% or more of their household income, are eligible. items.t: Labor Activist And Civil Rights Icon Dolores Huerta Dies At 96
items.x: Source: Michael Tullberg / Getty Dolores Huerta, co-founder of what became the United Farm Workers (UFW) union — the first nationally recognized union for farmworkers — has died at age 96. According to the New York Times , Huerta passed away Wednesday at her home in Bakersfield, California. Erik Olvera, a spokesman for her family, told the Times she died of cancer. Huerta — born on April 10, 1930, in the mining town of Dawson, New Mexico — was the first Latina inducted into the National Women’s Hall of Fame in 1993, and in 2012, she was awarded the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation’s highest civilian honor, by former President Barack Obama. According to NBC News , Matthew J. Garcia — the Dartmouth College professor who wrote the 2014 book, From the Jaws of Victory: The Triumph and Tragedy of Cesar Chavez and the Farm Worker Movement — called the Mexican-American activist “the most famous Latina that has ever been in the labor movement." The Supreme Court has cleared the way for New Hampshire to ban the use of student IDs as a backup form of voter identification during the upcoming midterm elections, handing Republicans another victory in the ongoing fight over access to the ballot box. On Thursday, the justices granted a Republican-backed emergency appeal, blocking student IDs from being used as an alternative method of identification at the polls. The court cited a longstanding legal principle that judges should avoid changing election rules too close to Election Day. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the only justice to publicly dissent, the Associated Press reports. New Hampshire lawmakers passed a law earlier this year that removed student IDs from the list of expressly accepted forms of identification for voters seeking a ballot. The state’s secretary of state subsequently issued guidance barring students from using those IDs as a backup method of verifying their identities. items.t: Meet the Black woman helping people buy land for less than $1,000 in just 5 days
items.x: For Black families, land has always meant more than property. It has meant freedom, stability, power, security, and something tangible to pass down. But over the last century, Black land ownership has declined dramatically. The Federation of Southern Cooperatives reports that Black farmland ownership peaked at roughly 16 to 19 million acres in 1910 and has fallen to less than 3 million acres today. The organization also estimates that more than 60% of Black-owned land is heirs’ property, leaving many families vulnerable to losing land that was meant to remain in the family. The ownership gap is still visible today. According to the U.S. Census Bureau, the Black homeownership rate was 44.0% in the first quarter of 2026, compared with 75.0% for non-Hispanic White households. That is the story Sis Shaneka is trying to help change. Through her free Land to Legacy Masterclass , she has taught more than 10,000 students at no cost, breaking down land ownership, funding, development, and legacy-building in a way everyday people can understand and use. items.t: Ex-NFL Player Jon Vaughn: ‘Who Protects Us from Our Protectors?’
items.x: By Jon Vaughn, Contributor I ended my last piece with a question, and I want to be honest about why I asked it. I did not pose it as a rhetorical flourish. I asked it because survivors have asked it of me, on the phone, late at night, after discovering what had been done with their names, their stories or their trust by people who said they were on their side. I asked it because I have had to ask it myself, about a room I walked into carrying evidence and walked out of as the problem. Who do I go to? Too often the true answer was: right now, nobody. That is not an accident. It is a design. We built our protectors the way the institutions built theirs. Every institution I have ever fought had the same shape. Power sat with one office. The people around that office owed their positions to it. Complaints traveled through the very desk they were complaining about. When something went wrong, the first instinct was not to fix it but to contain it. Look closely at much of the advocacy world and you will see the same architecture, drawn smaller. items.x: Source: Goodboy Picture Company / Getty A last name may look like a simple part of your identity, but for Black Americans, it can hold generations of history, survival, family separation, resistance and freedom. Some surnames connect families to the people who enslaved their ancestors. Others reflect the names people deliberately chose after emancipation to reclaim their identities and begin new chapters. And some carry stories that have been lost to time. The history of Black surnames in America is far more complicated than the familiar belief that formerly enslaved people simply adopted the last names of their enslavers. Behind these names are decisions made under extraordinary circumstances, family ties that survived slavery, and the determination of people who finally gained the legal freedom to decide what they and their children would be called and the future they would go on to forge for their lineage. To understand the story of Black surnames in America, we must look beyond the names themselves and examine the history that shaped them. items.t: Nathan Brown, convicted in 1976 murder of Bonnie Bolluch, released from prison and out on parole
items.x: CSRA (WJBF) – A man who was sentenced to life in prison in for a 1976 murder is now out on parole. Nathan Brown was released from prison on Tuesday, Oct. 27. He was convicted in the 1976 murder of Bonnie Bulloch in Taliaferro County . Bulloch, 11, was at a Crawfordville gas station with his stepfather, who was working a night shift, when he and his stepfather were kidnapped. A group of men, including Brown, shot Bulloch and his stepfather in the head. His stepfather survived and identified the killers. Brown, Jose High and Judson Ruffin were convicted of murder and sentenced to death in 1979. However, Brown and Ruffin got new trials and were resentenced to life in prison. Jose High was put to death in 2001. Ruffin remains in prison.

items.t: What does the referendum on Aiken County ballots mean?
items.x: AIKEN COUNTY, S.C. (WJBF) — Aiken County voters will decide November 3 whether to expand the county’s authority to use different funding sources for wastewater facilities and services. A 1976 referendum authorized Aiken County to build the Horse Creek Wastewater Treatment Plant. It also limited the county to a short list of funding options. Now, county leaders want voters to expand those options as they prepare to increase the plant’s capacity from 20 million to 26 million gallons per day. “When the referendum was passed for financing the plant, it enumerated specific financing options that were available at the time,” Bunker said. Those options include revenue from wholesale and non-wholesale customers, including scavenger waste haulers, Federal Housing Administration loans, and state and federal grants. Bunker says financing options have expanded in the past 50 years. He wants the county to consider other options, including capital project sales tax revenue, installment purchase revenue bonds, and traditional bonds sold on the open market. items.t: James Brown name set to come to new arena complex in Augusta
items.x: AUGSTA, Ga (WJBF) The name of the new Augusta arena remains undecided, but James Brown will still be a part of the project. The area housing the new arena and the Bell Auditorium will be the James Brown Entertainment Complex. The auditorium will connect to the arena with a grand hall. People are happy that Brown will continue to be honored at the arena. "I think it's a great thing," said Harrison Catalano. "Keeping that change going with the Godfather of soul." For a while it was unknown if Brown's legacy would still be a part of the arena. Now it will be bigger than just one building. "The entire complex is named after him, gives us an opportunity to continue to celebrate him, his family and his legacy," said Augusta Mayor Garnett Johnson. "I think it's a win win for Augusta, a win win for all those who support James Brown." The arena does not have its name yet. It is still open to have a corporate sponsor buy the naming rights. The Augusta-Richmond County Coliseum Authority voted unanimously to call it the James Brown Entertainment Complex. It will not be official until it is approved by Brown's estate.

items.t: Former WJBF sports director Stan Byrdy dies at 73
items.x: WJBF is saddened to announce that longtime sports anchor Stan Byrdy has died. Byrdy was Sports Director at WJBF from 1985 to 1994 and remained on the station's Masters Tournament coverage team through 2002. He later served as Sports Director at WAGT-TV in Augusta from 2006 to 2009. After his television career ended, he wrote four books on local history including "Alister Mackenzie's Masterpiece: Augusta National Golf Club". A local historian, he was a popular guest on talk shows and podcasts nationwide. He also served as coordinating executive producer for the Emmy-nominated documentary, “Augusta’s Master Plan; From Sherman’s March to Arnie’s Army”, for Georgia Public Broadcasting. Stan is survived by his wife and two children. He was 73.

items.t: Federal Reserve holds interest rates steady in face of persistent inflation
items.x: Federal Reserve officials held interest rates steady Wednesday despite stubborn inflation. The central bank's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) voted 10-2 to keep the benchmark federal funds rate range at 3.75 percent to 4 percent. "The committee believes that the accumulation of more information will help it determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the 2 percent goal," Fed Chair Kevin Warsh told reporters, reiterating the FOMC's statement. Fed board of governors member Lisa Cook and Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland's president Beth Hammack dissented in favor of a quarter-point increase. Hammack also backed a rate hike in late July, joining two of her colleagues in the minority when the central bank kept rates steady . Wednesday's decision came six weeks after officials raised rates by a quarter point , the first hike in more than three years. Inflation has risen this year amid the Iran war , creating a difficult set of circumstances for President Trump and the GOP this midterm cycle . items.t: New SNAP rules for South Carolina start Nov. 1
items.x: SOUTH CAROLINA (WJBF) Beginning November 1st, South Carolina will update the definition of SNAP-eligible foods. Candy, energy drinks, soft drinks, and other sweetened beverages will no longer be allowed for purchase with SNAP benefits. Diet and zero sugar soft drinks are allowed. This is all part of the Healthy Food SC project, a two-year initiative designed to help households receiving SNAP benefits make healthier food choices. The goal of this project is to promote healthier food choices among participants by encouraging the purchase of more nutritious foods while reducing the purchase of items with limited nutritional value. All South Carolina SNAP approved retailers will participate in this project, and SNAP households in South Carolina will not have the option to opt out of these food restrictions. For more information on the new program, please visit the Healthy Food SC website .

items.t: 68 dead in high-speed train collision, Spain’s 2nd deadly rail crash this year
items.x: URDA, Spain (AP) — A high-speed train slammed into another that had stopped on the tracks in Spain on Wednesday, killing at least 68 people and injuring dozens in the second deadly rail collision this year. The regional government of Castilla La Mancha confirmed the death toll and said another 58 people were receiving medical treatment at hospitals. Rescue workers searched the wreckage through the day for survivors and bodies. The collision came just nine months after another deadly crash involving high-speed trains operated by the same two companies in southern Spain in January. “Today all of Spain is grieving,” Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said from the crash site, where he announced that his government would declare three days of national mourning. items.t: Flying taxis could carry passengers by 2030
items.x: (TestMiles) A British aerospace company has demonstrated an electric flying taxi that could eventually offer a new way to escape crowded city roads. The Flying Car Is Moving Beyond Science Fiction Los Angeles has spent decades trying to solve its traffic problems. Freeways expand, transit systems improve, and technology promises more efficient journeys. Yet travelling across the city can still take a remarkable amount of time. A British aerospace company believes part of the solution might be above the roads rather than on them. Vertical Aerospace has demonstrated an electric aircraft capable of taking off vertically, transitioning into conventional forward flight, and landing without a runway. The technology was publicly displayed at the Farnborough International Airshow in Britain, marking an important development in the company's plans to introduce commercial passenger flights. The aircraft is part of a growing category known as electric vertical takeoff and landing, or eVTOL. Unlike a conventional airplane, it does not require a runway for every departure. items.t: Utah authorities connect 1974 cold case to serial killer Ted Bundy
items.x: SUMMIT COUNTY, Utah ( KTVX ) — Investigators in Summit County, Utah closed the 1974 cold case homicide of Melissa Ann Smith Tuesday, linking her murder to prominent serial killer Ted Bundy. Using DNA and other evidence, the Summit County Sheriff's Office and Summit County Attorney's Office formally closed the cold-case murder, saying that the evidence conclusively proves that Ted Bundy murdered 17-year-old Melissa Ann Smith. Bundy has long been considered a suspect in several cold cases in Utah, and Smith's murder was one of them. Hunters found her remains in Summit County on Oct. 27, 1974, 52 years ago today. "The work began with the investigators who handled the case in 1974, and it continued through the dedication and perseverance of those who carried it forward," Summit County Sheriff Kacey Bates said. "After 50 years, we have reached a point that so many have worked toward." During a City Council study session Monday, October 26, council members discussed allowing pedal-assist electric bicycles on the trail and establishing a 15-mile-per-hour speed limit for riders. No ordinance has been written or approved, and no date has been set for a vote. The discussion followed an inquiry from someone interested in opening an electric bike rental business in North Augusta. City leaders discussed whether those restrictions should be updated to accommodate electric bicycles, which have become increasingly popular among recreational riders. items.t: Recalled butter sold in 10 states receives risk warning: FDA
items.x: NEW JERSEY ( WPIX ) A popular plant-based butter has been recalled due to yeast, mold and E. coli, and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has now assigned it a risk level . The recall, which was initiated by Prosperity Organic Foods, Inc., headquartered in Boise, Idaho, involves 1,304 cases of Miyoko's Creamery European Style Salted Plant Milk Butter. The FDA assigned the recall as a Class II risk level on Friday, meaning a product may cause “temporary or medically reversible adverse health consequences.” The recall was initially announced Sept. 11. The affected butter, which is perishable and stored refrigerated or frozen, comes in six-packs of 8-ounce units, which can be identified with the following information: UPC 857554005773 Lot number and best-by on SBS carton: 07871, Nov. 5, 2026 Lot number and best-by date on the corrugated case for shipment: 1007871, Nov. 5, 2026 The affected products were also sold in Connecticut, Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Illinois, Indiana, Maryland, New Jersey, New Hampshire and Wisconsin.

items.t: ‘Who am I tipping here?’ Self-service kiosk at airport prompts customer to tip 18%, viral video shows
items.x: (NEXSTAR) – A viral video filmed by a traveler at Newark Liberty International Airport in New Jersey appears to show that he was prompted to leave a tip while purchasing a bottle of water — at a self-service kiosk. The traveler, a Florida-based physician with a large social media following, demonstrated the frustrating moment in an Instagram video published Oct. 16. items.x: Source: Isbjorn / Getty Lately, the debate over whether Black women should get our hair done in a corporate chair at a retail giant like Ulta or retreat to the privacy of an independent solo suite is moving us further away from the community space of Black beauty salons that historically have welcomed, shielded, and anchored us in self-care and community. I was a teenage girl, untethered and newly navigating the rough edges of the foster care system, when I somehow found my way into the basement beauty salon across the street from my high school. I didn’t know it then, but descending those steps would introduce me to Toni, who would open a new world and a new lens through which I saw myself. Toni was a queer gay man whose vibrancy overflowed the modest salon. He had survived the rough streets of Chicago and had been raised outside his biological family. Toni eventually found safety and community in San Diego, where he was able to blossom. He would regale me with stories of how free he felt living in his true self after a childhood spent feeling like living in his truth put him in grave danger. His wife, Lydia, revealed that the couple had been in a polygynous marriage for nearly three years before publicly introducing Minister Shakayla as his other wife. He made the announcement during the service, explaining that Shakayla was already familiar to many church members because of her ministry. She then invited the minister to join them onstage and welcomed her as her “sister in marriage.” The introduction revealed a family arrangement that the congregation may not have fully understood before the service. Shakayla addressed the audience after joining the couple, acknowledging that the revelation could prompt questions and concerns. She said she felt neither overlooked nor mistreated and believed the relationship had brought positive changes to her life. She also thanked God, Ford, and Lydia, explaining that she wanted to support their family and serve alongside them. “I have not been slighted not one bit. I have gained so much,” Shakayla said, according to Complex . She described their family d

items.t: LeBron James Brushes Off Trump’s Demand for an Apology Over National Anthem Criticism
items.x: Nationwide President Donald Trump has demanded an apology from LeBron James after footage showed the NBA star moving his arms during the national anthem. The president accused him of disrespecting the country, but the Philadelphia 76ers player brushed off the criticism after leading his team to a historic comeback win. The controversy began Tuesday before Philadelphia faced the reigning champion New York Knicks at Madison Square Garden. According to The Comeback , footage shared by ClutchPoints showed James swinging his arms as if practicing a golf swing before making a basketball shooting motion while the national anthem played. Most of his teammates remained still. The 76ers went on to win the game, spoiling the Knicks’ championship ring ceremony, but the pregame footage quickly gained attention on social media. Conservative commentators criticized James over the footage, prompting Trump to weigh in on Thursday. In a post on Truth Social, the president accused the basketball star of disrespecting the country and called him a “TOTAL DISGRACE.” He also demanded that James apologize to American service members who died defending the nation and its flag. items.t: Black Mom Says Police Were Called After Her 3-Year-Old Son Was Singled Out for Being Too Good at Soccer
items.x: Nationwide Nevada Pierre, a 3-year-old African American boy from Winter Park, Florida, has drawn widespread attention after a youth soccer league asked his family to leave a game following a dispute over his skills on the field. His mother, Martasia Griffin, disputes the league official’s allegations and says her son was singled out because he plays soccer extremely well. According to People , a league official called police to Martin Luther King Jr. Park in Winter Park and asked officers to speak with Nevada’s parents, Griffin and Don Pierre. Body camera footage released by the Winter Park Police Department later spread across social media, drawing attention to the dispute. In the footage, the official told officers that Nevada was more advanced than the other players and scored many goals. However, he also alleged that the boy pushed other children during games. The official said he had rotated players in previous matches to give everyone a chance to participate, but claimed Nevada’s parents objected to his decisions. He also accused them of arguing with other parents during the latest game and asked officers to help remove the family. The league offered to refund their participa

items.t: Family Still Seeks Justice Ten Years After 15-Year-Old Black Teen Was Burned Alive
items.x: Nationwide Demetrius Griffin Jr., an African American teen from Chicago, Illinois, was only 15 years old when firefighters found him burning inside a garbage can in a West Side alley. Ten years later, his murder remains unsolved, and his family is still searching for answers after years without meaningful updates from investigators. Firefighters discovered Demetrius on September 16, 2016, near the 5500 block of West Cortez Street in Chicago’s Austin neighborhood, just a block and a half from his home. The Cook County Medical Examiner determined that he was alive when the fire started. His aunt, Rochelle Sykes, continues to struggle with the brutality of his death and the unanswered questions surrounding his final moments. “Who would burn somebody alive? What could you possibly do to somebody that they would burn you alive?” she asked. She also said she still struggles with the thought that her nephew suffered and she could not help him. According to Fox 32 Chicago , Sykes said Demetrius had walked a young girl partway toward her home on the evening he disappeared before heading back toward his own house. The girl reportedly shared that account with the family, but Sykes has questio

items.t: Black Mom of 4 Who Was Missing For 5 Days Found Shot Dead in Shallow Grave
items.x: Nationwide Seraphina Pereira, a 35-year-old African American mother of four from New York, was found dead in a shallow grave at a Queens waterfront park five days after she disappeared. Police identified her death as a homicide after an autopsy revealed gunshot wounds to her head, neck, and torso. Police also took a person of interest into custody as the investigation continued. Her body was discovered around 9:40 p.m. Saturday in Rockaway Community Park near the Jamaica Bay shoreline, close to Beach 58th Street and Almeda Avenue. Her remains had begun to decompose when authorities found her buried at the site. The New York City Medical Examiner’s Office later determined that she died from gunshot wounds to her head, neck, and torso. Her death was ruled a homicide. Her family had been searching for her since October 19, when she left her apartment on Beach 54th Street around 11 a.m. and never returned. Relatives distributed missing-person flyers throughout the neighborhood and searched nearby areas in hopes of finding her. Her sister, Davonna Gray, traveled from Albany to help with the search. Gray said the family even went to the beach with flashlights because Pereira loved spendi

items.t: Black Mom With 9 Children Seeks Community Help to Move Family After Losing Her Home
items.x: Nationwide Melody Clay, an African American mother of nine from Seattle, Washington, is seeking community support to move her family after her landlord declined to renew her lease. After adopting five of her nieces and nephews to keep them together, she now faces another challenge as a broken car threatens to delay the move to a home that could accommodate her large family. Clay officially adopted her five nieces and nephews in May 2025. She was already raising four children of her own but stepped in after the younger children entered foster care. Their father had struggled with drug addiction following the death of his oldest child in gun violence. During the years Clay worked to bring the family together, she also lost her mother, while the children's father died from health complications. Despite these losses, Clay remained determined to provide a stable home for the children. She said their dependence on her gives her the strength to keep going. “When I look at them, that's what keeps me going. I'm like, they depend on me, I don't have the option of failing,” she told Fox 13 Seattle . She also reassured their father that the children would be safe and cared for in her home, pro

items.t: Reality Star Anika Rashaun Dies at 34, Just Months After Learning She Had Breast Cancer
items.x: Nationwide Former reality star Anika Rashaun, known for appearing on The Real World and The Challenge , has died at 34 after battling stage 4 breast cancer. She died on October 1, months after receiving a diagnosis that surprised her and speaking publicly about the importance of breast cancer awareness and early detection. Her friend Cyndi Rich announced her death in a Facebook post. Another longtime friend, Tiara Ramos, paid tribute to her in an October 5 Substack post titled “Breast Friends Forever: RIP to my Sister.” Ramos described the diagnosis as “a shock,” explaining that Rashaun had never been identified as high-risk despite her mother's history of breast cancer, according to People . She also raised concerns about the medical care her friend received, saying doctors had not advised her to prioritize mammograms. She appeared on The Real World: Bad Blood in 2016 before joining The Challenge: Invasion of the Champions in 2017. Beyond reality television, she worked as a dating coach and was training to become a licensed marriage and family therapist, according to her Instagram profile. Ramos, who had known her for more than 20 years, remembered her as someone who stood firmly

items.t: Nicki Minaj Could Become White House Press Secretary, Trump Allies Suggest
items.x: Nationwide Nicki Minaj has been floated as a possible replacement for the White House press secretary after two allies of President Donald Trump publicly suggested she could fill the role. The speculation followed a video of the rapper praising Trump during a conversation aboard Air Force One, though no formal offer has been confirmed. White House communications director Steven Cheung shared the video on X and said, "Ladies and gentlemen, I think we may have found the new White House Press Secretary!" Trump adviser Alex Bruesewitz also weighed in, asking Minaj’s fans, known as the Barbz, what they thought of the idea. The White House’s official account joined the exchange with an eyeballs emoji, as reported by TMZ . In the clip, Cheung asks Minaj about Trump’s leadership and the economy. She describes the president as a natural businessman, says nobody works harder than him, and claims he won three elections. The exchange ends with the rapper looking toward the camera and laughing as Cheung begins to speak. The suggestion comes as the White House press secretary position faces another transition. Katie Zacharia reportedly resigned after a rocky first appearance, leaving the adminis

items.t: Siblings of Black Woman Missing for 3 Months Raise Money to Hire Private Investigator
items.x: Nationwide Chantel Brooks, a 37-year-old African American woman from Fairfield, California, has been missing for more than three months, and her family refuses to give up the search. Her brothers, Calvin and Kevin Robinson, are organizing volunteer searches, sharing her story online and raising money for a private investigator as police suspect foul play in her disappearance. Surveillance footage captured Brooks leaving her job in the 700 block of Eddy Street in San Francisco around 12:20 a.m. on July 17. About 85 minutes later, cameras recorded her leaving a CVS store in Fairfield. She was last seen approaching her black 2021 Infiniti QX50 SUV in the parking lot. On Aug. 18, the Fairfield Police Department announced that investigators believed foul play was involved. Authorities have not publicly disclosed further details about what happened to her. Since learning that their sister was missing, both brothers have made finding her their priority. Calvin traveled from Los Angeles to the Bay Area as soon as he heard the news. He said he has put much of his life on hold while trying to bring her home. Known as CiCi within the family, Brooks runs a beauty business called Glamour House.

items.t: Innocent 68-Year-Old Black Woman Dies After Stray Bullet Hits Her While Sitting on Her Porch
items.x: Nationwide Pamela Shanks, a 68-year-old African American woman from Gastonia, North Carolina, was fatally struck by a stray bullet while sitting on the back porch of her home. Her death has left her family devastated as police investigate the shooting and search for those responsible. The shooting happened late Monday afternoon, October 19, at the Dwell Townhomes on Hillgate Avenue. According to KWTX , Shanks was sitting on her porch, which backs up to Laurel Lane, when gunfire erupted nearby. Her family believes the shooting may have stemmed from a dispute involving other people in the neighborhood. Police confirmed that she was not the intended target and died after a stray bullet hit her. Neighbors said they heard several gunshots before seeing multiple young people dressed in black flee the area. Police spent hours investigating the scene, cordoning off a large part of the townhome complex, including a playground. Investigators are working to determine how many people fired weapons and who they were targeting. As of Tuesday afternoon, authorities had not announced any arrests. Her sudden death has left her relatives struggling to cope with their loss. Her niece, who asked to re

items.t: Man Becomes Local Hero After Jumping onto Runaway School Bus, Saving More Than 18 Students
items.x: Nationwide Ebro Ahmed, a 27-year-old Somali American man from St. Paul, Minnesota, jumped onto a runaway school bus and brought it to a stop after its driver suffered a medical emergency. His quick response helped protect more than 18 students who were still on board as the bus moved down a street with its door open. Ahmed was working at Ya Bricks Snacks and Tobacco in St. Paul on Monday when he noticed the school bus moving without anyone seemingly in control, as reported by 11Alive . The bus's door was open, and he could see that the driver was incapacitated. At first, Ahmed struggled to believe what he was witnessing, but he soon realized he needed to act. In an interview, Ahmed said, "I kind of hesitated for a little bit, but I just, this was too crazy not to be real. I just jumped on there, did what I had to do." Surveillance footage from the nearby store captured the moment he climbed aboard as the bus continued down the street with its safety arm extended. The video also showed the bus moving in reverse before finally coming to a halt. Ahmed later explained that he accidentally shifted the bus into reverse when he first tried to gain control. items.t: Black Family of 9-Year-Old Beaten By His Teacher s Relative Wins $750K Lawsuit
items.x: Nationwide Jo’maury Champ, an African American boy from Chicago, Illinois, was 9 years old when a woman allegedly beat him with two leather belts inside his elementary school. His teacher, Kristen Haynes, was accused of arranging the punishment and providing the belts. Years later, Champ’s family won a $750,000 jury award in a federal civil rights lawsuit over the 2018 incident. The alleged beating happened on Sept. 20, 2018, at Tilton Elementary School in Chicago. The lawsuit states Haynes arranged for Juanita Tyler, Champ’s distant relative who did not work at the school, to come in and physically punish him. The lawsuit alleged that the teacher and Tyler took him to a boys’ bathroom, where Haynes left him alone with Tyler. Champ testified that Tyler then struck him with two belts about 20 times. The reason for the planned punishment was disputed, and the available account did not clearly establish what prompted it. Champ described the incident publicly for the first time during a federal civil rights trial about six years later. He told the jury that both women dragged him into the bathroom before Haynes left. items.t: Both Grandmothers of 1-Year-Old Black Baby Killed by White Cop Speak Out
items.x: Nationwide The family of 1-year-old Kohen Wiley is demanding accountability after a white police officer fatally shot the Black toddler in Senatobia, Mississippi. Both of his grandmothers have questioned the state's decision to rule the shooting justified, saying they cannot understand how officers' actions could be considered acceptable. Civil rights attorney Ben Crump, Memphis attorney Van Turner, and Kohen's relatives addressed the case during a press conference on Thursday, October 22, at Senatobia Church of Christ. The gathering came three days after the Mississippi Attorney General's Office concluded that the officers were justified in using deadly force. According to Local Memphis , Crump said the Mississippi Bureau of Investigation showed the family footage of the shooting that morning. However, Kohen's maternal grandmother, Veronica Robinson, said the family had already seen leaked footage and learned about the state's decision through media reports before officials presented the video to them. Crump condemned the officers' actions, arguing that the shooting was excessive from the start. He questioned why they approached the vehicle with their guns drawn and said their act

items.t: Congresswoman Ilhan Omar Says That Claims About Her Marrying Her Brother Are a Conspiracy
items.x: Nationwide Rep. Ilhan Omar has denied allegations that she married her brother to help him obtain U.S. citizenship, calling the claims baseless conspiracy theories spread by right-wing activists. In her first major interview since federal agents searched her Washington, D.C., home, the Minnesota Democrat also discussed the ongoing immigration investigation, questions about her family's finances and her plans to remain in Congress. During an interview with MS NOW host Chris Hayes, she was asked about her former husband, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, and whether he could have been her brother. When Hayes pressed her on whether there was any truth to the allegation, she responded, “Not to my knowledge.” She called the claims “insane” and said they originated on a Somali blog before conservative activists in Minneapolis began spreading them. Omar also disputed claims from people who allegedly said she had introduced Elmi as her brother, saying she did not know those individuals. She has repeatedly denied the allegations, and no established evidence has shown that Elmi is her brother. items.t: 15-Year-Old Black Teen Faces Four Charges in Shooting That Seriously Injured a Woman
items.x: Nationwide Martavious Grandberry, a 15-year-old African American teen from Yazoo City, Mississippi, faces four charges after police arrested him in connection with a shooting that injured 20-year-old Vaniyah Woodbury. Investigators said someone fired multiple shots at a car carrying Woodbury and two other women as they tried to leave a home. Yazoo City police began investigating on Sunday, Oct. 18, after learning that a woman with a gunshot wound had arrived at Baptist Memorial Hospital. Woodbury had been shot in the lower-left side of her back. Hospital staff treated her before transferring her to the University of Mississippi Medical Center in Jackson for further care. According to WLBT , investigators determined that Woodbury had argued verbally with her boyfriend at a home on Leach Street before the shooting. The argument reportedly happened before she and two other women attempted to leave the property in a gray Honda Accord. Authorities said an individual allegedly fired multiple shots at the vehicle as the women were leaving. items.t: 75-Year-Old Black Woman Dies After Her Car Plunges Into Contaminated Water
items.x: Nationwide Sheila Harris, a 75-year-old African American woman from Gary, Indiana, died after her car sank into contaminated water near Buffington Harbor on Saturday, Oct. 17. Emergency crews spent hours working to recover her vehicle because hazardous conditions prevented divers from reaching it safely. She called 911 after her white Hyundai entered the water and began sinking. Authorities responded to the emergency call but initially could not find the vehicle. Investigators later reviewed surveillance footage to determine where the car had entered the water. According to People , divers from the Indiana Department of Natural Resources could not reach the submerged vehicle because of the dangerous conditions and water contamination. Officials eventually located the car about 12 feet underwater. They paused recovery efforts while arranging specialized equipment to make the operation safer. The Gary Police Department said crews deployed pumps to remove the contaminated water and lower the water level. The work continued overnight as emergency personnel prepared to recover the vehicle. items.t: Black Firefighter Sues White Chief Over Alleged Racial Harassment After He Reported a Noose Around a CPR Dummy
items.x: Nationwide Randy Brown, an African American firefighter from Charleston, South Carolina, is suing his fire district and its chief after he found a noose around a Black CPR training mannequin at his station. He alleges that officials failed to identify who placed it there and later treated him as uncooperative instead of protecting him from racial harassment. Brown, who has worked for the Low Country Area Fire District for 18 years, discovered the noose in September 2025 after another crew temporarily staffed his station. He reported it to his captain and a battalion chief, asking officials to investigate and condemn the display. He initially wanted an apology and acknowledgment of the incident, not anyone's termination. However, internal investigators and outside counsel failed to identify the person responsible. The Charleston County Sheriff's Office also administered polygraph tests to some suspected crew members, but not everyone who had worked the preceding shift was tested. According to Atlanta Black Star , the lawsuit questions why officials did not investigate firefighter Joseph Crawford more closely after his polygraph results came back inconclusive. items.t: White Cop Accused of Choking Black Mom Has Been Named Officer of the Month
items.x: Nationwide Nadia Baxter, an African American mother from New Jersey, has filed a federal lawsuit against a school police officer who allegedly choked and arrested her while she was trying to bring menstrual products to her daughter. The case raises questions about the officer’s use of force and the department’s response, especially after an internal investigation cleared him and he was later named Officer of the Month. Baxter filed the federal lawsuit on Oct. 8, accusing officer Michael J. Marsh of using excessive force, malicious prosecution, and fabricating evidence. The complaint also alleges that school officials and police supervisors failed to intervene or hold those involved accountable. According to Atlanta Black Star , the dispute began when school staff refused to accept the menstrual-hygiene products she brought for her daughter. Although the school handbook discouraged certain drop-offs, it also designated a cabinet outside the main entrance for parents to leave items. After staff rejected the delivery, Baxter decided to take her daughter home for the rest of the day. items.t: Rapper Ja Rule Is Raising Up to $7 Million to Expand His Whiskey Brand Within the Next Year
items.x: Nationwide Rapper Ja Rule is raising $5 million to $7 million to expand his whiskey brand, Amber & Opal , into new markets. The business, which he launched with three longtime friends, takes a different approach to whiskey by combining traditional ingredients with honey and tea while appealing to a wider range of consumers. The group launched the brand after initially investing in whiskey barrels with plans to sell them for a profit years later. However, as the founders learned more about the industry, they saw an opportunity to create something different. Herb Rice, Sandy Sandiford, Kelvin Barton, and Ja Rule decided to build their own whiskey company and make the category more welcoming to people of color, women, and those who are curious about whiskey but unfamiliar with it. Rather than use their existing barrels for the first release, the founders developed a honey botanical whiskey with a distinct mix of ingredients. Amber & Opal combines rye whiskey with orange blossom honey, lapsang souchong tea, black tea, and herbal tea. The drink currently sells online for $69.99. The team plans to save the original barrels for a premium bourbon they could introduce in the future. Ja Rule

items.t: Daymond John Reveals Why He Turned Down A $1.3 Billion Bank Offer
items.x: Nationwide Entrepreneur Daymond John says he turned down a $1.3 billion credit line from a major bank because he did not want to spend the next 20 years building and managing a business empire. Although the deal could have increased his wealth, the FUBU founder said he chose to protect his time with family and focus on what matters most to him. John shared the story during a 2025 appearance on the BigDeal by Codie Sanchez podcast. Known for building FUBU into a successful fashion brand and investing in businesses on ABC’s Shark Tank , he said he often receives attractive business offers. One bank, which reportedly works with 1,000 of the world’s largest companies, proposed giving him access to $1.3 billion in credit to acquire other businesses and compete for major contracts, according to AfroTech . The bank had a specific expansion plan in mind. It offered to provide a mergers and acquisitions specialist to help him purchase companies in industries such as hospitality, flooring, lighting, and furniture. The bank also believed his business experience, television presence, and background as a minority entrepreneur could help him secure contracts through minority business initiatives

items.t: Kamala Harris Says She Has Yet to Decide Whether She Will Run for President Again in 2028
items.x: Nationwide Kamala Harris has not decided whether she will run for president again in 2028, leaving the door open to another White House campaign. During a recent podcast interview, the former vice president said Democrats should focus on the 2026 midterm elections before looking ahead to the next presidential race. She addressed the speculation during an appearance on Keke Palmer’s podcast, Baby, This Is Keke Palmer , released on October 13. Near the end of their conversation, Palmer asked whether she planned to seek the Democratic presidential nomination again. Harris laughed before answering, “I haven’t decided yet. I will, I promise.” She then shifted attention to the upcoming elections, stressing that Democrats must first succeed in 2026. “’28 doesn’t matter if we don’t do ’26 right,” she said, emphasizing the importance of addressing the political challenges facing the country now. Although she has not announced her next political move, Harris has continued supporting Democratic candidates and discussing issues that affect American families. items.t: Democrats see battleground map expand to South Carolina, Florida, Mississippi
items.x: Democrats are giddy about the possibility of a bigger blue wave than expected in the battle for the Senate as polls show that South Carolina , Florida and Mississippi — three seats that were long seen as safe Republican holds — are now competitive races. Democrats view the Republican candidates running in those states as mediocre political talents who must fight historic headwinds caused by President Trump’s unpopularity, voter anger over inflation and the war in Iran, and burgeoning Democratic voter enthusiasm. The Senate battleground map has steadily expanded throughout the 2026 midterm election cycle as political handicappers have shifted seats that were thought to be in solidly Republican territory — such as Alaska, Iowa, Kansas and Texas — to the “toss-up" category. But now Republicans have to worry about losing Senate seats in states that were unthinkable as realistic Democratic pickup opportunities at the start of the election cycle, most notably South Carolina, which last elected a Democrat, Fritz Hollings, to the Senate in 1998. items.t: Johnson signals he’ll remain atop GOP, scrambling leadership landscape
items.x: Speaker Mike Johnson’s (R-La.) recent hints that he intends to remain GOP leader even if Republicans lose the House have rattled the party’s leadership outlook and raised fresh new questions about the GOP’s future heading into the next Congress. Most House Speakers in recent decades have stepped out of Congress after losing the gavel. And Reps. Steve Scalise (R-La.), the majority leader, and Jim Jordan (R-Ohio), a conservative icon, are both expected to launch bids to lead House Republicans if Democrats flip the chamber, according to GOP lawmakers, aides and strategists. But Johnson recently muddled the leadership landscape by signaling his intention to keep his spot atop the party even if Republicans are knocked out of power. items.t: Illinois basketball dominates UIC in exhibition
items.x: CHAMPAIGN, Ill. (WCIA) Illinois men's basketball picked up a win on Wednesday night in the team's final exhibition game of the season. The Illini beat University of Illinois-Chicago 101-66. Illinois was short-handed in the win, as Andrej Stojakovic, Zvonimir Ivisic and David Mirkovic all missed the game due to injury. It was a balanced scoring attack for Brad Underwood's team on Wednesday, with seven different players finishing in double figures. Tomislav Ivisic led the scoring effort for the Orange and Blue with 14. Freshmen Lucas Morillo and Quentin Coleman led the team in rebounding with eight and seven respectively. Illinois won the rebounding battle 44-30. Click here to watch Brad Underwood's opening statement from his postgame press conference after the game. Up next, Illinois turns the page to its regular season opener on Monday, Nov. 2 at home against Fairleigh-Dickinson. The Illini then will host Penn on Thursday, Nov. 5.

The moratorium is an effort by the city to pause a potential federal plan to convert the Naval Information Warfare Systems Command (NAVWAR) site near Old Town into a 400-megawatt AI data center. items.t: Architectural firm proposes new domed stadium for Chicago Bears in Bridgeport
items.x: CHICAGO ( WGN ) A Chicago architectural firm has released a proposal that would move the Chicago Bears to a domed stadium in Bridgeport. The firm Skidmore, Owings and Merrill released renderings of the proposed stadium on Instagram Wednesday, saying the proposal would "create a new home for the Bears that is also a catalyst for lasting neighborhood investment." The proposal has the Bears moving to the area the Chicago White Sox currently call home. The White Sox, however, are currently in the process of exploring the possibility of leaving their home at Rate Field for a proposed new ballpark in South Loop . The proposed Bridgeport stadium would serve as the centerpiece of a mixed-use district that would also feature housing, entertainment, hospitality, parks and public recreation. The site would also have access to the CTA, Metra and the Dan Ryan Expressway. Skidmore, Owings and Merrill also said it has identified a large amount of publicly-owned land surrounding the proposed site that could transform the stadium into a district with more affordable and market-rate housing, along with civic amenities and new and improved pedestrian bridges. (WCIA) A domestic violence situation Tuesday led to a Decatur woman making her first court appearance the next day. 29-year-old Haley Tobin appeared in front of a judge Wednesday. She is accused of stabbing her 31-year-old boyfriend in his shoulder and neck, just before 11 a.m. Tuesday. items.t: Federal Reserve holds interest rates steady in face of persistent inflation
items.x: Federal Reserve officials held interest rates steady Wednesday despite stubborn inflation. The central bank's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) voted 10-2 to keep the benchmark federal funds rate range at 3.75 percent to 4 percent. "The committee believes that the accumulation of more information will help it determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the 2 percent goal," Fed Chair Kevin Warsh told reporters, reiterating the FOMC's statement. Fed board of governors member Lisa Cook and Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland's president Beth Hammack dissented in favor of a quarter-point increase. Hammack also backed a rate hike in late July, joining two of her colleagues in the minority when the central bank kept rates steady . Wednesday's decision came six weeks after officials raised rates by a quarter point , the first hike in more than three years. Inflation has risen this year amid the Iran war , creating a difficult set of circumstances for President Trump and the GOP this midterm cycle . items.t: Illinois sales tax holiday saved families more than $11M
items.x: CHICAGO (WMBD) The Office of the Governor announced on Monday that a sales tax holiday saved Illinois families millions of dollars this back-to-school season. The 2026 Back-to-School Sales Tax Holiday, held from Aug. 7 to Aug. 16, saved families an estimated $11.4 million, according to a news release from the Office of the Governor. This tax holiday waived the 5% state sales tax on school supplies, clothing and footwear. During the holiday, 2,284 stores sold $229.3 million in qualifying items. The savings applied to both in-store and online purchases and were applied automatically at checkout. “This initiative provided Illinois taxpayers with meaningful savings as they prepared for the new school year,” said Illinois Department of Revenue Director David Harris. “By reducing the state sales tax rate on qualifying purchases, the Back-to-School Sales Tax Holiday helped ease the cost of school essentials.” According to the news release, it was enacted as part of the FY27 state budget package.

items.t: Recalled butter sold in Illinois, other states receives risk warning: FDA
items.x: NEW JERSEY ( WPIX ) A popular plant-based butter has been recalled due to yeast, mold and E. coli, and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has now assigned it a risk level . The recall, which was initiated by Prosperity Organic Foods, Inc., headquartered in Boise, Idaho, involves 1,304 cases of Miyoko's Creamery European Style Salted Plant Milk Butter. The FDA assigned the recall as a Class II risk level on Friday, meaning a product may cause “temporary or medically reversible adverse health consequences.” The recall was initially announced Sept. 11. The affected butter, which is perishable and stored refrigerated or frozen, comes in six-packs of 8-ounce units, which can be identified with the following information: UPC 857554005773 Lot number and best-by on SBS carton: 07871, Nov. 5, 2026 Lot number and best-by date on the corrugated case for shipment: 1007871, Nov. 5, 2026 The affected products were also sold in Connecticut, Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Illinois, Indiana, Maryland, New Jersey, New Hampshire and Wisconsin.

items.t: Trump-led Rep. Ilhan Omar raid an attack on Houston
items.x: When a president repeatedly attacks a political opponent, questions her right to belong in the country she serves, and then watches federal agents raid her home weeks before an election, Americans should be alarmed. That is precisely why the Oct. 12 raid on U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar’s Washington, D.C., home should concern Houston. Omar, a Somali-born naturalized American citizen representing Minnesota, has endured years of insults and accusations from President Donald Trump. He has repeatedly demanded that she leave the country. Now, a federal investigation into alleged immigration paperwork irregularities has resulted in agents searching her home. Omar denies wrongdoing, and no charges had been filed as of the initial reports. The Justice Department says agents executed a judicially authorized search warrant. But legal authorization alone does not eliminate legitimate questions about political motivation, timing, and the weaponization of government power. Omar called the raid an attempt to “target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement.” She added, “I will not be silenced.” Neither should the American people remain silent. items.t: Young Black voters in Houston defy labels
items.x: When Evan Robinson cast his first ballot in the 2024 presidential election, poll workers rang a bell to celebrate a first-time voter. Two years later, the Texas Southern University student urges classmates to vote in every race, but he won't pledge loyalty to a party. Robinson, vice president of the NAACP's TSU unit, said most policies he supports lean Democratic, but he calls himself an Independent. "I just feel like choosing sides, in a sense, does yourself a disservice because people then treat it like sports," Robinson said. "They're like, oh yeah, my team is blue, or my team is red. And no matter what they do, they support that even if it's not in their best interest." With the Texas midterms weeks away, Robinson reflects on a new kind of Black voter emerging in Houston. These voters are younger and more digitally fluent. They study local races as closely as federal ones and expect candidates to earn their support. They also do not vote as a bloc. A proud daughter of an immigrant mother, granddaughter of trailblazers, and lifelong advocate for justice and equity, she embodies a family tradition of breaking barriers and serving others. Her grandfather made history as the first African-American judge in Texas and courageously desegregated the Harris County cafeteria system, helping lay the foundation for fairness and inclusion in local government. Her grandmother, a devoted educator, inspired generations through the power of learning. Her father served the Department of Defense and Harris Health as a dentist, dedicating his career to improving access to care for underserved communities. A product of Houston’s public school system, Dr. Plummer has been a successful small business owner for more than 25 years. Through her dental practice, she has provided compassionate care, mentored young professionals, and created jobs in her community. items.t: Stop calling Katie Zacharia a DEI hire
items.x: Recently, former White House press secretary Katie Zacharia was asked where she passed the bar exam and replied, "When I moved to China." Three days later, she was fired from her position. Online, she earned the nickname DEI hire. I understand the joke. The Trump administration spent nearly two years tearing down diversity, equity, and inclusion programs in the name of merit, then handed one of the government’s most visible jobs to someone who could not get through a 15-minute briefing. But the punchline only works if you accept that DEI means unqualified. That is the lie used against Black, brown, LGBTQ, and disabled professionals, and we should stop repeating it. She was hired for loyalty Zacharia was named press secretary on Oct. 9 to replace Karoline Leavitt. She later said she misheard the bar question, then admitted two days later that she never passed the exam. Her five days are the shortest tenure of any press secretary on record. items.t: Five arrested, three charged with murder in fatal Rockford shooting
items.x: ROCKFORD, Ill (WTVO) — Five people have been arrested and charged in connection with the death of 20-year-old Maleek Cofield, according to the Rockford Police Department. Police said on Tuesday, October 27, around 11:13 p.m., officers responded to the area of Yonge and Evergreen Streets for reports of shots fired. Shortly afterward, Cofield arrived at a hospital suffering from multiple gunshot wounds. He later died from his injuries. Officials said several vehicles and a nearby residence were also struck by gunfire. Investigators said 22-year-old Damarion Evans-Mackey, 21-year-old Aryanna Ozbirn, and a 17-year-old have each been charged with first-degree murder. Meanwhile, 20-year-old Willie McGee and 20-year-old Armonti Bryant have been charged with aggravated unlawful use of weapons. Mackey, Ozbirn, McGee, and Bryant are all being held in the Winnebago County Jail.

The Senate battleground map has steadily expanded throughout the 2026 midterm election cycle as political handicappers have shifted seats that were thought to be in solidly Republican territory — such as Alaska, Iowa, Kansas and Texas — to the “toss-up" category. While much of the time will be dry, enough moisture wrapping around the system could spark a few scattered showers from time to time, mainly Saturday morning and then again late in the afternoon into the evening. Rainfall amounts look like, and widespread washouts are not expected. but it may be enough that someone in your trick-or treat group will want to keep an umbrella on hand. Temperatures remain seasonably mild, but cooler than recent times in the low 60s for Saturday, then upper 60s for Sunday. items.t: Brewers beat the Rays to capture their first World Series championship
items.x: ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. (AP) — The small-ball Milwaukee Brewers playing in the smallest market in the majors are World Series champions for the first time. Hey, Milwaukee: grab a brat, raise a beer and prepare for that parade. Young ace Jacob Misiorowski threw 5 2/3 scoreless innings of two-hit ball, rookie Cooper Pratt got two more hits and two RBIs, and Milwaukee beat the Tampa Bay Rays 4-1 in Game 5 to set off a long-awaited celebration among thousands of Brewers fans in attendance at Tropicana Field. Misiorowski left the game because of a right calf cramp, but a stellar Milwaukee bullpen had little trouble closing it out. Jacob Misiorowski pitched with poise when he couldn't overwhelm with punishing heat, overcoming Tampa Bay batters and the Tropicana Field mound to lead the Milwaukee Brewers to their first World Series title. On a night when he tied his career low with only two strikeouts, baseball's hardest-throwing starting pitcher threw two-hit ball over 5 2/3 scoreless innings before leaving because of a leg cramp with a four-run lead.

items.t: Illinois woman arrested for alleged drug induced homicide
items.x: MCLEAN COUNTY, Ill. (WMBD) An East Peoria woman is under arrest for allegedly causing the death of another person in LeRoy last month. Mary Hammel, 40, was arrested on the single count of drug-induced homicide by deputies with the McLean County Sheriff's Office in connection with the Sept. 30 death. According to online court records, she has not yet been formally charged in court. That charge carries a possible 30-year prison term. She was arrested in Tazewell County, said McLean County Sheriff Matt Lane on Tuesday by agents with the U.S. Marshals Service. Lane, in a Facebook post , said the death investigation began on Sept. 30 near West Cherry and North Walnut Streets in LeRoy. Kathleen Yoder, the McLean County Coroner, determined the cause of death was the result of a drug overdose. The sheriff's office got invovlee at the request of the LeRoy Police Department. Lane said the investigation is ongoing. An attempt to reach Lane and Yoder was not immediately successful. This story will be updated when more information is available.

items.t: DOJ’s California ballot fight rejected by another judge
items.x: ( The Hill ) The Trump administration's bid to separate 20,000 mail ballots in California that it says are likely noncitizens met another defeat on Wednesday as a trial judge refused to intervene. U.S. District Judge David Carter ruled California can continue to accept the questioned ballots like any other. “This request violates longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections,” Carter wrote. “If Plaintiff’s last-minute request for relief were granted, either party could create chaos for their own political purposes to disrupt the election process,” he continued. “Over 20,000 registered Californians would potentially lose the right that generations of Americans have fought to preserve.” California has raised eyebrows at the veracity of the administration's list and says it's not obligated to verify voters’ citizenship in response. items.t: Stoughton man seriously injured after train strikes car in Rock County
items.x: FULTON, Wis. (WTVO) – A 21-year-old Stoughton man was seriously injured Wednesday afternoon when a train struck his vehicle at a railroad crossing in the Town of Fulton, according to the Rock County Sheriff's Office. Deputies said the crash happened around 2:45 p.m. on North Dallman Road south of County Highway N. Investigators said a northbound Honda Civic entered the railroad crossing and was struck on the driver's side by a train consisting of a locomotive and two freight cars. The driver was extricated from the vehicle by fire department personnel and flown to a hospital with serious injuries, authorities said. Officials said a 51-year-old man from McFarland, Wisconsin, operated the train. Three crew members aboard the train were not injured. According to investigators, the crossing was controlled by stop signs for northbound and southbound traffic, and those traffic control devices were functioning properly at the time of the crash. The Rock County Sheriff's Office said the crash remains under investigation. All facts in this report were gathered by journalists employed by WTVO. items.t: Harris advises Democrats against attempting to impeach Trump
items.x: ( The Hill ) Former Vice President Kamala Harris on Tuesday urged Democrats against making a third attempt to impeach President Trump if they win back the House after next week's midterm elections. "I think that going in the direction of impeachment is not a good idea, just to be honest with you," Harris told MeidasTouch's Aaron Parnas in an interview. "Just because we have limited resources and I think the energy and the resources need to put into accountability, need to be put into investigations." "And that's where the time should be spent," she added. "Remember, I was in the Senate for the last go-around, and the votes aren't there. "So, that's how I feel. But also, I think after the election, we all have to just also agree that our attitude has to be to get stuff done." Harris said Democrats should be "uncompromising" and "not sit around, you know, being genteel about the relationships," but maintain accountability when it comes to cuts to healthcare and oversight on the Iran war. The former vice president was days into her new role in 2021 when Democratic lawmakers impeached Trump in connection with the Jan. 6 Capitol Hill attack. In February 2021, the Senate acquitted Trump

Thunderstorms have quickly developed along the front from Iowa through Minnesota, with severe thunderstorms around Minneapolis, MN. Any threat for severe weather will remain well to our northwest through the evening. Breezy southerly winds will help keep temperatures in the 60s for most of the night, dropping only into the upper 50s around sunrise Thursday. As the cold front moves close to northern Illinois and southern Wisconsin, we'll see an uptick in cloud cover and eventually a few widely scattered showers move in during the overnight. A few of those showers may develop as early as 8pm across far northwest Illinois, but most likely we'll see the rain move in after Midnight. items.t: Winnebago County Housing Authority awarded $1.6 million federal grant to boost financial independence
items.x: ROCKFORD, Ill. (WTVO) — The Winnebago County Housing Authority has been awarded a $1.6 million federal grant to help public housing residents achieve financial independence. The funding comes from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development's Jobs Plus grant program and will be used over the next four years. The grant will specifically benefit residents in the Collier Garden community. Under the program, residents will be able to keep rent costs flat as their earnings increase, exempting them from the standard requirement to pay 30% of their income toward rent. The U.S. Department of Justice said Francisco Hernandez-Ramos, 51, was arrested in Harvard, Illinois, on August 7. At that time, he had been deported from the United States five times and was in the country illegally. Hernandez-Ramos had previously been convicted of criminal sexual assault of a minor, attempted possession of child pornography, illegal entry, and illegal re-entry. items.t: Federal Reserve holds interest rates steady in face of persistent inflation
items.x: Federal Reserve officials held interest rates steady Wednesday despite stubborn inflation. The central bank's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) voted 10-2 to keep the benchmark federal funds rate range at 3.75 percent to 4 percent. "The committee believes that the accumulation of more information will help it determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the 2 percent goal," Fed Chair Kevin Warsh told reporters, reiterating the FOMC's statement. Fed board of governors member Lisa Cook and Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland's president Beth Hammack dissented in favor of a quarter-point increase. Hammack also backed a rate hike in late July, joining two of her colleagues in the minority when the central bank kept rates steady . Wednesday's decision came six weeks after officials raised rates by a quarter point , the first hike in more than three years. Inflation has risen this year amid the Iran war , creating a difficult set of circumstances for President Trump and the GOP this midterm cycle . items.t: Police: Rockford man arrested after drug bust leads to cocaine, ecstasy, marijuana seizure
items.x: Winnebago County, Ill. — A Rockford man was arrested following a months-long drug investigation into the alleged sale of large quantities of cocaine in the Winnebago County area, according to the Winnebago County Sheriff's Office. Sheriff deputies said that, for several months, they had been receiving information about a suspect who was selling large amounts of cocaine in the area. The suspect was later identified as 27-year-old Deshon Johnson. Detectives said Johnson was located on Thursday, October 15, near Crosby and Summit Street. Authorities executed a search warrant in the 200 block of Longwood Street, where Investigators recovered more than one kilogram of cocaine, more than 20 pounds of psilocybin mushrooms, more than 40 pounds of marijuana, 33 grams of ecstasy, and a loaded handgun. Johnson faces multiple charges, including possession with intent to deliver cocaine and possession of a firearm. He is currently being held in the Winnebago County Jail.
