items.t: Mung beans sold in 22 states recalled after glass found
items.x: (NewsNation) — Shoppers of Natural Grocers stores, check your mung beans. Vitamin Cottage Natural Food Markets is recalling its organic mung bean products due to the potential presence of glass in its two-pound bulk bags. In a notice posted by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, the company warns of injury, including potential "damage to teeth, laceration of the mouth and throat, or perforation of the intestine." The company issued the recall after receiving customer complaints, though no injuries had been reported as of the Oct. 22 notice. The affected product was sold in clear plastic bags with Natural Grocers labeling in the following states: Arkansas, Arizona, Colorado, Iowa, Idaho, Kansas, Louisiana, Minnesota, Missouri, Montana, North Dakota, Nebraska, New Mexico, Nevada, Oklahoma, Oregon, South Dakota, Texas, Utah, Washington, Wisconsin and Wyoming. The affected lots began shipping on June 10 of this year, and the recalled beans bear the UPC 000080112600. Consumers should immediately stop using the beans and either throw them away or return them for a full refund or credit, the company advises.

"We want to honor the six wonderful years we had at Bryan Park by ensuring this next chapter is our most successful yet," the post reads in part. The move will take place in spring 2027, but Bryan Park will continue to host the market in the meantime, including during the winter 2026-27 season. A Thursday evening market will also return to the park in spring 2027, as well as the year-round Sunday South of the James Market in Forest Hill Park. items.t: Federal Reserve holds interest rates steady in face of persistent inflation
items.x: Federal Reserve officials held interest rates steady Wednesday despite stubborn inflation. The central bank's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) voted 10-2 to keep the benchmark federal funds rate range at 3.75 percent to 4 percent. "The committee believes that the accumulation of more information will help it determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the 2 percent goal," Fed Chair Kevin Warsh told reporters, reiterating the FOMC's statement. Fed board of governors member Lisa Cook and Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland's president Beth Hammack dissented in favor of a quarter-point increase. Hammack also backed a rate hike in late July, joining two of her colleagues in the minority when the central bank kept rates steady . Wednesday's decision came six weeks after officials raised rates by a quarter point , the first hike in more than three years. Inflation has risen this year amid the Iran war , creating a difficult set of circumstances for President Trump and the GOP this midterm cycle . items.t: Dolores Huerta, labor leader and activist, dies at 96
items.x: ( KTLA ) Activist Dolores Huerta, who helped co-found the National Farm Workers Association with César Chavez, has died. She was 96. Huerta's family said in a statement through her foundation that she died Wednesday at home. "We are deeply saddened to announce that our beloved mother, Dolores Huerta, has passed away today at the age of 96," her family said in a statement posted on social media. "As you can imagine, this is an incredibly difficult time for us, and we ask for privacy as we grieve this incredible loss to our family," the statement continued. "We know that many of you around the world share in our mourning, and we will be following up on plans to recognize and celebrate her incredible life and legacy." items.t: US stocks hold steady as the countdown ticks to a Federal Reserve decision on interest rates
items.x: NEW YORK (AP) — U.S. stocks are drifting Wednesday as the countdown ticks toward this afternoon’s announcement from the Federal Reserve on what it will do with interest rates . The S&P 500 rose 0.2% and pulled within 1% of its all-time high , which was set earlier this month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 176 points, or 0.3%, as of 11:45 a.m. Eastern time, and the Nasdaq composite was virtually unchanged. The day’s highlight will likely be what the Federal Reserve says, if anything, about where interest rates are heading. The Fed raised its main interest rate last month for the first time in three years in hopes of slowing the high inflation that’s squeezing the economy and discouraging Americans . The widespread expectation on Wall Street is that the Fed will leave the federal funds rate alone at this meeting, and the question is whether it will give hints about what may happen at later meetings. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh, though, has been adamant since taking over the Fed about wanting it to give fewer indications about its future moves. items.t: $39K Home Depot Boom Lift sold on Facebook Marketplace in Tennessee, police say
items.x: NASHVILLE, Tenn. (WKRN) — A 23-year-old woman is set to appear in Nashville court after allegedly helping a man flip a $39,000 piece of Home Depot equipment on Facebook Marketplace. Arrest documents show Rebecca Walpole and a male suspect entered the Madison, Tennessee, Home Depot on May 26 and rented a boom lift, which is commonly known as a cherry picker or basket crane. The equipment was towed using a silver Dodge Ram. According to court documents, the property was never returned. The male suspect was arrested in Michigan on Sept. 23, according to arrest documents. Investigators said he admitted to selling rented construction equipment to buyers on Facebook Marketplace. Walpole faces a felony theft of property charge, and she was recently booked in Davidson County. Her bond was set at $10,000.

items.x: (NewsNation) – A New York company is recalling more than 560 pounds of smoked fish over concerns about potential contamination with a bacterium that can cause life-threatening botulism. Haifa Smoked Fish of Queens, New York, has recalled Cold Smoked Sprats that were distributed in New Jersey, New York and Pennsylvania through retail stores, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration announced this week. Cold-smoked sprats from Haifa Smoked Fish Inc. are pictured in a photo distributed by the Food and Drug Administration. (FDA) The recall was initiated after an FDA inspection revealed that the firm "was producing cold-smoked sprats without required food safety controls to prevent Clostridium botulinum growth and toxin formation." Botulism is a potentially fatal form of food poisoning, the FDA added. It can cause general weakness, dizziness, double vision, trouble with speaking or swallowing, difficulty in breathing, weakness of other muscles, abdominal distension and constipation. Consumers should return the recalled product to the place of purchase for a refund, according to the FDA. They are also urged not to consume the product even if it doesn't look or smell spoiled. items.t: Chesterfield man sentenced to 11 years after supplying meth to undercover DEA agent
items.x: CHESTERFIELD COUNTY, Va. (WRIC) — A Chesterfield County man who supplied methamphetamine to an undercover Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) agent will spend 11 years in prison. According to the Department of Justice (DOJ), the sentence on Tuesday, Oct. 27, came after the DEA conducted a controlled purchase of 112.22 grams of methamphetamine, which was given to 33-year-old Elliot Davis on March 23, 2025. A third party coordinated the transaction, and Davis came to a parking lot with a quarter-pound of methamphetamine in his pants. The third party delivered the methamphetamine from Davis to the buyer, who was an undercover DEA agent. Davis had an additional pound and a half of methamphetamine in a hotel room, court documents show.

Kotlikoff after allegations of a 2024 gang rape at a campus fraternity that resulted in no criminal charges caused uproar around the country. A motion could be introduced to delay the no-confidence vote and set another meeting. items.t: Sabato’s Crystal Ball moves 16 House races toward Democrats
items.x: (The Hill) – Nonpartisan election forecaster Sabato’s Crystal Ball is shifting more than a dozen House races toward Democrats in the final week of the campaign , another sign of a worsening political environment for Republicans. Crystal Ball, a division of the University of Virginia’s Center for Politics, has moved dozens of races toward Democrats in recent weeks, including nearly 50 races in the month of October alone. The race changes include moving a few deep-red seats into the “toss up” column. Open congressional districts in Kentucky and Montana, as well as seats with GOP incumbents in Missouri, Virginia, Colorado and Pennsylvania moved into coin flip territory. Many of the seats Crystal Ball rates as a toss-up were places Trump carried by double digits in 2024. One notable race that moved from toss-up to “leans Democratic” is Texas’s 15th Congressional District, where Rep. Monica de la Cruz (R) is facing a tough challenge from Tejano music star Bobby Pulido (D). Unlike the other South Texas districts where Democrats are trying to hold onto redrawn seats, the 15th is a Republican-held district that Trump won by nearly 20 points in 2024. items.t: US cruise ship suspends voyage in Asia due to fuel costs, stranding 200 passengers
items.x: SIHANOUKVILLE, Cambodia (AP) — A U.S. cruise ship on an around-the-world voyage that touted its cabins as floating homes suspended its three-year voyage in Cambodia due to fuel costs, forcing hundreds of passengers to disembark. The MV Odyssey set sail two years ago on a voyage to the seven continents marketed as combining long-term living at sea with global travel. Its operator had offered to “make the Odyssey your permanent home,” with the purchase price of a suite for the lifetime of the vessel starting around $230,000. For now, it is docked at the Cambodian port of Sihanoukville on the Gulf of Thailand, with no certain departure date. The ship has been carrying 203 passengers, mostly Americans, along with 156 crew members, according to Cambodian officials. It has a 650-passenger capacity. Its Florida-based operator, Villa Vie Residences, said monthly fuel expenses per cabin that historically averaged $1,800 have reached an estimated $6,000 to $8,000 in parts of Asia due to the war in Iran. items.t: No clear winner yet in Israel’s national elections: What happens now?
items.x: JERUSALEM (AP) — No clear winner has emerged in Israel’s national elections as vote-counting continues, and weeks of negotiations may lie ahead as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and his main rival, Gadi Eisenkot, will scramble to build a governing coalition. The election was widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu, the country’s longest-serving prime minister, who gave a defiant speech to his supporters just after 3 a.m. on Wednesday in Jerusalem despite the unclear results. With around 70% of the votes counted on Wednesday afternoon, his party, Likud, appears to have gotten the most votes, capturing around 20% of the popular vote. This was a dip from the previous election in 2022, when Likud won 23.4% of the popular vote. But initial results indicate that support for other parties in Netanyahu's current coalition with far-right parties dropped significantly, putting his bloc below the 61 seats needed to form a government. Netanyahu’s chief rival, Gadi Eisenkot, has obtained nearly 16% of the popular vote. items.x: URDA, Spain (AP) — A high-speed train slammed into another that had stopped on the tracks in Spain on Wednesday, killing at least 68 people and injuring dozens in the second deadly rail collision this year. The regional government of Castilla La Mancha confirmed the death toll and said another 58 people were receiving medical treatment at hospitals. Rescue workers searched the wreckage through the day for survivors and bodies. items.t: Richmond seeks input on proposed protected bike lane designs on 6th Street
items.x: RICHMOND, Va. (WRIC) — Richmond’s Department of Transportation (RDOT) is asking the community for feedback on a proposed cycle track along 6th Street that could reduce both vehicle travel lanes and street parking to add a designated lane for bicyclists. The protected bike lane would run along 6th Street between Franklin and Canal Streets in Downtown Richmond. The goal is to improve access to downtown destinations, support the future Fall Line Trail and create a “safer, more comfortable connection” for cyclists, according to a release. The proposed cycle track comes as the city is resurfacing several streets downtown. "One thing we do in the Department of Transportation is take the opportunity, when we're repaving the streets, to see if that's a time when we can expand the bike network," said RDOT director Andy Boenau. For bicyclists, the proposal could provide a safer, more consistent route through downtown, where existing bike lanes are not always connected. “I just turned around because the further down you go, the bike lanes kind of disappear,” said cyclist Osvaldo Rivera. items.t: Toyota recalls more than 228,000 vehicles over risk of injury
items.x: (NewsNation) — Toyota is recalling more than 228,000 vehicles due to an issue with the second-row seat backs that could increase the risk of injury, according to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. A notice by NHTSA says if a crash happens, the second-row seat backs may fail to remain secured. According to the notice, around 228,367 vehicles from the Toyota Sienna Hybrid 2022-26 are impacted. Dealers plan to update the supplemental restraint system electronics control unit software. For vehicles equipped with the “Mobility as a Service” package, dealers plan to replace the two second-row seat backs free of charge, according to NHTSA. Owners should expect to receive notification letters in the mail around Dec. 7, according to the notice.

items.t: Utah authorities connect 1974 cold case to serial killer Ted Bundy
items.x: SUMMIT COUNTY, Utah (KTVX) — Investigators in Summit County, Utah closed the 1974 cold case homicide of Melissa Ann Smith Tuesday, linking her murder to prominent serial killer Ted Bundy. Using DNA and other evidence, the Summit County Sheriff's Office and Summit County Attorney's Office formally closed the cold-case murder, saying that the evidence conclusively proves that Ted Bundy murdered 17-year-old Melissa Ann Smith. Bundy has long been considered a suspect in several cold cases in Utah, and Smith's murder was one of them. Hunters found her remains in Summit County on Oct. 27, 1974, 52 years ago today. "The work began with the investigators who handled the case in 1974, and it continued through the dedication and perseverance of those who carried it forward," Summit County Sheriff Kacey Bates said. "After 50 years, we have reached a point that so many have worked toward." items.t: King Overton’s drowning death at SwimRVA ruled an accident, legal analyst reacts
items.x: HENRICO COUNTY, Va. (WRIC) — A final report from the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner has ruled a 9-year-old's drowning at SwimRVA over the summer an accident. On Tuesday, Oct. 27, Henrico Police said the medical examiner's June 15 ruling that King Overton’s death was accidental was preliminary. The final autopsy report was not available to police until the week of Oct. 19. Overton drowned while attending SwimRVA’s summer camp at its North location in Henrico County on June 15. King’s mother, LaTaisha Johnson, said it was his first day at the camp and staff knew he was unable to swim. The family’s attorney said a bystander pulled him from the pool, not a lifeguard or member of SwimRVA staff. Overton’s family has filed a wrongful death lawsuit against the swim school for over $100 million, saying their child's death was preventable. 8News legal analyst Russ Stone said the medical examiner must ensure they report accurate information before giving a final report. “When you have something as tragic as this, it doesn't shock me that the medical examiner wanted to make sure that all their i's were dotted and their t's were crossed before they actually issued an opinion,” Stone said.

items.t: St. Louis Fire Department to test drone technology for emergency responses
items.x: ST. LOUIS The St. Louis Fire Department will test drone technology to see how it could be incorporated into its operations. According to officials, the department will conduct a 30-day evaluation to determine how the technology can support emergency response efforts. Officials hope to gain a better understanding of the technology's capabilities, limitations and potential impact on decision-making. During the trial, the department will evaluate how aerial data could assist firefighters at various incidents, including fires, hazardous materials incidents and rescue operations. Old North St. Louis redevelopment delayed by reported squatters This is not the first time authorities in the St. Louis region have tested drones. items.t: Man injured after wall collapse in Litchfield, Illinois
items.x: LITCHFIELD, Ill. One man was seriously injured Wednesday after a partial wall collapse at an apartment building in Litchfield, officials say. The collapse happened around 4 p.m. Wednesday at the Elk Tower Apartment Building in the 400 block of Monroe Street. When first responders arrived, they found the injured man in the bucket of a man lift near the partially-collapsed wall. Firefighters used hydraulic rescue tools to cut through part of the lift's railing and move the man to safety, according to the Litchfield Fire Department . A short time later, the injured man was airlifted to two hospitals, including one in St. Louis, for further treatment. Investigators said there were no further updates on the man's condition as of Thursday morning. No other injuries were reported from the collapse. Firefighters monitored the area for unstable walls and falling debris, clearing several people from the immediate hazard area. As a precaution, access to one apartment building passageway has now been blocked. The Litchfield Fire Department did not immediately disclose the cause of the collapse.

items.t: AAA advises drivers about daylight saving time
items.x: ( WAVY ) – It's only a few days until we trade one extra hour of sleep for months of darkness as we leave work to drive home. And even though we're on the easier end of the time transition (from daylight saving time to standard time), the switch still takes its toll. Nexstar's WAVY went to AAA Tidewater Virginia to see what commuters can expect. "Well, the biggest thing for drivers will be the change in daylight when we leave work or school," said Holly Dalby with AAA. "At the end of the day, gone will be the bright sunshine, and we will find ourselves either driving into the glare from the setting sun or driving home in the dark. So it's a time to be particularly careful on the roads." Days will get way shorter in November: How much daylight will we lose? While lawmakers have tried to get rid of the time switch altogether, it doesn't appear to be going anywhere anytime soon, so your circadian rhythm will have to dance to a different beat for a while. items.t: Democrats see battleground map expand to South Carolina, Florida, Mississippi
items.x: Democrats are giddy about the possibility of a bigger blue wave than expected in the battle for the Senate as polls show that South Carolina , Florida and Mississippi — three seats that were long seen as safe Republican holds — are now competitive races. Democrats view the Republican candidates running in those states as mediocre political talents who must fight historic headwinds caused by President Trump’s unpopularity, voter anger over inflation and the war in Iran, and burgeoning Democratic voter enthusiasm. The Senate battleground map has steadily expanded throughout the 2026 midterm election cycle as political handicappers have shifted seats that were thought to be in solidly Republican territory — such as Alaska, Iowa, Kansas and Texas — to the “toss-up" category. But now Republicans have to worry about losing Senate seats in states that were unthinkable as realistic Democratic pickup opportunities at the start of the election cycle, most notably South Carolina, which last elected a Democrat, Fritz Hollings, to the Senate in 1998. items.t: Legal Lens: Dressing for Success in the Workplace
items.x: Sponsored – Attorney Andrea McNairy of Brown & Crouppen Law Firm explains that dressing appropriately at work depends on your workplace, job responsibilities, and employer’s dress code. Some workplaces require formal business attire, while others allow business casual clothing, jeans, or uniforms. To understand what is acceptable, review the employee handbook, ask about the dress code during your interview, or consult your supervisor or human resources department. If you are unsure whether an outfit, hairstyle, or accessory is appropriate, it is best to ask before wearing it. Keep in mind that dress expectations may change depending on the occasion, such as a regular workday, a client meeting, or a formal company event. The key to dressing appropriately is understanding and following your workplace’s expectations. Clarifying the rules ahead of time can help you look professional and avoid violating the dress code. items.t: Muzzleloader Deer Season Opens Oct. 31, Is Your Gun Ready?
items.x: NEW CASTLE, Va. (WFXR) Expect to hear the thunder of gunfire around Virginia soon. Deer muzzleloader season opens October 31. But, before you head into the woods, there is one very important thing to consider. "Is my gun ready?" The only way to tell is to fire it at a target to make sure the scope and gun are in synch, and that your aim is true. If not, you will need to make adjustments on the scope and possibly the gun. There are any number of things that can affect the scope. "Well, it's been been a whole year since we've done this, so bumping them in the closet or on the truck ride, you know, things happen," said expert deer hunter Randy Frango of Craig County. "It's a good practice to, you check your rifle prior to season." Having a gun dialed in can keep you from missing a deer, but it can also prevent something else, wounding a deer and not being able to track it. "You don't want to make a bad shot and wound an animal either," said Frango. "So yeah, check your rifle, whether it be a muzzleloader or rifle, rifle season is coming up, and make sure your firearm is hitting where it should." The other thing Frango emphasized is safety and especially avoiding double charging a gun.

items.t: Federal Reserve’s preferred measure of inflation rose slightly in September
items.x: ( The Hill ) Inflation increased slightly in September after declining in August , new data from the Bureau of Economic Analysis showed Thursday. The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index , the preferred inflation metric for the Federal Reserve, rose by 0.5 percent last month and was up 3.6 percent relative to September 2025. The Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland projected PCE inflation for last month at 0.5 percent month-over-month and 3.6 percent relative to September 2025. Annual inflation, according to the PCE, previously dipped from 3.7 percent in July to 3.4 percent in August. The price of gas and other energy goods rose by 9.2 percent from August to September, after increasing by 4.4 percent from July to August. Gasoline and energy costs have risen in six of nine months this year, as the Iran war sparked oil price shocks via the Islamic Republic's restrictions on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. Persistent inflation , which has remained above the Fed's 2 percent target for five-and-a-half years, spurred central bank officials to hike interest rates by a quarter point in mid-September. The draft policy posted online by Kennedy’s Department of Health and Human Services covers a handful of injectable peptides promoted within the wellness industry for uses such as building muscle, healing injuries and boosting energy. items.t: Health officials warn of new potent opioid impacting communities
items.x: ST. LOUIS Missouri health officials have issued a warning about a dangerous new opioid impacting communities across the country. According to the Missouri Department of Public Safety, health officials have raised concerns about cychlorphine, a new synthetic opioid that is considered up to 10 times more potent than fentanyl. Health officials said cychlorphine is known to suppress breathing, causing life-threatening respiratory and cardiovascular depression. According to officials, the drug is not detectable by fentanyl test strips and is being mixed into the illicit drug supply without users' knowledge. Old North St. Louis redevelopment delayed by reported squatters The White House Office of National Drug Control Policy reported in April that 55 deaths dating back to 2025 had been linked to the new opioid. Additionally, Los Angeles County has reported its first death linked to cychlorphine. In light of this new substance, residents are advised to treat any illicit drug as a potential risk. Officials also advise residents to carry naloxone but warn that multiple doses may be needed to reverse an opioid overdose.

items.t: Screwworm detected in dog in El Paso County
items.x: EL PASO, Texas (Border Report) The number of active New World screwworm cases rose to 18 on Wednesday, with several counties reporting their first case, including the populous El Paso County, Texas. According to the USDA, the five latest confirmed screwworm cases involved four dogs and a cat. Cochise County, Arizona, reported its first screwworm case on Wednesday, the first in that state. Texas state Rep. Mary Gonzalez, D-El Paso, issued a statement saying the screwworm was detected in a dog in the town of Socorro. She said her office has been in communication with the appropriate state agencies and will continue to monitor the situation. She urged the public to check on their pets and monitor them closely. "It is important that members of our community stay vigilant and go to their veterinarians if they believe their animal may have been impacted," she said. The border county of Luna, New Mexico, also confirmed its first screwworm case in a cow on Monday. The New World screwworm is a parasitic fly that lays eggs in open wounds. items.x: ST. LOUIS – St. Louis Mayor Cara Spencer is calling on the St. Louis Board of Police Commissioners to refocus their attention after publicly outlining her concerns Wednesday. Spencer, a longtime critic of the 2025 state lawmakers’ decision to return control of the St. Louis Metropolitan Police Department to a state-appointed board, said the board has failed to address basic issues. “In recent weeks, the board’s attention has gone for an executive pay raise and a reality TV show instead of the department’s needs,” Spencer told reporters. She alleged the board violated Missouri’s Sunshine Law by holding an emergency meeting to approve a contract that raised Police Chief Robert Tracy’s base salary substantially while shifting a larger share of the cost to the City of St. Louis. “There was no emergency, there was no required meeting, and we didn’t follow a 24-hour notice period,” Spencer said. “And I found that to be enormously egregious.” Old North St. Louis redevelopment delayed by reported squatters The board approved the new contract for Tracy, increasing his city-paid base salary to $295,000. Coffman, 38, walked up to the valet desk and asked if they had a Rivian. The person working at the desk gave Coffman the key, and he left with the vehicle. items.t: DOJ’s California ballot fight rejected by another judge
items.x: ( The Hill ) The Trump administration's bid to separate 20,000 mail ballots in California that it says are likely noncitizens met another defeat on Wednesday as a trial judge refused to intervene. U.S. District Judge David Carter ruled California can continue to accept the questioned ballots like any other. “This request violates longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections,” Carter wrote. “If Plaintiff’s last-minute request for relief were granted, either party could create chaos for their own political purposes to disrupt the election process,” he continued. “Over 20,000 registered Californians would potentially lose the right that generations of Americans have fought to preserve.” California has raised eyebrows at the veracity of the administration's list and says it's not obligated to verify voters’ citizenship in response. The state has conceded it's not feasible to segregate a ballot once it's processed. It would be counted even if later found to be fraudulent. items.x: CHICAGO ( WGN ) A Chicago architectural firm has released a proposal that would move the Chicago Bears to a domed stadium in Bridgeport. The firm Skidmore, Owings and Merrill released renderings of the proposed stadium on Instagram Wednesday, saying the proposal would "create a new home for the Bears that is also a catalyst for lasting neighborhood investment." The proposal has the Bears moving to the area the Chicago White Sox currently call home. The White Sox, however, are currently in the process of exploring the possibility of leaving their home at Rate Field for a proposed new ballpark in South Loop . The proposed Bridgeport stadium would serve as the centerpiece of a mixed-use district that would also feature housing, entertainment, hospitality, parks and public recreation. The site would also have access to the CTA, Metra and the Dan Ryan Expressway. Skidmore, Owings and Merrill also said it has identified a large amount of publicly-owned land surrounding the proposed site that could transform the stadium into a district with more affordable and market-rate housing, along with civic amenities and new and improved pedestrian bridges. items.t: Preservation group seeks millions to save historic water tower
items.x: ST. LOUIS – If you were to make a list of St. Louis landmarks, the one-of-a-kind Compton Hill Water Tower would likely be in the top five. The iconic Romanesque tower, located on one of the highest elevations in the city, used to provide water to people who lived in St. Louis. Designed by Harvey Ellis, it was built in 1890 to solve a problem: to get equal water pressure to this high point in the city. “This is what's called a standpipe,” Robert Atchisson, St. Louis Water Division spokesman, said. “They were constructed to help the flow of water and prevent surges that would rupture pipes.” It's one of seven standpipe towers that remain in the world; three of which are in St. Louis City off Grand Boulevard. But in 2019, the Compton Hill Water Tower was closed to the public for safety and structural concerns. items.x: McALLEN, Texas (Border Report) The Humanitarian Respite Center in McAllen used to help thousands of migrants who crossed the border during the Biden administration. But since Trump took over it has largely been empty. But on Wednesday dozens of faith-based and community leaders were at the center to speak out against hunger and food insecurities that are plaguing this South Texas border region. And to urge voters to elect leaders who will help. “In this election year Bread for the World is urging people of faith to vote to end hunger," Felipe Salinas of the Christian-based nonprofit group Bread for the World told the group. He says there are too many people in the region who cannot afford food for their families and he believes more public assistance is needed by the government. “It is very much a policy choice because for every meal a food bank or food pantry provides, the federally-funded Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, provides 9. items.t: Report: Off-duty border agent allegedly stabs, kills wife
items.x: EL PASO, Texas (Border Report) An off-duty U.S. Border Patrol agent allegedly stabbed and killed his wife early Wednesday morning in Laredo, Texas, according to the Laredo Morning Times. The newspaper reported that Abel Garza, 30, is charged with murder in the death of his wife, 28-year-old Mayra Alejandra Landeros. The newspaper also reported that U.S. Customs and Border Protection confirmed that Garza is a U.S. Border Patrol agent with the Laredo Sector, and that the agency’s Office of Professional Responsibility is reviewing the incident.

items.t: Harris advises Democrats against attempting to impeach Trump
items.x: ( The Hill ) Former Vice President Kamala Harris on Tuesday urged Democrats against making a third attempt to impeach President Trump if they win back the House after next week's midterm elections. "I think that going in the direction of impeachment is not a good idea, just to be honest with you," Harris told MeidasTouch's Aaron Parnas in an interview. "Just because we have limited resources and I think the energy and the resources need to put into accountability, need to be put into investigations." "And that's where the time should be spent," she added. "Remember, I was in the Senate for the last go-around, and the votes aren't there. "So, that's how I feel. But also, I think after the election, we all have to just also agree that our attitude has to be to get stuff done." Harris said Democrats should be "uncompromising" and "not sit around, you know, being genteel about the relationships," but maintain accountability when it comes to cuts to healthcare and oversight on the Iran war. items.t: St. Louis County working to fix online errors with senior property tax freeze
items.x: ST. LOUIS COUNTY, Mo. Some St. Louis County residents tell FOX 2 they're seeing property tax figures online that don't reflect their senior property tax freeze, prompting questions and concerns. FOX 2 received several phone calls and emails Tuesday over apparent errors pertaining to St. Louis County's senior property tax freeze. Some residents on the Nextdoor App reported seeing higher tax amounts online, and others said they have not received approval for their applications. According to a St. Louis County spokesperson, software errors caused the incorrect base years to be assigned to some senior tax freeze applicants. The St. Louis County Department of Revenue is working to address the technical issues, and the errors are expected to be corrected online in the coming days. St. Louis County property tax bills have not yet been mailed. The county expects to send them in November and says the bills will reflect the correct amounts.

items.t: Three brothers walk free in Missouri boy’s murder
items.x: BARRY COUNTY, Mo. — Prosecutors dropped murder charges against three brothers accused in a decades-old cold case. David Ray Scott was scheduled for a preliminary hearing on Tuesday, but the Missouri Attorney General's office did confirm the cases were dismissed. They would not confirm reports about a witness failing to testify as the reason all murder charges were dropped in the death of Justin Hocutt. We reached out to Amy Boxx, the current Barry County prosecutor, to ask questions about the dismissal but she has not returned our emails or messages. The A.G.'s office, which is assisting with the case, says they hope to have charges refiled. Now, Mark, David, and Bobby Scott, who are accused of killing the 14-year-old Seligman boy, are walking free. All three were released from the Barry County Jail just before noon yesterday. David Scott was arrested in Barry County in early July. Mark and Bobby Scott were both arrested in Pulaski County, Arkansas. Mark waived extradition and was brought back in late July. Bobby Scott fought his return and was extradited to Barry County jail on September 8. Hocutt went missing in October of 1999 and was found dead one day later on the train tracks

items.x: ( The Hill ) Conservative influencer James O’Keefe was charged in Minnesota Wednesday after he and fellow right-leaning commentator Cam Higby misrepresented themselves at a polling place during the state’s primary election earlier this year. Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty announced during a press conference the two men are facing felony unlawful voting and identity fraud charges. “Elections are the bedrock of democracy and their protection is one of our highest priorities,” Moriarty said in a statement . “Individuals engaging in unlawful conduct related to our elections will be held accountable.” On the state’s Aug. 11 primary election day, O’Keefe and Higby donned mock “ Muslim attire ,” spoke in fake accents at Minnesota polling places. O’Keefe and Higby began the state's unregistered voter vouching process under fake names but did not ultimately sign this oath or cast a vote, according to the county attorney. items.t: East St. Louis Korean War hero to be laid to rest Thursday
items.x: BELLEVILLE, Ill. — A Metro East soldier missing since the Korean War is finally home. After 75 years, U.S. Army Private First-Class John Robert Stovall returned to Illinois this week after his remains were identified, allowing family, veterans and community members to honor his service and sacrifice. Stovall, a native of East St. Louis, arrived at St. Louis Lambert International Airport on Oct. 27. The Illinois State Police escorted his remains to Kassly Mortuary in Fairview Heights, where members of the ISP Honor Guard participated in a ceremonial transfer. Stovall is scheduled to be laid to rest with full military honors Thursday, Oct. 29, at Mount Hope Cemetery in Belleville. He was just 19 years old when he went missing in July 1950. For decades, his name remained on the Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency's list of missing service members. In June 2025, the agency positively identified his remains. items.t: Cornell preps for no-confidence vote against president after Jane Doe’s allegations: What to know
items.x: ( The Hill ) The Cornell University Faculty Senate is set to debate a no-confidence vote on Wednesday against President Michael I. Kotlikoff after allegations of a 2024 gang rape at a campus fraternity that resulted in no criminal charges caused uproar around the country. The more than 75 members of the body will have their second meeting debating the resolution and the timing of a vote on it. A motion could be introduced to delay the no-confidence vote and set another meeting. But if that motion is not introduced or fails, members of the Faculty Senate will begin the no-confidence vote after Wednesday's meeting is over, and they typically have a week to cast their choice online. While a no-confidence vote has no authority to remove an official, its passing would show deep dissatisfaction from faculty with how Cornell leadership has handled accusations from Jane Doe that seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity raped her . What does the no-confidence vote entail? The resolution, led by Paul Ortiz, a professor of labor history, states the faculty has no confidence in Cornell's leadership to "address the ongoing crisis of sexual assault" at the school. items.t: Dolores Huerta, labor leader and activist, dies at 96
items.x: ( KTLA ) – Activist Dolores Huerta, who helped co-found the National Farm Workers Association with César Chavez, has died. She was 96. Huerta's family said in a statement through her foundation that she died Wednesday at home. "We are deeply saddened to announce that our beloved mother, Dolores Huerta, has passed away today at the age of 96," her family said in a statement posted on social media. "As you can imagine, this is an incredibly difficult time for us, and we ask for privacy as we grieve this incredible loss to our family," the statement continued. "We know that many of you around the world share in our mourning, and we will be following up on plans to recognize and celebrate her incredible life and legacy." items.t: Man sentenced in stabbing of Collinsville Walmart co-worker
items.x: MADISON COUNTY, Ill. A man who admitted to stabbing his co-worker at Walmart in Collinsville last year has been sentenced to decades behind bars. Kelvin F. Fuller, 20, was sentenced to 25 years in prison on Tuesday, according to Madison County State's Attorney Tom Haine. Fuller previously pleaded guilty to one count of attempted murder, a class X felony. Investigators say Fuller stabbed his co-worker with a knife multiple times on July 23, 2025. Customers and other employees stepped in to help the victim, prompting Fuller to flee the store. Fuller was taken into custody nearby, and told police he attacked the co-worker because he felt that she had “disrespected” him. “A workplace should be a place where people can do their jobs without fear of being attacked,” Haine said. “The actions of the employees and customers who stepped in to stop this attack may have prevented an even greater tragedy. I commend them for their intervention, and I commend law enforcement and our prosecution team for ensuring that this offender was held accountable for this violent crime.” A statement from Haine's Office did not immediately confirm whether Fuller will be eligible for parole or early release.

The S&P 500 rose 0.2% and pulled within 1% of its all-time high , which was set earlier this month. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 176 points, or 0.3%, as of 11:45 a.m. Eastern time, and the Nasdaq composite was virtually unchanged. The day’s highlight will likely be what the Federal Reserve says, if anything, about where interest rates are heading. The Fed raised its main interest rate last month for the first time in three years in hopes of slowing the high inflation that’s squeezing the economy and discouraging Americans . The widespread expectation on Wall Street is that the Fed will leave the federal funds rate alone at this meeting, and the question is whether it will give hints about what may happen at later meetings. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh, though, has been adamant since taking over the Fed about wanting it to give fewer indications about its future moves. items.t: Creve Coeur Lake to close five months for invasive carp removal

Officials from the Missouri Department of Conservation, U.S. Geological Survey and St. Louis County Parks and Recreation Department are all helping with the effort. Biologists say that invasive carp can negatively impact native fisheries by consuming large amounts of plankton, a food source for native fish and other aquatic organisms. The carp's feeding habits can also disrupt food chains and the health of ecosystems. According to MDC, beginning on Monday, Nov. 2, nets will be used to direct and concentrate invasive carp. items.x: ST. LOUIS Tower Grove Park is getting a major boost to help preserve one of its most recognizable landmarks. The park has been awarded a $750,000 federal Save America’s Treasures grant to restore the 154-year-old Music Stand Pavilion. The discovery comes as Lutheran South prepares for its next chapter with the construction of a new STEM Center. items.t: Federal Reserve holds interest rates steady in face of persistent inflation
items.x: Federal Reserve officials held interest rates steady Wednesday despite stubborn inflation. The central bank's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) voted 10-2 to keep the benchmark federal funds rate range at 3.75 percent to 4 percent. "The committee believes that the accumulation of more information will help it determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the 2 percent goal," Fed Chair Kevin Warsh told reporters, reiterating the FOMC's statement. Fed board of governors member Lisa Cook and Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland's president Beth Hammack dissented in favor of a quarter-point increase. Hammack also backed a rate hike in late July, joining two of her colleagues in the minority when the central bank kept rates steady . Wednesday's decision came six weeks after officials raised rates by a quarter point , the first hike in more than three years. Inflation has risen this year amid the Iran war , creating a difficult set of circumstances for President Trump and the GOP this midterm cycle . items.t: Woman dies after domestic dispute involving vehicle in Franklin County, police say
items.x: FRANKLIN COUNTY, Mo. A woman died Monday after a domestic dispute involving a vehicle in Franklin County, authorities say. The St. Clair (Missouri) Police Department responded to the situation around 1:15 p.m. Monday on Highway 47 near Miller Drive. According to a Facebook post from St. Clair Police Chief John Sikes , when officers arrived, one woman was found lying in the roadway with apparent injuries. The woman was rushed to a hospital for treatment, but she later died from her injuries. In a separate Facebook post Tuesday , Sikes reported that prosecutors had charged Bryan E. Thrower with second-degree murder and that he is being held at the Franklin County Detention Center without bond.

Democrats view the Republican candidates running in those states as mediocre political talents who must fight historic headwinds caused by President Trump’s unpopularity, voter anger over inflation and the war in Iran, and burgeoning Democratic voter enthusiasm. The Senate battleground map has steadily expanded throughout the 2026 midterm election cycle as political handicappers have shifted seats that were thought to be in solidly Republican territory — such as Alaska, Iowa, Kansas and Texas — to the “toss-up" category. But now Republicans have to worry about losing Senate seats in states that were unthinkable as realistic Democratic pickup opportunities at the start of the election cycle, most notably South Carolina, which last elected a Democrat, Fritz Hollings, to the Senate in 1998. items.t: Topeka man sentenced to life in prison after 2024 deadly shooting
items.x: TOPEKA ( KSNT ) – A judge has sentenced a man to prison after a local jury found him guilty of charges tied to a 2024 deadly shooting in Topeka. A Shawnee County judge sentenced Du'Jontez J. J. Owens, 26, of Topeka, to life in prison without the possibility of parole until he has served 51 years and eight months. The court ordered the sentences for several counts that involved criminal discharge of a firearm to run consecutively while all other sentences were ordered to run concurrently. A jury convicted Du'Jontez Owens of 20 separate charges earlier this year. Shawnee County District Attorney Mike Kagay said the charges stem from the 2024 fatal shooting of Ricky R. Washington Jr., the attempted murder of another person and a series of related violent crimes in Topeka. Du'Jontez Owens' charges included: First-degree premeditated murder Attempted first-degree premeditated murder Conspiracy to commit murder Three counts of criminal discharge at an occupied vehicle Multiple counts of criminal discharge of a firearm at occupied and unoccupied dwellings Criminal possession of a firearm by a convicted felon Aggravated battery Interference with law enforcement Mugshot of Du'Jontez Owens.

items.t: Veteran Salute: Robert Messineo reflects on Navy submarine service and helping fellow veterans
items.x: TOPEKA ( KSNT ) Robert Messineo knew he wanted to join the U.S. Navy from the time he was eight years old. Messineo served in the Navy from 1980 to 1985 as a machinist’s mate. He was stationed in Norfolk, Virginia, and deployed to the Mediterranean and North Atlantic. His job involved maintaining and working on mechanical equipment aboard his submarine, including hydraulic and pneumatic systems, atmosphere control and diesel equipment. “There are a million parts on a submarine. Any of them can fail and half will kill you and that's something you will have to learn very quickly to accept, very quickly if this is the life you want to have,” Messineo said. During his deployments, Messineo visited places including France, Norway and Scotland. He said the crew sometimes visited smaller communities rather than major tourist destinations, giving him a chance to experience everyday life in other countries. “We went to a little island called Santo Stefano," Messineo said. "So, you didn't see the tourist part of the country. You saw the country; you saw what it was like to live in a small town in Italy. France we were in Toulon and that was a NATO base. items.t: AAA advises drivers about daylight saving time
items.x: ( WAVY ) – It's only a few days until we trade one extra hour of sleep for months of darkness as we leave work to drive home. And even though we're on the easier end of the time transition (from daylight saving time to standard time), the switch still takes its toll. Nexstar's WAVY went to AAA Tidewater Virginia to see what commuters can expect. "Well, the biggest thing for drivers will be the change in daylight when we leave work or school," said Holly Dalby with AAA. "At the end of the day, gone will be the bright sunshine, and we will find ourselves either driving into the glare from the setting sun or driving home in the dark. So it's a time to be particularly careful on the roads." Days will get way shorter in November: How much daylight will we lose? While lawmakers have tried to get rid of the time switch altogether, it doesn't appear to be going anywhere anytime soon, so your circadian rhythm will have to dance to a different beat for a while. "It just messing with our sleep schedule can really add to our fatigue very quickly. And when we're fatigued, we can make mistakes," Dalby said. Asked if they will get it back, she said, "No, no, no, no." items.x: Wendy’s shares jumped more than 14% Wednesday after noted investor Nelson Peltz made an offer to buy the chain, which has been struggling with high beef prices and aging stores. Peltz’s Trian Fund Management and several partners are offering Wendy’s $7.35 per share in cash, or a premium of nearly 19% over the stock’s closing price on Tuesday, in a deal that would take the company private. The offer values Wendy's at $1.4 billion. Wendy's, which is based in Dublin, Ohio, confirmed receipt of the unsolicited proposal in a statement Wednesday and said its board has formed an independent committee to evaluate it. At the end of last year, Wendy's had 5,969 restaurants in the U.S. and 1,428 outlets in 38 countries. Wendy's, founded in 1969 by Dave Thomas and named after his daughter, is known for its square burgers and Frosty desserts. The fast-growing chain introduced the drive-thru window in 1970 and went public in 1976. In the 1980s, as it jockeyed for sales with McDonald's and Burger King, Wendy's launched salad bars and ran its iconic “Where's the beef?” ad campaign. items.t: Federal Reserve’s preferred measure of inflation rose slightly in September
items.x: ( The Hill ) Inflation increased slightly in September after declining in August , new data from the Bureau of Economic Analysis showed Thursday. The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index , the preferred inflation metric for the Federal Reserve, rose by 0.5 percent last month and was up 3.6 percent relative to September 2025. The Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland projected PCE inflation for last month at 0.5 percent month-over-month and 3.6 percent relative to September 2025. Annual inflation, according to the PCE, previously dipped from 3.7 percent in July to 3.4 percent in August. The price of gas and other energy goods rose by 9.2 percent from August to September, after increasing by 4.4 percent from July to August. Gasoline and energy costs have risen in six of nine months this year, as the Iran war sparked oil price shocks via the Islamic Republic's restrictions on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz. Persistent inflation , which has remained above the Fed's 2 percent target for five-and-a-half years, spurred central bank officials to hike interest rates by a quarter point in mid-September. items.x: DoorDash is gobbling up Instacart in a $17 billion acquisition that will supercharge its grocery delivery business. DoorDash said the Instacart brand name and app will remain, and Instacart shoppers can continue fulfilling orders for Instacart. Grocers can also choose to work with Instacart or DoorDash. Instacart customers will now have access to 50,000 additional stores covered by DoorDash, the company said. Instacart, founded in 2012, specializes in grocery and convenience store delivery in the U.S. and Canada. Its 600,000 “shoppers” — who are independent contractors — completed 338 million orders last year, according to company filings. Instacart has a market value of $14 billion. DoorDash, founded in San Francisco in 2013, began as a restaurant delivery business but has expanded to pet food and electronics. Operating in 40 countries, it completed more than 3 billion orders last year using a network of 9 million independent delivery workers. It has a market value of $73 billion. DoorDash began delivering groceries in 2020 amid a surge in pandemic-era demand. Grocers were initially cautious. items.t: RFK Jr. eases access to unproven peptides despite opposition from FDA scientists
items.x: WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration on Wednesday acted to ease access to unproven peptide drugs favored by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr . Food and Drug Administration scientific staffers had little input on the decision and opposed the changes, according to six people familiar with its development. The draft policy posted online by Kennedy’s Department of Health and Human Services covers a handful of injectable peptides promoted within the wellness industry for uses such as building muscle, healing injuries and boosting energy. The government will take comments for two weeks before finalizing the measure. The document, primarily written by officials at HHS, faced overwhelming pushback among FDA drug staffers who warned it could undermine the agency’s long-standing mission of keeping unsafe health products off the U.S. market, according to the people familiar with its development. items.t: A close up look at Fort Riley’s Bradley fighting vehicles
items.x: TOPEKA ( KSNT ) – Soldiers at Fort Riley showed off their Bradley fighting vehicles Wednesday. Officials said training and operating weapons for gunnery is a foundational skill in the Army. Service members train for four to six weeks on the platform of driver training. Then from there, they do the GST gunnery skills test. It's for developing the basics, such as how to load ammunition and how to identify targets in the field. "Anything that we plan is an operation. We start really for plan and prepare. And for us to be successful, we have to rehearse and make sure everyone is on the same page," said LTC Bernard Mabini, commander, 1 st Battalion, 16 th Infantry Regiment. Staff Sergeant Jacob Kreager is a vehicle commander at Fort Riley. He has been driving Bradley's for the past two years. His job is to tell the gunner where and what to fire while giving the driver directions. "Think of it like the brain," Kreager said. "And then they're like me. My arms and legs, so. Yeah. Just keep keeping the crew alive. Keeping us where we're going. Make sure we're going to the right place." Kreager talked about how important the little details are when it comes to operating a fighting vehicle. "

"Just because we have limited resources and I think the energy and the resources need to put into accountability, need to be put into investigations." items.x: TOPEKA ( KSNT ) Halloween is only a few days away, and some four-legged friends may be put at risk by certain holiday traditions. Experts say keeping your pets safe this Halloween starts with keeping them inside and away from the front door. Trick-or-treaters, doorbells and costumes can be stressful, especially for dogs. People should make sure their pets wear an ID tag and are microchipped in case they get out. If your pet is wearing a costume, make sure it's comfortable. Second best, just put a bandana on, and a Halloween-themed bandana. That's usually a safer route to go. items.t: Federal Reserve holds interest rates steady in face of persistent inflation
items.x: Federal Reserve officials held interest rates steady Wednesday despite stubborn inflation. The central bank's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) voted 10-2 to keep the benchmark federal funds rate range at 3.75 percent to 4 percent. "The committee believes that the accumulation of more information will help it determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the 2 percent goal," Fed Chair Kevin Warsh told reporters, reiterating the FOMC's statement. Fed board of governors member Lisa Cook and Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland's president Beth Hammack dissented in favor of a quarter-point increase. Hammack also backed a rate hike in late July, joining two of her colleagues in the minority when the central bank kept rates steady . Wednesday's decision came six weeks after officials raised rates by a quarter point , the first hike in more than three years. Inflation has risen this year amid the Iran war , creating a difficult set of circumstances for President Trump and the GOP this midterm cycle . items.x: ( The Hill ) Alvin Hellerstein, a longtime federal judge who was set to oversee the criminal trial of deposed Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro, has passed away, according to a court official. He was 92. Nominated by then-President Bill Clinton in 1998, Hellerstein oversaw many high-profile disputes during his nearly three decades on the bench in New York City. He was back in the national limelight presiding over the proceedings for Maduro , who was captured and brought to the U.S. earlier this year over accusations of narco-terrorism. Maduro and his wife were in the judge's courtroom less than two weeks ago to plead not guilty to a new set of criminal charges. Before the Maduro operation, Hellerstein had long clashed with President Donald Trump in court. The judge at one point agreed that Trump’s fixer-turned-foe, Michael Cohen, could be released from prison to home confinement. Cohen has cast his prosecution as retribution by Trump. Separately, Hellerstein repeatedly denied Trump's efforts to move his hush money criminal prosecution into federal court, forcing the president to try his luck in New York's state system. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was up 176 points, or 0.3%, as of 11:45 a.m. Eastern time, and the Nasdaq composite was virtually unchanged. The day’s highlight will likely be what the Federal Reserve says, if anything, about where interest rates are heading. The Fed raised its main interest rate last month for the first time in three years in hopes of slowing the high inflation that’s squeezing the economy and discouraging Americans . items.t: Hazmat teams respond to diesel fuel spill in south Topeka
items.x: TOPEKA ( KSNT ) – Topeka firefighters and hazmat personnel responded to a diesel fuel spill situation Tuesday. City of Topeka spokeswoman Kim Qualls said in a press release that personnel with the Topeka Fire Department (TFD) responded to reports of diesel fuel leaking from a fueling facility just before 10:55 a.m. on Oct. 27 at 4201 SW Burlingame Rd. in Topeka. Fire crews arriving at the scene spotted diesel fuel leaking from the facility into a nearby drainage ditch. TFD personnel and hazardous materials crews built a dam using nearby soil to contain the spill and stop it from spreading further. Qualls said the property owner is responsible for coordinating cleanup efforts, including removal of all contaminated soil. items.x: AMSTERDAM (AP) — A longtime zookeeper at a safari park in the Netherlands died Tuesday from injuries she suffered when she was attacked by a leopard in its enclosure over the weekend. The Beekse Bergen Safari Park said in a statement that the woman, whose name has been withheld in accordance with Dutch privacy law, had passed away after she suffered serious wounds to her head and neck on Saturday while working in an enclosure with two male Persian leopards. “Her passing deeply affects us all, and we sympathize intensely with her family, friends, and loved ones,” the zoo, in the southern town of Hilvarenbeek, said in a statement, which was made together with her family. The woman began working at the zoo when she was 17 and spent nearly all of her 40-year career there. items.t: Cause of death revealed for ‘Office Space’ actor Richard Riehle: Reports
items.x: (NEXSTAR) – The cause of death for longtime actor Richard Riehle has been revealed, according to reports. The 78-year-old died earlier this month in Los Angeles, friends told TMZ , which was the first to report the news. The outlet and People , citing his death certificate, reported Tuesday that the "Office Space" actor experienced a stroke and had oropharyngeal cancer. He had been in a rehabilitation center at the time of his death in mid-October, according to People. Oropharyngeal cancer , which can be asymptomatic, impacts the middle portion of your throat, including the base of your tongue and the tonsils. While there are multiple types of oropharyngeal cancers, Johns Hopkins Medicine says the majority are squamous cell carcinomas, which are further divided into HPV-related and HPV-unrelated. The former is caused by HPV, while the latter is commonly caused by tobacco or alcohol. Details about Riehle's condition were not released. items.t: After two-year search, woman’s coworker turns out to be a match for kidney transplant
items.x: SALT LAKE CITY, Utah ( ABC4 ) — Katie Hood and Reina Child became fast friends five years ago when they met as coworkers at Charlie's Produce in Salt Lake City. Then two years ago, Katie, 41, was diagnosed with renal failure. Family, friends and even coworkers began getting tested to see if they were a match. Reina, 47, knew she needed to be tested. And guess what? She is a perfect match. Vanderbilt develops new technique for child heart transplants Now, the bond the two ladies share will grow even stronger because on Tuesday, Nov. 3, they're scheduled for kidney transplant surgery. "She's an inspiration to so many because even though she's struggling, she's smiles and laughs with you," Reina said about Katie. It all started in October 2024. "I had been really swollen for a while, and it got to the point where walking upstairs was just hard," explained Katie. She decided to go to the doctor, which led to an emergency room visit. That visit changed Katie's life. She was diagnosed with heart and kidney failure. "And I've been doing dialysis for three times a week for two years and yeah, just kind of on this crazy journey." items.t: Democrats see battleground map expand to South Carolina, Florida, Mississippi
items.x: Democrats are giddy about the possibility of a bigger blue wave than expected in the battle for the Senate as polls show that South Carolina , Florida and Mississippi — three seats that were long seen as safe Republican holds — are now competitive races. Democrats view the Republican candidates running in those states as mediocre political talents who must fight historic headwinds caused by President Trump’s unpopularity, voter anger over inflation and the war in Iran, and burgeoning Democratic voter enthusiasm. The Senate battleground map has steadily expanded throughout the 2026 midterm election cycle as political handicappers have shifted seats that were thought to be in solidly Republican territory — such as Alaska, Iowa, Kansas and Texas — to the “toss-up" category. But now Republicans have to worry about losing Senate seats in states that were unthinkable as realistic Democratic pickup opportunities at the start of the election cycle, most notably South Carolina, which last elected a Democrat, Fritz Hollings, to the Senate in 1998. items.t: AAA advises drivers about daylight saving time
items.x: ( WAVY ) – It's only a few days until we trade one extra hour of sleep for months of darkness as we leave work to drive home. And even though we're on the easier end of the time transition (from daylight saving time to standard time), the switch still takes its toll. Days will get way shorter in November: How much daylight we’ll lose in Nashville News 2's sister station, WAVY, went to AAA Tidewater Virginia to see what commuters can expect. "Well, the biggest thing for drivers will be the change in daylight when we leave work or school," said Holly Dalby with AAA. "At the end of the day, gone will be the bright sunshine, and we will find ourselves either driving into the glare from the setting sun or driving home in the dark. So it's a time to be particularly careful on the roads." While lawmakers have tried to get rid of the time switch altogether, it doesn't appear to be going anywhere anytime soon, so your circadian rhythm will have to dance to a different beat for a while. Instacart customers will now have access to 50,000 additional stores covered by DoorDash, the company said. Instacart, founded in 2012, specializes in grocery and convenience store delivery in the U.S. and Canada. Its 600,000 “shoppers” — who are independent contractors — completed 338 million orders last year, according to company filings. items.t: Federal Reserve’s preferred measure of inflation rose slightly in September
items.x: ( The Hill ) Inflation increased slightly in September after declining in August , new data from the Bureau of Economic Analysis showed Thursday. The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index , the preferred inflation metric for the Federal Reserve, rose by 0.5 percent last month and was up 3.6 percent relative to September 2025. The Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland projected PCE inflation for last month at 0.5 percent month-over-month and 3.6 percent relative to September 2025. Federal Reserve holds interest rates steady in face of persistent inflation Annual inflation, according to the PCE, previously dipped from 3.7 percent in July to 3.4 percent in August. The price of gas and other energy goods rose by 9.2 percent from August to September, after increasing by 4.4 percent from July to August. items.t: Wendy’s gets buyout offer while struggling with beef prices and growing competition
items.x: Wendy’s shares jumped more than 14% Wednesday after noted investor Nelson Peltz made an offer to buy the chain, which has been struggling with high beef prices and aging stores. Peltz’s Trian Fund Management and several partners are offering Wendy’s $7.35 per share in cash, or a premium of nearly 19% over the stock’s closing price on Tuesday, in a deal that would take the company private. The offer values Wendy's at $1.4 billion. Wendy's, which is based in Dublin, Ohio, confirmed receipt of the unsolicited proposal in a statement Wednesday and said its board has formed an independent committee to evaluate it. At the end of last year, Wendy's had 5,969 restaurants in the U.S. and 1,428 outlets in 38 countries. Wendy's, founded in 1969 by Dave Thomas and named after his daughter, is known for its square burgers and Frosty desserts. The fast-growing chain introduced the drive-thru window in 1970 and went public in 1976. In the 1980s, as it jockeyed for sales with McDonald's and Burger King, Wendy's launched salad bars and ran its iconic “Where's the beef?” ad campaign. items.t: Inside Tennessee Farmers Cooperative’s La Vergne headquarters
items.x: LA VERGNE, Tenn. (WKRN) — While La Vergne is not necessarily known for agriculture, the city is home to the headquarters of the Tennessee Farmers Cooperative (TFC), a central hub for the state's federated farm supply cooperative system. Chief Development Officer Joe Huffine explained TFC was founded in 1945, with different supply operations realizing they could be stronger together. “They’re price takers and not price makers. So the only way they could increase profitability would be to lower their input costs," Huffine said. La Vergne police chief highlights progress over last 3 years The Tennessee Farm Bureau, UT Extension and Tennessee Department of Agriculture studied cooperatives across the U.S. and recommended a federated co-op in Tennessee. That meant ownership would be at the grassroots level—with farmers buying a share of stock, and profits being returned to them, Huffine explained. “Farmers buy at fair market value, and at the end of the year, if there’s a profitability, then they’re paid back based on that," Huffine said. “Over the past 10 years, TFC has paid over $200 million in cash, and those local co-ops have paid over $180 million in cash to the farmer owners." items.t: Running dry: Two Middle Tennessee cities urge water conservation as severe drought strains supplies
items.x: FRANKLIN, Tenn. (WKRN) — Two Middle Tennessee cities are urging residents to conserve water as severe drought conditions put pressure on local supplies, leaving Franklin unable to draw drinking water from the Harpeth River. After months of dry conditions, the river has dropped so low that Franklin has stopped withdrawing water from it, forcing the city to rely on stored water and other sources to keep the taps flowing. "If we were canoeing the Harpeth River right now, we would be dragging our canoe," Franklin Water Management Department Director Michelle Hatcher said. Hatcher said the city has experienced more than two months without significant rainfall, causing water levels in the Harpeth River to fall below the threshold at which the state permits the city to withdraw water. ⏩ Read today's top stories on wkrn.com "It's just rainfall dependent. It's just been a dry year," Hatcher said. "We had a crazy summer that was very wet early on and then everything has dried up since then." Franklin has a 110-million-gallon reservoir that stores water drawn from the river before it is treated for drinking. items.t: FTC, TN, other states sue Dollar General over ‘deceptive pricing’ allegations
items.x: GOODLETTSVILLE, Tenn. (WKRN) — The Federal Trade Commission and 20 states, including Tennessee, have sued Goodlettsville-based Dollar General for alleged deceptive pricing. The federal lawsuit accuses the bargain chain of routinely charging customers more at the register than prices displayed on shelves and in advertisements. “Dollar General has betrayed the trust of millions of American consumers and imposed significant financial harm on communities and consumers who are already struggling to make their paychecks last,” said Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection, according to a press release . News 2 obtained dozens of complaints Dollar General customers filed with the Tennessee Attorney General's office alleging price discrepancies. One customer noted "product shelf price of $3.95 is not what was charged at the register of $4.15," while another said in a complaint, "I bought Christmas lights which were advertised at $1.37 per set. They rang up at $2.75 per set." Nashville, TN Super 8 sued over nearly $150K in unpaid bills Dollar General denied the FTC's claims, saying "nothing could be further from the truth" in a statement provided to News 2.

items.t: Hayden Panettiere death ruled accidental by police in South Carolina
items.x: GREENVILLE, S.C. ( WSPA ) – Police in South Carolina have officially closed the investigation into the death of Hayden Panettiere, according to a Wednesday news release. Greenville Police Department officials said that Panettiere's death has been ruled accidental, based on findings in the investigation and the medical examiner's determination. On August 16, Panettiere was found unresponsive in an apartment at the Judson Mill Lofts on Easley Bridge Road. Police said that Brian Hickerson, Panettiere's on-and-off boyfriend, along with his brother, Zach Hickerson, were at the residence. EMS attempted life-saving measures before pronouncing Panettiere dead at 2:31 p.m. According to the Greenville County Coroner's Office, Panettiere had died from an accidental overdose of fentanyl, 4-ANPP, Alprazolam, Methocarbamol and Quetiapine. Panettiere had spoken openly about challenges in her personal life, including emotional scars from her childhood fame, postpartum depression after giving birth to her daughter, and struggles with alcohol addiction. items.t: Federal Reserve holds interest rates steady in face of persistent inflation
items.x: Federal Reserve officials held interest rates steady Wednesday despite stubborn inflation. The central bank's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) voted 10-2 to keep the benchmark federal funds rate range at 3.75 percent to 4 percent. "The committee believes that the accumulation of more information will help it determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the 2 percent goal," Fed Chair Kevin Warsh told reporters, reiterating the FOMC's statement. Fed board of governors member Lisa Cook and Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland's president Beth Hammack dissented in favor of a quarter-point increase. Hammack also backed a rate hike in late July, joining two of her colleagues in the minority when the central bank kept rates steady . Wednesday's decision came six weeks after officials raised rates by a quarter point , the first hike in more than three years. Inflation has risen this year amid the Iran war , creating a difficult set of circumstances for President Trump and the GOP this midterm cycle . items.x: ( The Hill ) Alvin Hellerstein, a longtime federal judge who was set to oversee the criminal trial of deposed Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro, has passed away, according to a court official. He was 92. Nominated by then-President Bill Clinton in 1998, Hellerstein oversaw many high-profile disputes during his nearly three decades on the bench in New York City. He was back in the national limelight presiding over the proceedings for Maduro , who was captured and brought to the U.S. earlier this year over accusations of narco-terrorism. Maduro and his wife were in the judge's courtroom less than two weeks ago to plead not guilty to a new set of criminal charges. Before the Maduro operation, Hellerstein had long clashed with President Donald Trump in court. The judge at one point agreed that Trump’s fixer-turned-foe, Michael Cohen, could be released from prison to home confinement. Cohen has cast his prosecution as retribution by Trump. Separately, Hellerstein repeatedly denied Trump's efforts to move his hush money criminal prosecution into federal court, forcing the president to try his luck in New York's state system. items.x: ( KTLA ) – Activist Dolores Huerta, who helped co-found the National Farm Workers Association with César Chavez, has died. She was 96. Huerta's family said in a statement through her foundation that she died Wednesday at home. items.t: FEC electronic filing system hit with hours-long outage
items.x: The Federal Election Commission's electronic filing system has been down for hours on Tuesday, according to a spokesperson who confirmed the agency's IT teams are working to restore the service. According to the FEC's incident update page, the agency said Monday night it is "investigating this issue," stating the FEC filing system is down. An update shortly after 9:30 a.m. EDT Tuesday said the agency is "continuing to investigate this issue." "At this time, we can point to the status update posted to the FEC’s website that the electronic filing system is currently offline and our IT staff are actively working to restore service," the spokesperson said in a statement to The Hill. The FEC's website search function used to find campaign donations, recipients and political action committee information is not impacted by the outage. It is not clear what caused the outage, though Reuters , citing an email, reported the FEC website was targeted by a hacker or hackers. The incident comes just over a week until voters across the country will head to the polls for the midterm elections. The FEC's functions should not impact the electoral process. DEVELOPING

The 78-year-old died earlier this month in Los Angeles, friends told TMZ , which was the first to report the news. He had been in a rehabilitation center at the time of his death in mid-October, according to People. ⏩ Read today's top stories on wkrn.com Oropharyngeal cancer , which can be asymptomatic, impacts the middle portion of your throat, including the base of your tongue and the tonsils. While there are multiple types of oropharyngeal cancers, Johns Hopkins Medicine says the majority are squamous cell carcinomas, which are further divided into HPV-related and HPV-unrelated. The former is caused by HPV, while the latter is commonly caused by tobacco or alcohol. Details about Riehle's condition were not released. items.t: Claude AI reportedly bypassed paywall to access Georgia voter data
items.x: ( NewsNation ) — Anthropic’s Claude AI model reportedly accessed publicly available Georgia election data without human authorization, raising fresh questions about AI security and human oversight ahead of the midterm elections. The company told Axios that Claude accessed aggregate vote counts as part of an internal statistics project, bypassing a paywall to retrieve information that Georgia typically makes available for a fee. An Anthropic spokesperson told the outlet that the model didn't access the state’s voter registration system, retrieve individual voter records or alter any voting records. AI giant Anthropic files to make stock market debut According to The Guardian , Claude exploited a loophole in an older version of the Georgia agency’s website, which issued digital access tokens that allowed users to reach the data. The outlet reported that the model requested a token without being instructed to do so. Anthropic said it has since implemented safeguards to prevent similar actions. And guess what? She is a perfect match. items.t: Democrats see battleground map expand to South Carolina, Florida, Mississippi
items.x: Democrats are giddy about the possibility of a bigger blue wave than expected in the battle for the Senate as polls show that South Carolina , Florida and Mississippi — three seats that were long seen as safe Republican holds — are now competitive races. Democrats view the Republican candidates running in those states as mediocre political talents who must fight historic headwinds caused by President Trump’s unpopularity, voter anger over inflation and the war in Iran, and burgeoning Democratic voter enthusiasm. The Senate battleground map has steadily expanded throughout the 2026 midterm election cycle as political handicappers have shifted seats that were thought to be in solidly Republican territory — such as Alaska, Iowa, Kansas and Texas — to the “toss-up" category. But now Republicans have to worry about losing Senate seats in states that were unthinkable as realistic Democratic pickup opportunities at the start of the election cycle, most notably South Carolina, which last elected a Democrat, Fritz Hollings, to the Senate in 1998. items.t: AAA advises drivers about daylight saving time
items.x: ( WAVY ) – It's only a few days until we trade one extra hour of sleep for months of darkness as we leave work to drive home. And even though we're on the easier end of the time transition (from daylight saving time to standard time), the switch still takes its toll. Days will get way shorter in November: How much daylight we’ll lose in Nashville News 2's sister station, WAVY, went to AAA Tidewater Virginia to see what commuters can expect. "Well, the biggest thing for drivers will be the change in daylight when we leave work or school," said Holly Dalby with AAA. "At the end of the day, gone will be the bright sunshine, and we will find ourselves either driving into the glare from the setting sun or driving home in the dark. So it's a time to be particularly careful on the roads." While lawmakers have tried to get rid of the time switch altogether, it doesn't appear to be going anywhere anytime soon, so your circadian rhythm will have to dance to a different beat for a while.
