items.t: Texas says 9 islands in Rio Grande belong to state, not Mexico
items.x: HARLINGEN, Texas ( Border Report ) The State of Texas on Tuesday declared that nine river islands in the middle of the Rio Grande belong to the state, not to Mexico. For years, river islands have provided what officials says are safe havens for cartels that smuggle drugs and migrants into the U.S. from Mexico, giving them a place to hide and wait out border patrols in those areas. A couple years ago, however, the Texas General Land Office declared some islands a part of the state and cleared them of vegetation. Some islands have had military troops land on them recently, and some are also used as border security staging zones. items.t: Florida cocaine case exposes alleged Sinaloa cartel route through El Paso
items.x: EL PASO, Texas (Border Report) — Florida authorities announced charges Tuesday against 10 people accused of participating in a Sinaloa cartel-linked cocaine network that used El Paso as a transportation hub for shipments to the Tampa Bay area. Investigators allege the organization moved cocaine from Mexico through El Paso before transporting it across the country in commercial trucks. El Paso police and Homeland Security Investigations assisted Florida detectives, authorities said. Prosecutors described the operation as a Juárez-based branch of the Sinaloa cartel that supplied Florida with monthly cocaine shipments from at least December 2025 through July 2026. Investigators say traffickers used inoperable truck tractors as cover to transport cocaine from El Paso to Florida as part of an alleged Sinaloa cartel-linked network. (Photo: Courtesy of Pinellas County Sheeriff's Office) Authorities identified Jorge Ramiro Zamonsett as an alleged logistics coordinator in El Paso who arranged trucks and accompanying vehicles for the trips to Florida. items.t: Austin man shot by ICE officer pleads not guilty to federal assault charge
items.x: ( The Texas Tribune ) The Venezuelan man shot by a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer last month in Austin has pleaded not guilty to a federal charge of assaulting a federal officer while resisting arrest. Wilber Rafael Garces Perez entered the not guilty plea in a court filing Tuesday, a week after a grand jury indicted him on one count of assaulting, resisting, impeding and obstructing a federal officer. He also waived his appearance at an arraignment hearing that was scheduled for Thursday. Garces Perez could face up to 20 years in prison if convicted, the U.S. Justice Department has said. Garces Perez entered the country legally under the Biden administration via the CBP One App, according to immigration attorney Kate Lincoln-Goldfinch. He applied for asylum, but an immigration judge issued a deportation order after he missed a court appearance. The notice for the hearing had been sent to the wrong address, the attorney said. He also received a work permit, which expired in December 2025, according to Lincoln-Goldfinch. Garces Perez was shot on Sept. 20 after he had been pulled over while making a food delivery. items.t: When could it freeze in Austin?
items.x: AUSTIN (KXAN) As cold fronts move warm fall air out of our area and bring us milder temperatures, some parts of the country have already seen their first freezes. So, when could Central Texas drop below 32º? We're now less than two months from the official start of winter which is also the shortest day of the year. As days shorten temperatures will gradually continue dropping, ushering in the first freezes to Central Texas since last spring. Typically, November brings the first freezes for most of Central Texas, but in the last five years it has been later. Average first freeze According to data from the National Weather Service in Austin/San Antonio , the average first freeze in the western Hill Country can be as early as Halloween through the first week of November. The majority of the Hill Country gets the first freeze by mid-November with areas near and east of Interstate 35 seeing the average first freeze during the second half of November. Austin, thanks to the urban heat island effect, holds onto the heat a little longer with an average first freeze in the final days of November into the first few days of December. items.t: Aging Untold: How to spot the early signs of Parkinson’s and when to talk to a doctor
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we examine the subtle, easily overlooked early warning signs of Parkinson’s disease and discuss when to talk with a physician. Plus, we explore what to consider when starting antidepressants, emphasizing the importance of setting realistic expectations and building a comprehensive support plan. Then, we share how a grieving Michigan family turned heartbreak into hope by helping pair veterans and first responders with lifesaving service dogs. Parkinson’s doesn’t always start with a tremor — here’s what to watch for Parkinson’s disease can start long before a tremor and the subtle changes are easy to miss. Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said the loss of smell, constipation or changes in handwriting can be early signs. By the time tremors appear, Rogers said, significant damage has often already been done. Resources are available for people living with Parkinson’s. Read the full article here. items.t: ‘Amazed that she’s alive’: 18-year-old driver in ICU after hitting moose on icy road
items.x: ANCHORAGE, Alaska ( KTUU /Gray News) - A mother in Alaska said her 18-year-old daughter is lucky to be alive after hitting a moose Monday night while driving down an icy Anchorage road. “That’s what we’ve been hearing this entire ordeal, from the EMTs to the doctors; they are amazed that she’s alive,” Megan Stone said about her daughter’s crash. According to Stone, the collision occurred when her daughter Autumn was driving home and a moose appeared in the roadway. Stone said she does not believe her daughter had any time to brake. When firefighters arrived, they found a badly damaged vehicle with Autumn trapped inside. It took several crews to cut her out with the Jaws of Life hydraulic rescue tools. Anchorage firefighter Jason Dolph said moose are particularly dangerous when they are hit at highway speeds. “Typically when a car strikes a moose, that moose becomes suspended in the air,” Dolph said. “And when that moose then lands on the vehicle. In this case, it landed on the hood and kind of the windshield and roof area. items.t: Ukraine war continues despite Trump’s promise to end it
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The war in Ukraine has lasted more than four-and-a-half years, and fighting continues despite repeated efforts by President Donald Trump to end the conflict. Trump made a pledge on the campaign trail dozens of times during the last presidential campaign. “Before I even arrive at the Oval Office shortly after I win the presidency, I will have the horrible war between Russia and Ukraine settled,” Trump said at a July 7, 2023, rally in Council Bluffs, Iowa. “Somebody said, are you on Russia’s side? Are you on Ukraine’s side? You know what? The side — I want people to stop dying. That’s the side I’m on.” That campaign promise has not been fulfilled. Trump has met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy twice at the White House. He met once with Russian President Vladimir Putin, in August 2025 in Anchorage, Alaska. “I will say that I believe we had a very productive meeting,” Trump said. “There were many, many points that we agreed on. Most of them, I would say. A couple of big ones that we haven’t quite got there, but we’ve made some headway. ( Aging Untold ) — Members of the military and first responders run toward crisis and the repeated trauma can take a serious toll on mental health. A growing number of veterans and first responders are dying by suicide, struggling with the invisible wounds of service. The U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs estimates an average of 22 veterans take their own lives each day, and hundreds of first responders die by suicide annually. Two Michigan nonprofits are working together to help, providing free therapy and service dogs to veterans and first responders. For Tonya and Scott Shea, the mission is personal. Their son, Army Specialist Connor Shea, was a quiet, old soul with a passion for fishing and Johnny Cash. “His peaceful part of him was fishing. And he would just go on the lakes with his buddies or by himself, put in some headphones, listen to some Johnny Cash, cast some reels, and he was just simple,” Tonya Shea said. items.x: SEVIERVILLE, Tenn. ( WVLT /Gray News) - A Tennessee toddler died after being hit by a car at a pumpkin patch, according to her family. The family of 21-month-old Nyxailia Hinton said they want answers after she died Tuesday. The Sevier County Sheriff’s Office said she fell and was hit by a car driven by a family friend at a pumpkin patch. However, details have not been given about how or where she fell. “She just lit up the room,” said Peandra Hinton, the child’s mother. “If you were having a bad day, you see Zayla, she’s gonna turn it all around.” Hinton said her daughter was with a babysitter who took her to the pumpkin patch without permission. She said her daughter was with a group of people she did not know. Hinton rushed to the hospital, where her daughter died from her injuries Tuesday, according to the sheriff’s office. Hinton said the past 48 hours have been a whirlwind, adding the hardest part has been waking up without her daughter. “The fact that I couldn’t wake up this morning to my baby, it really tore me up,” Hinton said. items.x: (Gray News) - Barbara Barrie, known for her 1979 role in “Breaking Away,” died Wednesday by medically assisted suicide, according to her daughter in a statement to The New York Times . Barrie was 95. Barrie had been diagnosed with terminal cancer and died in her New York City home, according to her daughter, Jane Harwick. Barrie’s agent, Gary Gersh, said her passing was “medically assisted in accordance with the New York State Medical Aid in Dying Law,” according to USA Today . In addition to “Breaking Away,” which earned her an Oscar nomination, Barrie also starred in several TV shows, including “Barney Miller” and “Suddenly Susan.” She also received a Tony nomination for her performance in the original production of “Company.”

items.t: Relocation offers on the rise as cities try big cash incentives to attract remote workers
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Remote work opportunities continue to thrive years after the COVID-19 pandemic made working from home mainstream. Now some communities across the U.S. are competing to attract new residents who are fully employed but can live anywhere, offering increasingly large cash incentives to lure remote workers. Cumberland, Maryland launched “Choose Cumberland,” a pilot program offering $20,000 to up to 10 people who agree to move to the city. The Appalachian Mountains community, located about 130 miles outside Washington D.C., saw its population decline from over 40,000 to less than 19,000 after several manufacturing companies and other large employers closed their doors starting in the 1970s. “At one time, the population of Cumberland was over 40,000 people,” said Mayor Ray Morriss. Program details and requirements The Cumberland incentive splits the money into two payments : $10,000 in relocation cash $10,000 for a down payment or approved home renovations Recipients must make Cumberland their primary residence for at least five years. “The people we are trying to entice are the people who are bringing their jobs with them,” Morriss said. items.t: Gen Z has more debt than Millennials did at the same age
items.x: ( InvestigateTV ) — Gen Z carries more debt than Millennials did at the same age, even after adjusting for inflation, according to TransUnion data cited by a credit counseling expert. Ted Rossman, with nonprofit credit counseling agency Money Management International , said the agency has seen a 35% increase in demand from Gen Z clients in the past year. Their debt loads are about 12% higher than they were a year ago. Student loans, high rents and buy now, pay later plans are adding up and leaving many young adults living paycheck to paycheck with little savings. “That’s really showcasing a lot of these early career pressures,” Rossman said. “You have student loans, you have high housing costs. Those household formation years are very expensive, so GenZer’s actually have more debt than Millennials did at the same age, even adjusted for inflation according to TransUnion.” For Gen Z, Rossman said the starting point is the basics: knowing your budget and watching buy now, pay later spending. “It’s very popular among people in their 20’s, but it’s still debt,” Rossman said. “It can work in your favor. items.t: Antidepressants: What to know before you decide
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Feeling low, disconnected or not like yourself for weeks or months is different from a bad day. When it starts to affect sleep, energy or everyday life, it’s time to talk about support and treatment options. For some people, that could include an antidepressant. Start with a conversation with your provider Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said the decision looks different for everyone. “Everybody is individualized so you can just talk with your provider,” Rogers said. Rogers said to recognize whether you’re feeling depressed and to look at signs such as loss of sleep, loss of energy or loss of motivation. Some people might also experience a triggering event that starts a downward spiral, which they can’t pull themself out of, she said. “When your quality of life is being affected, then you might want to look into antidepressant therapy,” Rogers said. Antidepressants are not “happy pills” Rogers cautioned that antidepressants do not take away sadness. “They’re not happy pills. They don’t take away the sadness, but they will be a way for you to work on how you got there or what else is going on,” Rogers said. She listed chronic stress, a thyroid imbala

items.t: The barbershop quartet tradition is alive in New Orleans
items.x: NEW ORLEANS ( InvestigateTV ) - On a Mid City evening, a four-part harmony rang out just off Canal Street. The group, Southern Tradition, has been around since 1999. The quartet is a place where a traditional American art form forges a friendship. “The main attribute to be a barbershop quartet singer is to not be embarrassed, just keep going,” said Karl Hansen. Four men with four different careers create one sound. Hansen is a doctor who sings bass. Hansen Eschette is a med tech singing tenor. Joe Jacquat is a civil engineer who sings baritone. Johnnie Oufnac is the only actual barber in this barbershop quartet, singing lead. “Being together for a long time helps us harmonize and understand where the other person is going,” Hansen said. Barbershop quartets have been around for more than a century. Though they can be found all over the world, ties to New Orleans are strong. “It really is the nexus of American music at its most basic level and a lot of it comes from New Orleans,” said Zachary Matherne. items.t: Nearly 11 million people in the U.S. could be living with undiagnosed diabetes
items.x: CHARLOTTE, N.C. ( InvestigateTV ) - Diabetes is the seventh leading cause of death in the United States, the No. 1 cause of kidney disease, and an estimated 40 million people are living with it nationwide. Despite decades of prevention education and major breakthroughs in treatment, doctors say diabetes continues to hit the South especially hard — including North Carolina. It can create serious long-term complications, including coronary artery disease, heart attacks, never damage, and amputations. But many people who have the disease may not know it. The CDC estimates around 11 million live with undiagnosed diabetes. “Every day, almost every hour” battle Andrew Tucker has lived with Type 2 diabetes for nearly two decades. He’s made major lifestyle changes but said managing the disease is still a daily fight. Tucker was diagnosed about 15 years ago, when he was 35. “Yes, for me, it is truly an everyday, almost every hour watching what I do,” Tucker said. Type 2 diabetes develops when the body doesn’t make enough insulin or doesn’t use insulin properly. Doctors say obesity is a major risk factor. items.t: This veteran is using his service dog to regain independence
items.x: ST. LOUIS, Mo. ( InvestigateTV ) - Veteran James Poggi served in the Marine Corps working in aviation. His time in the military led to a lifelong strain on his body, including five back surgeries and a below-the-knee amputation. “You go from being six foot three, 250 pounds and able to travel halfway across the world and do whatever they ask you to do, to being relying on wheelchairs, walkers, mobility devices, things like that, you become a vulnerable person that you never thought you’d be,” Poggi said. Poggi said he was in multiple accidents, hard landings, PT accidents and a car crash. He also developed spinal meningitis. “And that was all while I was active,” he said. To help ease some of the emotional toll, Poggi’s wife, who is also his caregiver, suggested he get a service dog. Service dog provides daily support Poggi got Teddy, a Goldendoodle, who serves as his service dog and daily lifeline. “You never went anywhere without your battle buddy. And he always, always better have your back. And that’s how it is. He’s always got my back,” Poggi said. items.t: Weekend rain chances dwindle as cooler temperatures arrive: Charlotte forecast
items.x: CHARLOTTE, N.C. (WBTV) - An unusually warm and dry stretch of weather will persist into Halloween weekend in Charlotte. Unseasonably warm Temperatures Thursday started off warmer, thanks to a layer of clouds in the upper levels of the atmosphere. Those clouds won’t do much to slow down the warmup though, with highs reaching the mid-70s in the afternoon. The warmest day this week will be Friday, when the high in Charlotte will reach just above 80 degrees. While that is a dozen degrees above average, it falls short of the daily record of 84 degrees. Calm Halloween weekend Clouds will increase on Saturday, although the trick-or-treat forecast still looks dry and mild. Temperatures will be in the low 70s before sunset, steadily cooling into the 60s later in the evening. Cooler temperatures remain in the forecast Sunday and Monday, but the rain chances have significantly diminished. Measurable rain is unlikely on Sunday, just a few sprinkles here and there. A few showers on Monday and Tuesday won’t amount to much either, with rain chances only around 20%. Long-range pattern shift The long-range outlooks point to an unsettled pattern setting up later next week and farther into November.

items.t: Economist explains how the ‘K-shaped economy’ is impacting the midterms
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - As voters prepare to head to the polls for the midterm elections, a conflicting economic sentiment is once again emerging on the campaign trail. “Voters reflect the perception of the cost of living as they experienced, as opposed to what is in the data,” said Alessandro Rebucci, an economics professor at Johns Hopkins Carey Business School. “In the data, you have an economy that is very strong as a whole. How that pie is distributed affects how a large segment of the population and the voters are feeling about the economy right now.” The contradiction has been described by many economists recently, as the “k-shaped” economy, using a graph to depict how high-income earners and asset owners are doing compared to middle and lower-income earners. “To be concrete, the wealthiest households are presumed to spend much more than the lowest ones, not only in absolute terms, which is obvious, but also as a share of their income and in their wealth,” Rebucci said. (AP) — Liel Abada scored a career-high three goals in a 15-minute span and Charlotte FC beat CF Montreal 4-0 on Wednesday night to clinch a berth in the 2026 MLS Cup playoffs. Idan Toklomati had a goal and an assist for Charlotte (14-10-8), which snapped a three-game winless streak. Pep Biel added three assists. Abada had his first career hat trick and the third in club history, joining Toklomati and Daniel Rios. Montreal (6-19-7) is winless, with four losses, in its last five. Montreal has the fewest points (25) and worst goal differential (minus-30) in the Eastern Conference. Toklomati opened the scoring in the seventh minute. Allan Saint-Maximin, near the left corner of the penalty box, spun toward the end line to evade a defender and then played a perfectly-placed cross to Toklomati for a header from the center of the area. Abada subbed on for Rodolfo Aloko in the 65th minute and scored goals in the 67th, 79th and 83rd. The 25-year-old forward has all of his career-high eight goals this season since the All-Star break. items.t: College professor among 2 found dead in home; suspect in custody, police say
items.x: LORAIN COUNTY, Ohio. ( WOIO /Gray News) - An Ohio college professor and a woman were found shot to death in a home, and a suspect is in custody, according to authorities. Wednesday morning, police responded to the Oberlin College Conservatory lot at 77 E. College St. to assist firefighters with a vehicle smoking and possibly on fire. When crews arrived, they tried to find the registered vehicle owner, identified as Daniel Jones, 31, to conduct a welfare check. When officers arrived at Jones’ home to check on his family, they found the victims dead inside the home. Pipo Nguyen-Duy, a professor of studio art and photography at Oberlin College, was found dead on the first floor with an apparent gunshot wound. A woman found dead on the second floor was not immediately identified. She also had an apparent gunshot wound. Jones was located aat bout 10:20 a.m. and taken into custody. Charges are pending. The investigation is ongoing.

items.t: Hundreds of UNC Charlotte students march to polls during early voting
items.x: CHARLOTTE, N.C. (WBTV) - In the final days of early voting, hundreds of UNC Charlotte students marched about a mile from the student union to their closest polling location to cast their ballots. Students representing about 20 campus organizations gathered with signs encouraging voting around 3 p.m. on Tuesday, Oct. 28, for the march to the polls. The line of young voters wrapped into the parking lot of the former University City Regional Library. For some of the students, this will be the first time they vote. The group said they were excited to be part of the process and wanted their voices to be heard. “It’s very empowering and it’s a very nice change to know that we as students can make a change and I’m glad that we’re out here today doing it,” said Jada Jewel, a UNC Charlotte student. “People before me have always been fighting for us to have a message and voice so I want to use my voice and do what my ancestors fought for their whole life,” said Nyzia Heath, a UNC Charlotte student. items.t: International fugitive sentenced for one of the largest health care fraud schemes in U.S. history
items.x: COLUMBIA, S.C. ( WIS /Gray News) - A man whom federal prosecutors called the architect of one of the largest health care fraud schemes in U.S. history was sentenced Monday. Herbert Kimble was sentenced to 20 years’ imprisonment with three years of court-ordered supervision. He was also ordered to pay more than $199 million in restitution to Medicare and forfeit more than $195 million in what prosecutors described as “ill-gotten gains.” Kimble pleaded guilty in 2019 to conspiring to commit health care fraud, violate the anti-kickback statute, and defraud the United States in connection with a telemedicine and durable medical equipment scheme involving back, shoulder, wrist, and knee braces. Prosecutors say Kimble ran offshore call centers that recruited elderly Medicare beneficiaries, paid kickbacks to telemedicine companies for signed prescriptions, then sold those orders to medical equipment companies that billed Medicare. Court filings put the intended loss at more than $400 million, with Kimble personally gaining more than $195 million. items.t: Charlotte leaders tout pedestrian safety improvements ahead of Halloween
items.x: CHARLOTTE, N.C. (WBTV) - Ahead of Halloween, Charlotte leaders are highlighting efforts to slow down drivers and keep pedestrians safe, pledging even more investments for walkers and bikers next year. Within the last year, the Charlotte Department of Transportation has built 13 hybrid crossing beacons, giving people a place to cross between two major intersections, including a recently installed beacon at Park Road and Sunset Drive in south Charlotte. The Charlotte Department of Transportation installed the crossing beacon as part of a year of pedestrian upgrades, including more than 1,300 street lights and 22 new traffic signals. Pushing a stroller across Park Road, Clay Hevey calls the crosswalk a saving grace, allowing him to walk with his son to and from school. “The safer I feel the more I’m willing to go out,” Hevey said. Hevey, who lives near Park Road, said without the beacon they would drive instead. “We would be in the car because we wouldn’t feel safe crossing Park Road here at this intersection. items.t: For politics, what is an October surprise?
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - An October surprise is an event that could shake up an election, but does it often make the difference? Matt Dallek, a professor of political management at George Washington University, described it as “an event that, at least in theory, has the potential to shake up an election, something that people did not foresee coming that upends the debate.” He said the term dates back to around the 1980 election, when President Jimmy Carter failed to secure the release of American hostages being held in Iran before November 4, 1980, election day. Carter lost to Republican rival Ronald Reagan. Several surprises have occurred in the years since. Surprises can be driven by a campaign or by news events. Examples include Iran-Contra-related indictments in 1992 and the global financial collapse in 2008. Dallek said those surprises likely did not change the outcome of the election that November. “There’s no evidence that they flip a dynamic that was already in place,” Dallek said. “What’s more typical is that an event occurs, it dominates the news cycle and the trend line starts to move further toward the candidate who was already doing well, who was already likely to prevai

items.t: Library says person threw box of cockroaches at a staff member, prompting closure
items.x: TOLEDO, Ohio ( WTVG /Gray News) - A cockroach attack forced the closure of a library in Ohio this week. Surveillance footage was released by the Toledo Lucas County Public Library, appearing to show a person throwing a box of cockroaches at a staff member on Tuesday at the Kent Branch Library. Surveillance footage apparently shows someone throwing a box of cockroaches at a library employee in Ohio. (Source: Toledo Lucas County Public Library) A library spokesperson confirmed the throwing of the box of cockroaches at the library worker on Collingwood Blvd. But it wasn’t immediately shared what led up to the cockroach attack. The library was said to have gone into restricted access before closing for the rest of the day for cleanup and remediation. The Kent Branch Library reopened Wednesday. Officials did not say whether anyone would be facing any charges.

items.t: Rock Hill teachers help former student rebuild after deadly house fire

The teachers who helped get him to graduation are stepping in to help him rebuild. “I’m gonna miss… I’m gonna miss my mama," said 21-year-old Kheam Weldon. Firefighters responded to a home on Maple Street just before 11 p.m. on Wednesday, Oct. 21. They found heavy flames coming from the front of the house when they got there. Weldon and his mother — 53-year-old Mary Weldon — were taken to the hospital where Mary Weldon died. When Erin Poepping heard the news of what happened she knew she wanted to help the 21-year-old have somewhere familiar to turn. “To be a familiar face and comfortability for him at a time when he didn’t have anyone else showing up for him, that was, you know again we felt like where we needed to be,” said Poepping. Poepping and Myra Hargrove were Kheam Weldon’s special education teachers at South Pointe. items.t: North Carolina governor, attorney general campaign in Mecklenburg County House race

Republican Tricia Cotham is facing Democrat Ken McCool . Cotham is the incumbent and a longtime member of the state House. McCool is a former Matthews town commissioner who says he first gained an interest in politics when Cotham visited his 10th-grade journalism class. “She was the person who really introduced me to politics,” McCool told WBTV. “Kind of lit a fire under me,” he said. At the time of that high school visit, Cotham was a Democrat. Her switch to the Republican Party in 2023 came as a shock to her constituents and handed the NCGOP a supermajority, allowing Republicans to override vetoes from then-Gov. items.t: Grandmother not indicted in baby’s death after police say she left her in hot car for 8 hours while she worked
items.x: MADISONVILLE, Ky. ( WFIE /Gray News) — A Kentucky doctor who accidentally left her grandchild unattended in a hot car for about eight hours will not be indicted for the baby’s death. Madisonville police said 10-month-old Scottie Crowell died in August . On Tuesday, a grand jury found there was insufficient probable cause for an indictment. Police said Scottie’s grandmother picked her up in the morning of Aug. 13 and was supposed to take her to daycare. She forgot the child was in the car and went to work, police said. She arrived at Owensboro Health Multi-Care, where she works as a doctor, around 8 a.m. The baby’s father called his wife after trying to pick up Scottie from daycare, but the child was not there. The baby’s mother called the grandmother at work, and the grandmother ran outside and saw Scottie was still in the vehicle around 4 p.m., police said. After 911 was called, first responders tried to administer lifesaving measures, but the baby died. “I would ask that you keep the infant’s parents and family in your thoughts and prayers as they continue to grieve and process this unimaginable loss,” said Commonwealth’s Attorney Hannah Kington-Jarvis.

items.t: Widow searches for lost wedding ring when husband dies 3 days after getting married in Las Vegas
items.x: LAS VEGAS ( KVVU /Gray News) — A South Dakota woman is asking for help finding the wedding ring her husband lost in Las Vegas the night they married. Tammy Bishop and Will Mulroy were married Oct. 20 at the Viva Las Vegas Chapel. Bishop said they celebrated on a party bus and toured the Strip. At a bar, though, she says Mulroy looked down and realized his ring was gone. “We got to a bar. He looked down and his band was gone. He lost it. He started crying,” Bishop said. According to Bishop, he told her the ring was two sizes too big because he had lost weight. She said the ring may have slid off on the bus or while he moved into his wheelchair. It may also have come off while he rolled down the Strip. “We backtracked our steps. We told the bus driver. We had everyone looking. We couldn’t find it,” she said. The next day, she joked with him: “You didn’t even have your ring on for 24 hours and you lost it.” Everyone laughed, she said. “I said it’s not a big deal; we will buy you a new one, but now that he is gone it is a big deal to me,” Bishop said. items.t: ‘I miss her like crazy’: Loved ones remembering post office worker hit and killed by car
items.x: FORT THOMAS, Ky. ( WXIX /Gray News) - Loved ones and a Kentucky community are mourning a post office worker who was hit and killed by a car while walking earlier this month. Marchelle Bertram worked at the front desk of the Fort Thomas Post Office for years, helping people who came in. Sadly, she lost her life in a collision in Bellevue on Oct. 15. Her daughter, Whitney Bertram, said she is remembering her mother while seeing a large amount of support from the community following her death. “There are so many people I don’t know whose lives she’s touched and affected,” Whitney Bertram said. The crash occurred while Marchelle Bertram was walking on Memorial Parkway near her home. Her daughter said she rushed to the hospital after learning her mother had been hit by a vehicle. “Given the grave amount of injuries she sustained, there was no way she was going to survive,” she said. Marchelle Bertram died at the hospital. Whitney Bertram said the driver stayed at the scene and believes the crash was an accident. “I miss her like crazy; I try not to think about it too hard because I’ll break down,” she said. items.t: Ernie Johnson announces this will be his final season on ‘Inside The NBA’
items.x: (Gray News) - Ernie Johnson announced he will be stepping down as host of “Inside the NBA” at the end of the season. The Sports Broadcasting Hall of Famer took to social media on Wednesday to explain his decision to step away, saying, “It’s just time.” Johnson, 70, stated that he would not be retiring, but cutting back. “This is by no means the end. It’s just a turning of the page,” Johnson said. “And I’ll forever cherish every chapter we have written with ‘Inside the NBA.’” Johnson said he plans to continue to work, including covering the NCAA men’s basketball tournament for CBS and Turner Sports. The six-time Sports Emmy Award winner acknowledged that he has dealt with heart issues in recent years, but that isn’t the reason he’s stepping away from the show. “I just want to slow down a bit,” he added in his social media post. Johnson joined Turner Sports in 1989 and has hosted “Inside the NBA” since 1990. He thanked his TNT Sports and ESPN crews for their support over the years, as well as the viewers. “I just want to say thanks to you. Thanks for your loyalty, for your love, for your support. And on this day, for your understanding,” Johnson said.

items.t: Police department closes its investigation into Hayden Panettiere’s death
items.x: GREENVILLE, S.C. ( WHNS /Gray News) - The Greenville Police Department said it has officially closed its investigation into the death of Hayden Panettiere. Police said Panettiere’s death has been ruled accidental based on the medical examiner’s determination and the findings of the investigation. Panettiere, 36, died from an accidental overdose involving multiple prescription medications and fentanyl, according to findings previously released by the Greenville County Coroner’s Office. Toxicology testing determined the cause of death to be the toxic effects of fentanyl, 4-ANPP, alprazolam, methocarbamol and quetiapine. An autopsy showed no signs of contributing trauma. On Aug. 16, Panettiere was found unresponsive inside an apartment in Greenville, where she had been temporarily staying. Dispatchers received a 911 call reporting a woman in cardiac arrest at approximately 1:51 p.m. She was pronounced dead at 2:32 p.m. Her on-and-off boyfriend Brian Hickerson and his brother Zach Hickerson were at the apartment where she died. President Donald Trump, who has named it “super intelligence,” insists the U.S. will beat China in the AI competition. Trump said while campaigning for president that tariffs would form the crux of the bilateral relationship. The U.S. and China, the world’s two largest economies, have been engaged in a trade war during both of Trump’s terms. Speaking Sept. 13 in Ireland, Trump said the U.S. is leading China in AI. “We’re leading China in AI, we’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins,” Trump said. During a state visit to Beijing in May, Trump praised Chinese President Xi Jinping. “And it’s to me an honor. We’ve had a fantastic relationship. We’ve gotten along. When they were difficulties, we worked it out,” Trump said. Trump hosted Xi at the White House in September for a state visit. He touted what he called “the tremendous strides” he and Xi had already made on national security, trade and technology. items.t: Man loses more than $4,000 after scammers spoof father’s number, claim parents are at gunpoint
items.x: SCOTTSDALE, Ariz. ( KPHO /Gray News) - A man lost thousands of dollars after getting a call that appeared to come from his father’s phone number, with a stranger claiming his parents were being held at gunpoint. Curtis Indyke was asleep around 11:30 p.m. on Oct. 21 when he got a call that appeared to be from his dad, who lives in Virginia. Indyke lives in Arizona. “I answer the phone and it’s not my dad. It’s some other male saying he has my parents basically at gunpoint,” Indyke said. The caller told him to pay or his parents would be shot. While still on the phone, Indyke said he texted 911 to report his parents were being held hostage in Virginia. The person who claimed to be holding Indyke’s parents hostage continued making threats. In a panic, Indyke sent more than $4,000 through Apple Pay to two separate phone numbers. “And they also wanted $1,000 worth of crypto gift cards, which I’ve never even heard of. I’m in IT and I’ve never even heard of them,” Indyke said. Indyke said his bank blocked that purchase. items.t: 8-month-old dies after left alone in running bathtub, police say
items.x: STERLING, Va. (Gray News) - A Virginia woman was arrested after her 8-month-old died after being left unattended in a bathtub, according to authorities. Rosellena Pisani, 30, was arrested and charged with homicide, two counts of child abuse and three counts of child endangerment, a press release said. On Sept. 12, emergency medical personnel and sheriff’s deputies responded to the residence after receiving a call about an unresponsive infant. Investigators determined the baby had been left unsupervised in a bathtub with the water running. Three children, ranging in age from 8 months to 8 years old, were at home during the incident, according to police. Loudoun County Sheriff Mike Chapman called the baby’s death heartbreaking, saying caregivers have a fundamental duty to protect children. He added investigators remain committed to seeking justice in the case.

The Missouri State Highway Patrol previously issued an Endangered Person Advisory for Dylan Fernando Zendejas-Gonzalez, 7. To learn more about Hobart Wealth, visit https://hobartwealth.com/ . You may have spent decades building your retirement savings, only to feel uneasy the first time you start using them. That hesitation can be surprising. You did what you were supposed to do. You saved consistently, invested for the future and learned to think carefully before spending. Now the future you planned for has arrived, and paying for a long-awaited trip or helping a family member can feel like breaking a rule. For years, saving gave you a clear way to measure progress. Contributions went in, account balances grew over time, and leaving the money alone felt responsible. Retirement changes the routine. An account you worked hard to build may now need to help pay for the life you want. Even when withdrawals are part of the plan, seeing money leave an investment account can feel very different from spending a paycheck. Of course, there are good reasons to be careful.

items.t: Long-term care costs rose about 50% in five years, report finds
items.x: ( InvestigateTV ) — The cost of long-term care jumped nearly 50% in five years, while income for older households rose just 22%, according to a new AARP report . The report found long-term services and supports are becoming even less affordable for middle-class Americans. Alan Weil, senior vice president for public policy at AARP, said the gap is the most important finding. “Between 2019 and 2024, a five-year period, the cost of most long-term care services went up about 50%, but the incomes for older households only went up by about 22%,” Weil said. “So the gap between what people can afford and what it costs has grown.” The AARP also looked at what different types of care cost. Weil said the more skilled the service, the higher the price. “If you need someone to come in and help you prepare food, that’s less expensive than if you need someone to come in and provide nursing-level care,” Weil said. “Although I’ll also say that we’ve learned that a lot of caregivers are being forced to provide nursing care that they can’t afford to pay someone else to do, even though they’ve never been trained in nursing. items.x: ST. LOUIS, Mo. ( InvestigateTV ) - A family traveled from Turkey to St. Louis for their daughter’s surgery to treat a rare condition affecting fewer than 100 people worldwide. She was diagnosed with Ulnar Dimelia, also known as Mirror Hand Syndrome. “Mirror Hand is incredibly uncommon, and even surgeons like myself who take care of a great deal of kids almost never see this in their career. So, it’s really uncommon. Numbers are hard to come by, but one in a million or less is probably about right,” said Dr. Charles Goldfarb, Chief of Orthopedic Surgery at St. Louis Children’s Hospital. Deputies say Mullins and his fiancée were at a truck-or-treat event on Saturday in the Man area when he received an emergency call from the sheriff’s department. items.x: WASHINGTON, Ga. ( WRDW /Gray News) - A woman was arrested Tuesday morning after a 4-year-old boy was found dead more than an hour away in an Atlanta townhome, authorities said. Wilkes County Sheriff Darrell Powers said Jasmaine Smoak was arrested and booked into the Wilkes County Detention Center. According to WRDW’s sister station, Atlanta News First , Atlanta police responded to a gated community in the 3500 block of Cardinal Drive SW on Monday night for a welfare check. The Appalachian Mountains community, located about 130 miles outside Washington D.C., saw its population decline from over 40,000 to less than 19,000 after several manufacturing companies and other large employers closed their doors starting in the 1970s. “At one time, the population of Cumberland was over 40,000 people,” said Mayor Ray Morriss. items.t: Antidepressants: What to know before you decide
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Feeling low, disconnected or not like yourself for weeks or months is different from a bad day. When it starts to affect sleep, energy or everyday life, it’s time to talk about support and treatment options. For some people, that could include an antidepressant. Start with a conversation with your provider Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said the decision looks different for everyone. “Everybody is individualized so you can just talk with your provider,” Rogers said. Rogers said to recognize whether you’re feeling depressed and to look at signs such as loss of sleep, loss of energy or loss of motivation. Some people might also experience a triggering event that starts a downward spiral, which they can’t pull themself out of, she said. “When your quality of life is being affected, then you might want to look into antidepressant therapy,” Rogers said. Antidepressants are not “happy pills” Rogers cautioned that antidepressants do not take away sadness. “They’re not happy pills. The quartet is a place where a traditional American art form forges a friendship. “The main attribute to be a barbershop quartet singer is to not be embarrassed, just keep going,” said Karl Hansen. Four men with four different careers create one sound. Hansen is a doctor who sings bass. Hansen Eschette is a med tech singing tenor. Joe Jacquat is a civil engineer who sings baritone. Johnnie Oufnac is the only actual barber in this barbershop quartet, singing lead. “Being together for a long time helps us harmonize and understand where the other person is going,” Hansen said. Barbershop quartets have been around for more than a century. Though they can be found all over the world, ties to New Orleans are strong. “It really is the nexus of American music at its most basic level and a lot of it comes from New Orleans,” said Zachary Matherne. ( InvestigateTV ) - Diabetes is the seventh leading cause of death in the United States, the No. 1 cause of kidney disease, and an estimated 40 million people are living with it nationwide. Despite decades of prevention education and major breakthroughs in treatment, doctors say diabetes continues to hit the South especially hard — including North Carolina. It can create serious long-term complications, including coronary artery disease, heart attacks, never damage, and amputations. But many people who have the disease may not know it. He’s made major lifestyle changes but said managing the disease is still a daily fight. items.t: This veteran is using his service dog to regain independence
items.x: ST. LOUIS, Mo. ( InvestigateTV ) - Veteran James Poggi served in the Marine Corps working in aviation. His time in the military led to a lifelong strain on his body, including five back surgeries and a below-the-knee amputation. “You go from being six foot three, 250 pounds and able to travel halfway across the world and do whatever they ask you to do, to being relying on wheelchairs, walkers, mobility devices, things like that, you become a vulnerable person that you never thought you’d be,” Poggi said. Poggi said he was in multiple accidents, hard landings, PT accidents and a car crash. He also developed spinal meningitis. “And that was all while I was active,” he said. To help ease some of the emotional toll, Poggi’s wife, who is also his caregiver, suggested he get a service dog. And he always, always better have your back. And that’s how it is. He’s always got my back,” Poggi said. Bill Lee said he suspects Christa Pike’s sentence will remain the same following her failed execution last month, unless the courts determine otherwise. items.t: Economist explains how the ‘K-shaped economy’ is impacting the midterms
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - As voters prepare to head to the polls for the midterm elections, a conflicting economic sentiment is once again emerging on the campaign trail. “Voters reflect the perception of the cost of living as they experienced, as opposed to what is in the data,” said Alessandro Rebucci, an economics professor at Johns Hopkins Carey Business School. “In the data, you have an economy that is very strong as a whole. How that pie is distributed affects how a large segment of the population and the voters are feeling about the economy right now.” The contradiction has been described by many economists recently, as the “k-shaped” economy, using a graph to depict how high-income earners and asset owners are doing compared to middle and lower-income earners. “To be concrete, the wealthiest households are presumed to spend much more than the lowest ones, not only in absolute terms, which is obvious, but also as a share of their income and in their wealth,” Rebucci said. items.t: Benton Harbor awarded $22M grant for riverfront transportation improvements
items.x: BENTON HARBOR, Mich. (WNDU) - The city of Benton Harbor just landed major funding to rethink its riverfront. The city was awarded $22 million through the U.S. Transportation Department’s BUILD grant. The state of Michigan committed another $1 million. The money is set to fund transportation improvements along the city’s riverfront. It will build on the waterfront and downtown study now underway with Cornerstone Alliance and the University of Notre Dame. Goals include better public access to the waterfront and reducing risks and damage from rising lake levels, flooding and high water tables. The city said it is exploring ideas, including redesigning parts of the riverfront and creating more space for residents to walk and gather. Changes to Riverview Drive and surrounding streets may also be considered, though no designs have been finalized. Benton Harbor expects to start using the grant in the latter part of 2027. Las mareas comenzaron con la luna llena de principios de semana y podrían provocar inundaciones en algunas zonas hasta el fin de semana, según meteorólogos. Las mareas reales de esta semana se han visto agravadas por factores adicionales, indicaron los meteorólogos el miércoles. items.t: For politics, what is an October surprise?
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - An October surprise is an event that could shake up an election, but does it often make the difference? Matt Dallek, a professor of political management at George Washington University, described it as “an event that, at least in theory, has the potential to shake up an election, something that people did not foresee coming that upends the debate.” He said the term dates back to around the 1980 election, when President Jimmy Carter failed to secure the release of American hostages being held in Iran before November 4, 1980, election day. Carter lost to Republican rival Ronald Reagan. Several surprises have occurred in the years since. Surprises can be driven by a campaign or by news events. Examples include Iran-Contra-related indictments in 1992 and the global financial collapse in 2008. Dallek said those surprises likely did not change the outcome of the election that November. “There’s no evidence that they flip a dynamic that was already in place,” Dallek said. “What’s more typical is that an event occurs, it dominates the news cycle and the trend line starts to move further toward the candidate who was already doing well, who was already likely to prevai

items.t: Grandmother not indicted in baby’s death after police say she left her in hot car for 8 hours while she worked
items.x: MADISONVILLE, Ky. ( WFIE /Gray News) — A Kentucky doctor who accidentally left her grandchild unattended in a hot car for about eight hours will not be indicted for the baby’s death. Madisonville police said 10-month-old Scottie Crowell died in August . On Tuesday, a grand jury found there was insufficient probable cause for an indictment. Police said Scottie’s grandmother picked her up in the morning of Aug. 13 and was supposed to take her to daycare. She forgot the child was in the car and went to work, police said. She arrived at Owensboro Health Multi-Care, where she works as a doctor, around 8 a.m. The baby’s father called his wife after trying to pick up Scottie from daycare, but the child was not there. The baby’s mother called the grandmother at work, and the grandmother ran outside and saw Scottie was still in the vehicle around 4 p.m., police said. After 911 was called, first responders tried to administer lifesaving measures, but the baby died. “I would ask that you keep the infant’s parents and family in your thoughts and prayers as they continue to grieve and process this unimaginable loss,” said Commonwealth’s Attorney Hannah Kington-Jarvis.

(WNDU) - South Bend Community School Corp. board members and Superintendent Mansour Eid will meet in executive session Thursday afternoon to discuss whether the district will appeal a judge’s ruling involving the former Clay High School building. The ruling orders South Bend schools to make the building available to, Career Academy, a charter school in South Bend. The ruling reversed a decision made earlier in 2026 that allowed the district to keep control of the building and reinstates a decision from two years ago granting the charter school’s petition to get the building . Eid said the decision can be appealed and that the district received legal advice within the past 24 hours confirming that it is an appealable decision. According to Eid, the board will listen to attorneys during the executive session, but the decision will be publicly voted upon at Monday’s board meeting. “A lot of people in this community are upset with this decision because it gives away a building that they had paid for to an entity that is a for-profit entity for one dollar,” Eid said. items.t: Restorative Justice Collaborative Hub holds ribbon cutting in South Bend
items.x: SOUTH BEND, Ind. (WNDU) - A ribbon cutting in South Bend on Wednesday marked a new chapter for the Restorative Justice Collaborative Hub. The nonprofit, which helps people impacted by serious crime, officially opened its first office at the Colfax Cultural Center on Lincolnway West. Executive Director Dalila Huerta joined Mayor James Mueller to welcome community members. They were invited to tour the new client offices and art studio and hear how restorative justice can support healing. The hub is offering one-on-one support, arts-based programs and other services for survivors. “I think when people experience crime and violence, one of the things that they suffer the most is isolation,” Huerta said. “We provide a community support program where people can come together through peer support, through art workshops, through different activities that really address the core needs that result from experiencing crime.” A $130,000 accelerator grant from the state helped create the space. items.t: Critchlow invites Beacon Heights seniors to Portage Commons during renovations
items.x: SOUTH BEND, Ind. (WNDU) - Seniors at Beacon Heights Apartments are getting a place to go while renovations are underway. Portage Township Trustee Jason Critchlow is inviting seniors at the complex to spend their days at Portage Commons while work is being done on their homes. When the renovation was announced in June, residents were told they’d be out of their apartments for about 10 days. It is now scheduled to take 17 days. Residents said the new notice promised a temporary dwelling, which has not happened. Critchlow said residents deserve straight answers in writing. His office said it has tried to reach the relocation coordinator and has not heard back. Portage Commons is open Monday through Friday, 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. It offers art, fitness and wellness classes, bingo and games. Stay up to date on local news with WNDU on-air and online. items.t: Widow searches for lost wedding ring when husband dies 3 days after getting married in Las Vegas
items.x: LAS VEGAS ( KVVU /Gray News) — A South Dakota woman is asking for help finding the wedding ring her husband lost in Las Vegas the night they married. Tammy Bishop and Will Mulroy were married Oct. 20 at the Viva Las Vegas Chapel. Bishop said they celebrated on a party bus and toured the Strip. At a bar, though, she says Mulroy looked down and realized his ring was gone. “We got to a bar. He looked down and his band was gone. He lost it. He started crying,” Bishop said. According to Bishop, he told her the ring was two sizes too big because he had lost weight. She said the ring may have slid off on the bus or while he moved into his wheelchair. It may also have come off while he rolled down the Strip. “We backtracked our steps. We told the bus driver. We had everyone looking. We couldn’t find it,” she said. The next day, she joked with him: “You didn’t even have your ring on for 24 hours and you lost it.” Everyone laughed, she said. “I said it’s not a big deal; we will buy you a new one, but now that he is gone it is a big deal to me,” Bishop said. items.t: How data centers are defining some local Indiana elections
items.x: PERU, Ind. ( Free Press Indiana ) - Jason McClure, an apple farmer in Miami County, said he didn’t have any plans to run for political office this year. But that changed when the Miami County Plan Commission voted in May to give a favorable recommendation to a data center ordinance and lift a temporary moratorium on the projects. Hundreds of residents attended the meeting to speak out against it. That included McClure, who wants to reinstate the moratorium. The day after the meeting, he went to the courthouse to file as an independent to challenge two-term Republican County Commissioner Fred Musselman, who serves on the board and voted to pass the ordinance. “It was the straw that broke my back to get into the race,” McClure said. “Enough is enough. My neighbors are showing up and they’re not being heard.” ‘This election’s boogeyman’ As proposals to build hyperscale data centers rapidly ramp up across Indiana, the controversial developments have become the defining issue in many local races where elected officials are considering the issue. items.t: ‘I miss her like crazy’: Loved ones remembering post office worker hit and killed by car
items.x: FORT THOMAS, Ky. ( WXIX /Gray News) - Loved ones and a Kentucky community are mourning a post office worker who was hit and killed by a car while walking earlier this month. Marchelle Bertram worked at the front desk of the Fort Thomas Post Office for years, helping people who came in. Sadly, she lost her life in a collision in Bellevue on Oct. 15. Her daughter, Whitney Bertram, said she is remembering her mother while seeing a large amount of support from the community following her death. “There are so many people I don’t know whose lives she’s touched and affected,” Whitney Bertram said. The crash occurred while Marchelle Bertram was walking on Memorial Parkway near her home. Her daughter said she rushed to the hospital after learning her mother had been hit by a vehicle. “Given the grave amount of injuries she sustained, there was no way she was going to survive,” she said. Marchelle Bertram died at the hospital. Whitney Bertram said the driver stayed at the scene and believes the crash was an accident. “I miss her like crazy; I try not to think about it too hard because I’ll break down,” she said. items.t: Ernie Johnson announces this will be his final season on ‘Inside The NBA’
items.x: (Gray News) - Ernie Johnson announced he will be stepping down as host of “Inside the NBA” at the end of the season. The Sports Broadcasting Hall of Famer took to social media on Wednesday to explain his decision to step away, saying, “It’s just time.” Johnson, 70, stated that he would not be retiring, but cutting back. “This is by no means the end. It’s just a turning of the page,” Johnson said. “And I’ll forever cherish every chapter we have written with ‘Inside the NBA.’” Johnson said he plans to continue to work, including covering the NCAA men’s basketball tournament for CBS and Turner Sports. The six-time Sports Emmy Award winner acknowledged that he has dealt with heart issues in recent years, but that isn’t the reason he’s stepping away from the show. “I just want to slow down a bit,” he added in his social media post. Johnson joined Turner Sports in 1989 and has hosted “Inside the NBA” since 1990. He thanked his TNT Sports and ESPN crews for their support over the years, as well as the viewers. “I just want to say thanks to you. Thanks for your loyalty, for your love, for your support. And on this day, for your understanding,” Johnson said.

items.t: Police department closes its investigation into Hayden Panettiere’s death
items.x: GREENVILLE, S.C. ( WHNS /Gray News) - The Greenville Police Department said it has officially closed its investigation into the death of Hayden Panettiere. Police said Panettiere’s death has been ruled accidental based on the medical examiner’s determination and the findings of the investigation. Panettiere, 36, died from an accidental overdose involving multiple prescription medications and fentanyl, according to findings previously released by the Greenville County Coroner’s Office. Toxicology testing determined the cause of death to be the toxic effects of fentanyl, 4-ANPP, alprazolam, methocarbamol and quetiapine. An autopsy showed no signs of contributing trauma. On Aug. 16, Panettiere was found unresponsive inside an apartment in Greenville, where she had been temporarily staying. Dispatchers received a 911 call reporting a woman in cardiac arrest at approximately 1:51 p.m. She was pronounced dead at 2:32 p.m. Her on-and-off boyfriend Brian Hickerson and his brother Zach Hickerson were at the apartment where she died. items.t: Trump says US will beat China in AI as technology emerges
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Artificial intelligence has emerged as the critical sticking point between the U.S. and China. President Donald Trump, who has named it “super intelligence,” insists the U.S. will beat China in the AI competition. Trump said while campaigning for president that tariffs would form the crux of the bilateral relationship. The U.S. and China, the world’s two largest economies, have been engaged in a trade war during both of Trump’s terms. Speaking Sept. 13 in Ireland, Trump said the U.S. is leading China in AI. “We’re leading China in AI, we’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins,” Trump said. During a state visit to Beijing in May, Trump praised Chinese President Xi Jinping. “And it’s to me an honor. We’ve had a fantastic relationship. We’ve gotten along. When they were difficulties, we worked it out,” Trump said. Trump hosted Xi at the White House in September for a state visit. He touted what he called “the tremendous strides” he and Xi had already made on national security, trade and technology. While still on the phone, Indyke said he texted 911 to report his parents were being held hostage in Virginia. The person who claimed to be holding Indyke’s parents hostage continued making threats. items.t: 8-month-old dies after left alone in running bathtub, police say
items.x: STERLING, Va. (Gray News) - A Virginia woman was arrested after her 8-month-old died after being left unattended in a bathtub, according to authorities. Rosellena Pisani, 30, was arrested and charged with homicide, two counts of child abuse and three counts of child endangerment, a press release said. On Sept. 12, emergency medical personnel and sheriff’s deputies responded to the residence after receiving a call about an unresponsive infant. Investigators determined the baby had been left unsupervised in a bathtub with the water running. Three children, ranging in age from 8 months to 8 years old, were at home during the incident, according to police. Loudoun County Sheriff Mike Chapman called the baby’s death heartbreaking, saying caregivers have a fundamental duty to protect children. He added investigators remain committed to seeking justice in the case.

items.t: Elkhart man accused of child molestation, other charges
items.x: ELKHART, Ind. (WNDU) - Elkhart police arrested a 21-year-old who is accused of sex crimes involving a 13-year-old. Police arrested Henry Cantarero on October 27. Cantarero faces the following charges: Child molest (2 counts) Possession of child sexual abuse material (1 count) Dissemination of matter harmful to minors (5 counts) According to Elkhart police, Cantarero allegedly engaged in sexual intercourse with the 13-year-old and recorded some of the acts. Elkhart police said Cantarero was booked without bond, pending a hearing on November 5. The Indiana Jail Public Portal shows Cantarero is on an immigration detainer. The Immigration and Customs Enforcement website says an immigration detainer is a request from ICE for federal, state or local law enforcement agencies to hold a non-U.S. citizen up to 48 hours after the time they’d typically be released so DHS can have time to act in accordance with federal immigration law. items.t: Elkhart County reports first measles case of the year
items.x: ELKHART COUNTY, Ind. (WNDU) - The Elkhart County Health Department is reporting its first measles case of the year. The Indiana Department of Health has reported 73 cases statewide as of Oct. 27. In Michiana, 11 cases have been reported in LaGrange County and one case has been reported in Kosciusko County. Measles is a viral rash illness that spreads easily from person to person. It is rare in the United States because most people are vaccinated or have had the disease, but cases still occur because of travel to or from parts of the world where measles is more common. Measles symptoms and complications People with measles often appear very ill. Early symptoms can include: Runny nose Cough Tiredness or sleepiness Loss of appetite Fever Spots inside the mouth that look like grains of salt, known as Koplik spots Sensitivity to light Conjunctivitis, or pink eye Around the fourth day of illness, the fever often rises, frequently to more than 101 degrees Fahrenheit. A blotchy, red rash can appear on the face or near the hairline before spreading downward and outward to the rest of the body. items.t: Meet the volunteers who bring flowers from weddings and funerals to hospice patients
items.x: LOUISVILLE, Ky. ( Aging Untold ) — Inside Crescent Hill Baptist Church in Louisville, a group of volunteers gathers each week surrounded by color, creativity and collaboration. They call themselves the Flower Buds. From events to those in need The Flower Buds take donated flowers from weddings, funerals, wholesalers, supermarkets, florists, galas, banquets and other community events. They cut, clean and arrange the blooms into vases, then deliver them to nursing homes, the VA hospital, assisted living facilities and shelters. “Amazingly gifted with so many flowers from places like Kroger who have overbought and can’t sell them, and they allow us to pick them up and then bring them here, and then we cut them, clean them and vase them. Then we take them to nursing homes, the VA hospital, assisted living facilities,” Jodie Raible, a Flower Buds volunteer, said. The group sends out about 100 vases every week. “I take flowers to Up for Women and Children, it’s a day homeless shelter for women,” Stephanie Mullins, a Flower Buds volunteer, said. Delivering to the VA Volunteer Clem Russell is a veteran and takes particular pride in delivering flowers to the VA hospital. “We deliver to the

items.t: Illegal moonshine distillery explodes, catches fire in mountains, officials say
items.x: WILKES COUNTY, N.C. ( WBTV /Gray News) - An explosion at an illegal moonshine distillery sparked a fire in the North Carolina mountains on Monday, according to authorities. Special agents from North Carolina’s Alcohol Law Enforcement Division were called to investigate the explosion in Wilkes County, North Carolina. Agents found an active 200-gallon illegal distillery. They seized about 1,800 gallons of mash, which is used to make moonshine, and 161 gallons of illegal moonshine. North Carolina officials shared photos showing the charred inside of a metal building. Distilling equipment was also damaged. Billy Ray Anderson, 69, was arrested and charged with manufacturing a non-taxpaid alcoholic beverage, possession for sale of a non-taxpaid alcoholic beverage, possession of a non-taxpaid alcoholic beverage, possession of distillery equipment, possession of distillery ingredients and allowing property to be used for the manufacture of a non-taxpaid alcoholic beverage. Moonshine is believed to have originated in North Carolina and was once an important source of income, particularly for rural residents.

items.t: Some packaged salads recalled for undeclared allergens
items.x: (Gray News) - Packaged salads produced by Taylor Farms have been recalled due to an undeclared allergen. According to the Food and Drug Administration, Taylor Farms is recalling its H-E-B Backyard BBQ Chop Salad because it may contain undeclared soy and tree nuts, specifically almonds. “People who have sensitivity or allergy to soy and tree nuts (almonds) may be at risk of a serious adverse reaction if they consume this product,” an FDA press release said. So far there have not been any illnesses or “adverse reactions” reported in connection with the recall. The salads were sold in H-E-B stores across Texas. They can be identified by their UPC code, 041220300457, and their best-by date, Oct. 30, 2026. Customers are asked not to eat the recalled salads and to throw them away or return them to the store for a refund.

items.t: How to spot fake crystals and avoid costly mistakes

What to know about fake crystals Shannon Wimberly, a crystal collector for several years, said she has encountered fake crystals and now scrutinizes purchases more carefully. “I absolutely know I’ve run into getting fake ones, so I started scrutinizing other things more and more,” Wimberly said. items.t: Flávio Bolsonaro aterriza en Miami tras huir de Brasil
items.x: MIAMI (AP) — El derrotado candidato presidencial brasileño Flávio Bolsonaro y su familia aterrizaron en Miami el miércoles tras huir de Brasil. La sorprendente decisión se produce después de 48 horas en las que Bolsonaro se negó a reconocer la derrota ante el presidente brasileño Luíz Inácio Lula da Silva y luego amenazó con intentar anular el resultado electoral. El padre de Bolsonaro, Jair Bolsonaro, también huyó a Florida tras perder las elecciones presidenciales de 2022 frente a Lula antes de regresar a Brasil tres meses después. Estados Unidos dijo el lunes que concedería visas a Flávio Bolsonaro y a su familia. Bolsonaro, aliado de Trump, visitó la Casa Blanca en mayo. Bolsonaro huyó primero de Brasil a Argentina y luego a Ecuador junto a su esposa y sus dos hijas, informó el miércoles la autoridad migratoria de Argentina, un día después de que al senador de 45 años y a su familia se les concedieran visas de Estados Unidos por parte del gobierno del presidente Donald Trump. Bolsonaro está siendo investigado por el Supremo Tribunal Federal de Brasil por presunta corrupción, lavado de dinero y evasión fiscal en dos casos. items.t: State closes daycare after video shows kids fighting inside operator’s home
items.x: SOUTH BEND, Ind. (WNDU) - The State of Indiana has closed a daycare in South Bend after the operator was arrested on felony charges involving alleged child neglect and battery. In a letter given to parents, the Indiana Office of Early Childhood and Out of School Learning said Heavenly Harmony Hope Ministry Inc. is to be closed immediately. The letter cites failure to report child abuse or neglect to law enforcement or DCFS as the reason. Tysharae Jones, the operator, pleaded not guilty to charges of neglect of a dependent, battery with injury to a person under 14 years and contributing to the delinquency of a minor. This stems from a viral video that allegedly showed two children fighting at Jones’ home. Court documents say an 11-year-old battered a 5 and 6-year-old brother and sister inside Jones’ home in June. Investigators allege that not only did Jones not stop the fight, but she is also accused of coaching one of the children who was fighting. items.t: Caregiver advocate shares 3 policies that could help family caregivers
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — More than 60 million Americans are family caregivers, balancing work, kids and care for an aging parent or loved one. Jason Resendez, president and CEO of the National Alliance for Caregiving, recently testified before the U.S. Senate Special Committee on Aging. He joined gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck to talk through the solutions he presented. The three policies he brought to lawmakers Resendez said the National Alliance for Caregiving is championing changes “to address so many of the pain points that family caregivers face every day.” 1) Older Americans Act funding He said one priority is reauthorization and funding of the Older Americans Act. Resendez said the law provides dollars for state Area Agencies on Aging to deliver services for older adults, such as Meals on Wheels and caregiver support. “One of the only federal line items for caregiving comes through the Older Americans Act, and it’s called the National Family Caregiver Support Program,” Resendez said. He said the program funds respite, which gives caregivers the chance to take breaks. items.t: Long-term care costs rose about 50% in five years, report finds
items.x: ( InvestigateTV ) — The cost of long-term care jumped nearly 50% in five years, while income for older households rose just 22%, according to a new AARP report . The report found long-term services and supports are becoming even less affordable for middle-class Americans. Alan Weil, senior vice president for public policy at AARP, said the gap is the most important finding. “Between 2019 and 2024, a five-year period, the cost of most long-term care services went up about 50%, but the incomes for older households only went up by about 22%,” Weil said. “So the gap between what people can afford and what it costs has grown.” The AARP also looked at what different types of care cost. Weil said the more skilled the service, the higher the price. “If you need someone to come in and help you prepare food, that’s less expensive than if you need someone to come in and provide nursing-level care,” Weil said. “Although I’ll also say that we’ve learned that a lot of caregivers are being forced to provide nursing care that they can’t afford to pay someone else to do, even though they’ve never been trained in nursing. So that’s where the burden falls back on the family.” The financial burden oft

items.t: She was born with eight fingers on one hand. Her family traveled to America for the surgery
items.x: ST. LOUIS, Mo. ( InvestigateTV ) - A family traveled from Turkey to St. Louis for their daughter’s surgery to treat a rare condition affecting fewer than 100 people worldwide. Elisa, an 18-month-old, was born with eight fingers on her left hand. She was diagnosed with Ulnar Dimelia, also known as Mirror Hand Syndrome. “Mirror Hand is incredibly uncommon, and even surgeons like myself who take care of a great deal of kids almost never see this in their career. So, it’s really uncommon. Numbers are hard to come by, but one in a million or less is probably about right,” said Dr. Charles Goldfarb, Chief of Orthopedic Surgery at St. Louis Children’s Hospital. The condition leaves patients without a radius bone. This means significant limitations in wrist and elbow motion and preserved shoulder movements. “From the very beginning, he was really warm, genuine, and gave us a lot of hope. Honestly, the trust and support he gave us played a huge role in our decision to come to St. Louis,” said Emircan Buga, Elisa’s father. items.t: Al menos 64 muertos en choque de trenes en España
items.x: BARCELONA, España (AP) — Un tren de alta velocidad chocó contra la parte trasera de otro tren que se había detenido en la vía el miércoles en el centro de España, lo que hizo descarrilar dos vagones y causó la muerte de al menos 64 personas, informaron las autoridades. La oficina del gobierno central para Castilla-La Mancha confirmó que el número de muertos había aumentado. La agencia noticiosa estatal EFE y otros medios informaron más tarde que el número de muertos había aumentado a al menos 30. Fue el segundo gran accidente ferroviario en España este año. El operador del sistema ferroviario de España, ADIF, indicó que el incidente ocurrió la mañana del miércoles en la provincia de Toledo. El servicio ferroviario está suspendido entre Madrid, Ciudad Real y Andalucía. items.t: Canned fruit sold at Walmart recalled in several states
items.x: (Gray News) - A voluntary recall over lead concerns has been issued for cans of Walmart fruit cocktail distributed to stores in at least seven states. The Food and Drug Administration said the recall applies to 15-ounce containers of Great Value Fruit Cocktail in Fruit Juice from Concentrate. Where the product was distributed More than 1,830 cases, or approximately 44,000 individual cans, were distributed to Walmart locations in Alabama, Arizona, Louisiana, New Mexico, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wyoming, the FDA said. How to identify the product The product is marked with lot number “6FCB 04 C2263” and a best if used by date of Sept. 1, 2027. Recall details The FDA initiated the recall for “potential contamination with elevated levels of lead” on Oct. 1. It was reclassified as a Class II recall on Oct. 20. According to the FDA, Class II recalls are issued when a product can cause temporary health effects with a remote possibility of serious issues. What customers should do Customers should throw the item away or return it to Walmart.

items.t: 24-year-old deputy killed in crash with coal truck while on duty, sheriff’s office says
items.x: LOGAN COUNTY, W. Va ( WSAZ /Gray News) - A 24-year-old sheriff’s deputy was killed in a crash while responding to a call, authorities said. The Logan County Sheriff’s Department identified the deputy as 24-year-old Caden Mullins. Deputy Mullins’ fiancée was airlifted from the scene of the crash to a hospital. Deputies say Mullins and his fiancée were at a truck-or-treat event on Saturday in the Man area when he received an emergency call from the sheriff’s department. The sheriff’s department says Deputy Caden Mullins, 24, died in the crash. Mullins was on his way to drop his fiancée off and head to the call when the crash occurred around 5 p.m., deputies say. Deputies say the crash happened at the intersection of Rum Creek Road and Route 10 when a coal truck pulled off the road and hit Mullins’ vehicle. Mullins worked for the Charleston Police Department for about a year before joining the Logan County Sheriff’s Department to be closer to family, the department said.

items.t: Woman found fatally shot inside Summit County home

items.t: Ohio Decides: Final push, records set
items.x: CLEVELAND, Ohio (WOIO) - There are just days before the Nov. 3rd election and records are being shattered for the amount of Ohioans voting early in-person at their county board of elections. In 2018, 177,046 total had voted early, in person the week before the election according to the Ohio Secretary of State, Frank LaRose. In 2022, that number was 265,062 votes. As of Wednesday morning, 770,601 people have already voted in the 2026 mid-term elections in Ohio. According to Case Western Reserve University professor Jonathan Entin there are a couple of reasons for the explosion of votes. For one, the ease and comfortability of people going to their board of elections and getting their votes recorded. Another possibility, people may fear putting their ballots in the mail. The rules have changed in Ohio this year, and if your mail-in ballot is not received by the close of polls on Nov. 3, 7:30pm, it will not be counted. In the past there was a grace period and ballots were still counted days after the elections. That will not happen this year. items.t: ‘Amazed that she’s alive’: 18-year-old driver in ICU after hitting moose on icy road
items.x: ANCHORAGE, Alaska ( KTUU /Gray News) - A mother in Alaska said her 18-year-old daughter is lucky to be alive after hitting a moose Monday night while driving down an icy Anchorage road. “That’s what we’ve been hearing this entire ordeal, from the EMTs to the doctors; they are amazed that she’s alive,” Megan Stone said about her daughter’s crash. According to Stone, the collision occurred when her daughter Autumn was driving home and a moose appeared in the roadway. Stone said she does not believe her daughter had any time to brake. When firefighters arrived, they found a badly damaged vehicle with Autumn trapped inside. It took several crews to cut her out with the Jaws of Life hydraulic rescue tools. Anchorage firefighter Jason Dolph said moose are particularly dangerous when they are hit at highway speeds. “Typically when a car strikes a moose, that moose becomes suspended in the air,” Dolph said. “And when that moose then lands on the vehicle. In this case, it landed on the hood and kind of the windshield and roof area. items.t: Claims line created for North Toledo chemical leak
