items.t: Canned fruit sold at Walmart recalled in several states
items.x: (Gray News) - A voluntary recall over lead concerns has been issued for cans of Walmart fruit cocktail distributed to stores in at least seven states. The Food and Drug Administration said the recall applies to 15-ounce containers of Great Value Fruit Cocktail in Fruit Juice from Concentrate. Where the product was distributed More than 1,830 cases, or approximately 44,000 individual cans, were distributed to Walmart locations in Alabama, Arizona, Louisiana, New Mexico, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wyoming, the FDA said. How to identify the product The product is marked with lot number “6FCB 04 C2263” and a best if used by date of Sept. 1, 2027. Recall details The FDA initiated the recall for “potential contamination with elevated levels of lead” on Oct. 1. It was reclassified as a Class II recall on Oct. 20. According to the FDA, Class II recalls are issued when a product can cause temporary health effects with a remote possibility of serious issues. What customers should do Customers should throw the item away or return it to Walmart.

items.t: 24-year-old deputy killed in crash with coal truck while on duty, sheriff’s office says
items.x: LOGAN COUNTY, W. Va ( WSAZ /Gray News) - A 24-year-old sheriff’s deputy was killed in a crash while responding to a call, authorities said. The Logan County Sheriff’s Department identified the deputy as 24-year-old Caden Mullins. Deputy Mullins’ fiancée was airlifted from the scene of the crash to a hospital. Deputies say Mullins and his fiancée were at a truck-or-treat event on Saturday in the Man area when he received an emergency call from the sheriff’s department. The sheriff’s department says Deputy Caden Mullins, 24, died in the crash. Mullins was on his way to drop his fiancée off and head to the call when the crash occurred around 5 p.m., deputies say. Deputies say the crash happened at the intersection of Rum Creek Road and Route 10 when a coal truck pulled off the road and hit Mullins’ vehicle. Mullins worked for the Charleston Police Department for about a year before joining the Logan County Sheriff’s Department to be closer to family, the department said.

items.t: Woman arrested after 4-year-old found dead in Atlanta townhome
items.x: WASHINGTON, Ga. ( WRDW /Gray News) - A woman was arrested Tuesday morning after a 4-year-old boy was found dead more than an hour away in an Atlanta townhome, authorities said. According to WRDW’s sister station, Atlanta News First , Atlanta police responded to a gated community in the 3500 block of Cardinal Drive SW on Monday night for a welfare check. items.t: Aging Untold: How to spot the early signs of Parkinson’s and when to talk to a doctor

Then, we share how a grieving Michigan family turned heartbreak into hope by helping pair veterans and first responders with lifesaving service dogs. items.t: ‘Breaking Away’ actress Barbara Barrie dies by medically assisted suicide, reports say
items.x: (Gray News) - Barbara Barrie, known for her 1979 role in “Breaking Away,” died Wednesday by medically assisted suicide, according to her daughter in a statement to The New York Times . Barrie was 95. Barrie had been diagnosed with terminal cancer and died in her New York City home, according to her daughter, Jane Harwick. Barrie’s agent, Gary Gersh, said her passing was “medically assisted in accordance with the New York State Medical Aid in Dying Law,” according to USA Today . items.t: Relocation offers on the rise as cities try big cash incentives to attract remote workers

Cumberland, Maryland launched “Choose Cumberland,” a pilot program offering $20,000 to up to 10 people who agree to move to the city. The Appalachian Mountains community, located about 130 miles outside Washington D.C., saw its population decline from over 40,000 to less than 19,000 after several manufacturing companies and other large employers closed their doors starting in the 1970s. “At one time, the population of Cumberland was over 40,000 people,” said Mayor Ray Morriss. Program details and requirements The Cumberland incentive splits the money into two payments : $10,000 in relocation cash $10,000 for a down payment or approved home renovations Recipients must make Cumberland their primary residence for at least five years. “The people we are trying to entice are the people who are bringing their jobs with them,” Morriss said. items.t: Gen Z has more debt than Millennials did at the same age

Ted Rossman, with nonprofit credit counseling agency Money Management International , said the agency has seen a 35% increase in demand from Gen Z clients in the past year. Their debt loads are about 12% higher than they were a year ago. Student loans, high rents and buy now, pay later plans are adding up and leaving many young adults living paycheck to paycheck with little savings. “That’s really showcasing a lot of these early career pressures,” Rossman said. “You have student loans, you have high housing costs. Those household formation years are very expensive, so GenZer’s actually have more debt than Millennials did at the same age, even adjusted for inflation according to TransUnion.” For Gen Z, Rossman said the starting point is the basics: knowing your budget and watching buy now, pay later spending. “It’s very popular among people in their 20’s, but it’s still debt,” Rossman said. “It can work in your favor. items.t: Antidepressants: What to know before you decide
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Feeling low, disconnected or not like yourself for weeks or months is different from a bad day. When it starts to affect sleep, energy or everyday life, it’s time to talk about support and treatment options. For some people, that could include an antidepressant. Start with a conversation with your provider Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said the decision looks different for everyone. “Everybody is individualized so you can just talk with your provider,” Rogers said. Rogers said to recognize whether you’re feeling depressed and to look at signs such as loss of sleep, loss of energy or loss of motivation. Some people might also experience a triggering event that starts a downward spiral, which they can’t pull themself out of, she said. “When your quality of life is being affected, then you might want to look into antidepressant therapy,” Rogers said. Antidepressants are not “happy pills” Rogers cautioned that antidepressants do not take away sadness. “They’re not happy pills. items.t: InvestigateTV+: Tracking the trackers
items.x: ( InvestigateTV ) — As the number of cameras capturing vehicle information multiplies, so do concerns of privacy for everyday people. InvestigateTV+ explores what can happen when the tool is misused and meet one man on a mission to track every police camera in the country. Plus, four-legged companions jump into action to help heal our heroes. We share the recent gift bringing military members support in the form of service animals. Tracking the trackers Flock Safety says its cameras don’t track people. But the company’s own training videos show police using the system to track suspects “from location to location to location.” And some of its cameras are designed to follow people as they walk. “And they quite literally use AI to zoom in and follow you around whether you’re a person of interest or not,” said Benn Jordan , a security researcher who found dozens of Flock cameras streaming openly online. items.t: The barbershop quartet tradition is alive in New Orleans
items.x: NEW ORLEANS ( InvestigateTV ) - On a Mid City evening, a four-part harmony rang out just off Canal Street. The group, Southern Tradition, has been around since 1999. The quartet is a place where a traditional American art form forges a friendship. “The main attribute to be a barbershop quartet singer is to not be embarrassed, just keep going,” said Karl Hansen. Four men with four different careers create one sound. Hansen is a doctor who sings bass. Hansen Eschette is a med tech singing tenor. Joe Jacquat is a civil engineer who sings baritone. Johnnie Oufnac is the only actual barber in this barbershop quartet, singing lead. “Being together for a long time helps us harmonize and understand where the other person is going,” Hansen said. Barbershop quartets have been around for more than a century. Though they can be found all over the world, ties to New Orleans are strong. “It really is the nexus of American music at its most basic level and a lot of it comes from New Orleans,” said Zachary Matherne. items.t: Nearly 11 million people in the U.S. could be living with undiagnosed diabetes
items.x: CHARLOTTE, N.C. ( InvestigateTV ) - Diabetes is the seventh leading cause of death in the United States, the No. 1 cause of kidney disease, and an estimated 40 million people are living with it nationwide. Despite decades of prevention education and major breakthroughs in treatment, doctors say diabetes continues to hit the South especially hard — including North Carolina. It can create serious long-term complications, including coronary artery disease, heart attacks, never damage, and amputations. But many people who have the disease may not know it. The CDC estimates around 11 million live with undiagnosed diabetes. “Every day, almost every hour” battle Andrew Tucker has lived with Type 2 diabetes for nearly two decades. He’s made major lifestyle changes but said managing the disease is still a daily fight. Tucker was diagnosed about 15 years ago, when he was 35. “Yes, for me, it is truly an everyday, almost every hour watching what I do,” Tucker said. Type 2 diabetes develops when the body doesn’t make enough insulin or doesn’t use insulin properly. Doctors say obesity is a major risk factor. items.t: This veteran is using his service dog to regain independence
items.x: ST. LOUIS, Mo. ( InvestigateTV ) - Veteran James Poggi served in the Marine Corps working in aviation. His time in the military led to a lifelong strain on his body, including five back surgeries and a below-the-knee amputation. “You go from being six foot three, 250 pounds and able to travel halfway across the world and do whatever they ask you to do, to being relying on wheelchairs, walkers, mobility devices, things like that, you become a vulnerable person that you never thought you’d be,” Poggi said. Poggi said he was in multiple accidents, hard landings, PT accidents and a car crash. He also developed spinal meningitis. “And that was all while I was active,” he said. To help ease some of the emotional toll, Poggi’s wife, who is also his caregiver, suggested he get a service dog. Service dog provides daily support Poggi got Teddy, a Goldendoodle, who serves as his service dog and daily lifeline. “You never went anywhere without your battle buddy. And he always, always better have your back. And that’s how it is. He’s always got my back,” Poggi said. items.t: FIRST ALERT FORECAST: Sunny today but changes are on the way
items.x: HAZARD, Ky. (WYMT) - We have one more bright, sunny day ahead before the weather pattern slowly begins to change. Halloween weekend is still looking mild and dry, though clouds and rain chances will build as we head into next week. Today will be absolutely sunny, with highs reaching the mid to upper 70s. That is still about 10 degrees above average for this time of year, making it another great afternoon to get outside and enjoy the warm fall weather. Tonight will remain clear, with lows dipping into the mid 40s. It will be a comfortable, quiet night before cloud cover begins to gradually increase. Tomorrow will bring a little more cloud cover, with highs in the low to mid 70s. It will still be a mild and pleasant day, but it will signal the start of a shift toward a more unsettled pattern. The Halloween weekend ahead looks fairly pleasant, dry, and warmer than average. Clouds will continue to build toward next week, when rain chances and a few cold fronts are expected to move through the region.

Bill Lee said he suspects Christa Pike’s sentence will remain the same following her failed execution last month, unless the courts determine otherwise. Lee’s comments on Pike Lee was asked Wednesday whether the state will try to execute Pike again or if he will commute her sentence to life in prison. “As it related to a particular individual like Christa Pike and her crime, she’s still incarcerated under the laws of the state of Tennessee,” Lee said. “I suspect her sentence will be the same as before unless determined otherwise by the courts.” Pike’s condition Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer. In September, Pike survived two doses of the lethal injection drug. The execution attempt failed. Pike is back in prison after spending days in the hospital. She is now able to speak in full sentences and walk on her own. Pike survived two doses of the lethal injection drug.(DEPARTMENT OF EMERGENCY COMMUNICATIONS, TENNESSEE DEPARTMENT OF CORRECTION, ASSOCIATED PRESS) Executions paused, commissioner resigns Lee has paused executions through the end of the year to determine what went wrong in Pike’s attempt.

items.t: Economist explains how the ‘K-shaped economy’ is impacting the midterms
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - As voters prepare to head to the polls for the midterm elections, a conflicting economic sentiment is once again emerging on the campaign trail. “Voters reflect the perception of the cost of living as they experienced, as opposed to what is in the data,” said Alessandro Rebucci, an economics professor at Johns Hopkins Carey Business School. “In the data, you have an economy that is very strong as a whole. How that pie is distributed affects how a large segment of the population and the voters are feeling about the economy right now.” The contradiction has been described by many economists recently, as the “k-shaped” economy, using a graph to depict how high-income earners and asset owners are doing compared to middle and lower-income earners. “To be concrete, the wealthiest households are presumed to spend much more than the lowest ones, not only in absolute terms, which is obvious, but also as a share of their income and in their wealth,” Rebucci said. Families seek answers Marsha Miniard said the search for answers is personal. She is now on hospice, alert but weak, and has lived well past that timeline. items.t: Kentucky joins 33 other states in settlement with crypto kiosk operator
items.x: FRANKFORT, Ky. (WKYT) - Gov. Andy Beshear announced Wednesday that Kentucky has joined 33 other states in a $2.5 million settlement with Coin-Me, a cryptocurrency money transmitter and kiosk operator. Kentucky’s share of the settlement is just under $63,000. The company is accused of violating anti-money laundering and bank secrecy laws. The laws are designed to stop criminals from moving money. Under the settlement, Coin-Me must hire an independent consultant to fix its compliance program. The company also must shut down its virtual currency kiosks by Jan. 1 or face another $4 million in penalties.

items.t: Powell County Schools investigating security concern at high school
items.x: POWELL COUNTY, Ky. (WKYT) - Powell County Schools said late Wednesday that it is investigating a security threat at the district’s high school. Two students at Powell County High School said that they heard another student say, “Don’t come to school tomorrow. It won’t be a good idea,” according to a district news release. After district officials gathered information and reviewed video footage, the student who allegedly made the comment was identified. The student denied any wrongdoing when confronted by district officials, but has been asked to stay home pending an investigation by local law enforcement. The district asks anyone with information about the incident to submit a form that can be found here .

The sheriff’s office and FBI conducted a joint investigation on Friday at the teen’s home after investigators learned he was having online conversations with members and supporters of the Islamic State group, also known as ISIS. Investigators say the teen asked for help to build drones and explosives to attack people at an unknown location. Authorities spoke with the 15-year-old’s parents, who allowed them to search the boy’s phone. They reportedly found files containing instructions for making explosive devices and chemical compounds, as well as ISIS propaganda. On Monday, investigators searched the teen’s home with his parents’ consent after they revealed the information found on the phone. Inside, they found two jars in his bedroom. items.t: Two people charged with meth trafficking, fentanyl possession
items.x: PIKE COUNTY, Ky. (WYMT) - A Pike County couple faces drug trafficking charges following a search that uncovered a large quantity of suspected illegal narcotics at an Elkhorn City home. According to Kentucky State Police, troopers and detectives with the Post 9 Street Crimes Unit executed a search warrant on Tuesday at a residence along Mill Mountain Branch as part of an ongoing drug investigation. During the search, investigators seized approximately one pound of suspected meth and 14 grams of suspected fentanyl. Authorities arrested Keshia Adkins, 40, and Jordan Clark, 31, both of Elkhorn City. Both were taken to the Pike County Detention Center. Adkins and Clark were each charged with first-degree trafficking in a controlled substance (meth) and first-degree possession of a controlled substance (fentanyl).

items.t: College professor among 2 found dead in home; suspect in custody, police say
items.x: LORAIN COUNTY, Ohio. ( WOIO /Gray News) - An Ohio college professor and a woman were found shot to death in a home, and a suspect is in custody, according to authorities. Wednesday morning, police responded to the Oberlin College Conservatory lot at 77 E. College St. to assist firefighters with a vehicle smoking and possibly on fire. When crews arrived, they tried to find the registered vehicle owner, identified as Daniel Jones, 31, to conduct a welfare check. When officers arrived at Jones’ home to check on his family, they found the victims dead inside the home. Pipo Nguyen-Duy, a professor of studio art and photography at Oberlin College, was found dead on the first floor with an apparent gunshot wound. A woman found dead on the second floor was not immediately identified. She also had an apparent gunshot wound. Jones was located aat bout 10:20 a.m. and taken into custody. Charges are pending. The investigation is ongoing.

items.t: Fact✓Check |Medicaid and rural hospital claims from Estill County debate
items.x: ESTILL COUNTY, Ky. (WKYT) - Voters at Tuesday night’s debate in Estill County heard different warnings about Medicaid and rural hospitals. A review of the big numbers cited by candidates Dembo and Alvarado found some are supported by data and others are estimates or disputed. Claim on Medicaid coverage loss Dembo said, “We have a law that’s about to go into effect in 2027 that could kick 200,000 Kentuckians off their Medicaid.” State and federal health records show Kentucky relies heavily on Medicaid. The impact of any future law depends on how work requirements and eligibility rules are written, and on how many people lose coverage versus move to other insurance. Estimates of exactly 200,000 people losing Medicaid are projections, not a final count. Claim on Medicaid use in the district Dembo also said, “Twenty-six percent of us in this district rely on Medicaid. Fifty percent here in Estill County.” County-by-county data shows rural areas such as Estill have high Medicaid use, especially for children, people with disabilities and nursing home care. items.t: International fugitive sentenced for one of the largest health care fraud schemes in U.S. history
items.x: COLUMBIA, S.C. ( WIS /Gray News) - A man whom federal prosecutors called the architect of one of the largest health care fraud schemes in U.S. history was sentenced Monday. Herbert Kimble was sentenced to 20 years’ imprisonment with three years of court-ordered supervision. He was also ordered to pay more than $199 million in restitution to Medicare and forfeit more than $195 million in what prosecutors described as “ill-gotten gains.” Kimble pleaded guilty in 2019 to conspiring to commit health care fraud, violate the anti-kickback statute, and defraud the United States in connection with a telemedicine and durable medical equipment scheme involving back, shoulder, wrist, and knee braces. Prosecutors say Kimble ran offshore call centers that recruited elderly Medicare beneficiaries, paid kickbacks to telemedicine companies for signed prescriptions, then sold those orders to medical equipment companies that billed Medicare. Court filings put the intended loss at more than $400 million, with Kimble personally gaining more than $195 million. items.t: For politics, what is an October surprise?
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - An October surprise is an event that could shake up an election, but does it often make the difference? Matt Dallek, a professor of political management at George Washington University, described it as “an event that, at least in theory, has the potential to shake up an election, something that people did not foresee coming that upends the debate.” He said the term dates back to around the 1980 election, when President Jimmy Carter failed to secure the release of American hostages being held in Iran before November 4, 1980, election day. Carter lost to Republican rival Ronald Reagan. Several surprises have occurred in the years since. Surprises can be driven by a campaign or by news events. Examples include Iran-Contra-related indictments in 1992 and the global financial collapse in 2008. Dallek said those surprises likely did not change the outcome of the election that November. “There’s no evidence that they flip a dynamic that was already in place,” Dallek said. “What’s more typical is that an event occurs, it dominates the news cycle and the trend line starts to move further toward the candidate who was already doing well, who was already likely to prevai

items.x: HAZARD, Ky. (WYMT) - One woman is in the hospital after an overnight house fire in Hazard spread to three homes. Hazard Fire Chief Robert Keith said crews got the call around 1:20 a.m. Wednesday. He said the fire started in an abandoned home, spread to an unoccupied house on High Street, then to an occupied home on Broadway. The occupant of that Broadway home is 70-year-old Karen Longworth. Her daughter, April Martin, said Longworth was trapped in her upstairs bedroom, and had to jump to escape. Martin said her mother helped her two dogs escape. One survived, one died. According to her daughter, Longworth has a fractured pelvis, a broken left wrist and five broken ribs. Martin said her mother recently lost her husband to terminal liver cancer in August and was still grieving when she lost her home. As of Wednesday evening, Keith said the fire was burning deep in debris, making it hard to fully extinguish. He said crews will stay on scene for a day or two to keep it under control. Keith said nearby homes and an apartment building on High Street had minor heat damage and parts of the area are still without power because of damage to power lines. items.t: Library says person threw box of cockroaches at a staff member, prompting closure
items.x: TOLEDO, Ohio ( WTVG /Gray News) - A cockroach attack forced the closure of a library in Ohio this week. Surveillance footage was released by the Toledo Lucas County Public Library, appearing to show a person throwing a box of cockroaches at a staff member on Tuesday at the Kent Branch Library. Surveillance footage apparently shows someone throwing a box of cockroaches at a library employee in Ohio. (Source: Toledo Lucas County Public Library) A library spokesperson confirmed the throwing of the box of cockroaches at the library worker on Collingwood Blvd. But it wasn’t immediately shared what led up to the cockroach attack. The library was said to have gone into restricted access before closing for the rest of the day for cleanup and remediation. The Kent Branch Library reopened Wednesday. Officials did not say whether anyone would be facing any charges.

items.t: UK sues CVS in federal court, alleges company owes it millions of dollars
items.x: LEXINGTON, Ky. (WKYT) - The University of Kentucky has sued CVS Health Corporation in United States federal court, according to a report by the Lexington Herald-Leader . The suit, which was filed on Tuesday, accuses CVS and its subsidiary companies of civil racketeering, fraud and breach of contract. The university claims in the suit that the company diverted around $41 million in 340B prescription revenue that was supposed to go to its pharmacies over a five-year period, according to the Herald-Leader. The 310B program allows hospitals to buy drugs at prorated rates and then use the savings to assist patients with the cost of care. UK is asking for damages under the RICO Act. CVS has yet to respond to the suit.

items.t: ‘He had a heart for others’: Pastor, friend remember man killed in Lake Cumberland boat crash
items.x: LEXINGTON, Ky. (WKYT) - Eddie Plaster, who died Saturday after a boat collision on Lake Cumberland in Russell County, is being remembered by his pastor and friends for his work helping others. Plaster’s body was recovered from the lake Tuesday afternoon. He died after officials say another boat collided with the boat he and another person were fishing on. After several days of searching, he was found in 117 feet of water. An autopsy will determine his cause of death. ‘Fisher of men’ Plaster was a fisherman. His pastor said he was literally a “fisher of men,” reaching people struggling with addiction or with life in general. Pat Finley of Grace Baptist Church in Clark County said Plaster understood the people he helped. “Boy, he had a heart for those people. Because he came from that. He knew what they thought. He knew what they were dealing with,” Finley said. “He came from that world, and God had delivered him from all that.” Business, jail ministry and helping others When he was not on the water, people said Plaster ran his business. They also said he was devoted to a jail ministry. People said he helped underprivileged children and people with addictions. Friend Brad Myers said

items.t: Grandmother not indicted in baby’s death after police say she left her in hot car for 8 hours while she worked
items.x: MADISONVILLE, Ky. ( WFIE /Gray News) — A Kentucky doctor who accidentally left her grandchild unattended in a hot car for about eight hours will not be indicted for the baby’s death. Madisonville police said 10-month-old Scottie Crowell died in August . On Tuesday, a grand jury found there was insufficient probable cause for an indictment. Police said Scottie’s grandmother picked her up in the morning of Aug. 13 and was supposed to take her to daycare. She forgot the child was in the car and went to work, police said. She arrived at Owensboro Health Multi-Care, where she works as a doctor, around 8 a.m. The baby’s father called his wife after trying to pick up Scottie from daycare, but the child was not there. The baby’s mother called the grandmother at work, and the grandmother ran outside and saw Scottie was still in the vehicle around 4 p.m., police said. After 911 was called, first responders tried to administer lifesaving measures, but the baby died. “I would ask that you keep the infant’s parents and family in your thoughts and prayers as they continue to grieve and process this unimaginable loss,” said Commonwealth’s Attorney Hannah Kington-Jarvis.

items.t: Man dies following single-vehicle crash
items.x: JOHNSON, Ky. (WYMT) - A man is dead following a single-vehicle crash in Johnson County early Wednesday morning. Paintsville Police identified the victim as Joshua Hogsten, 37. Officers say the crash happened around 2:30 a.m. on Kentucky Route 321. Police say Hogsten’s vehicle struck a rock cliff at a high rate of speed before flipping multiple times. He was taken to Paintsville ARH, where he was pronounced dead.

items.t: Clocks fall back Nov. 1: Sleep specialist on health impacts and how to adjust
items.x: LEXINGTON, Ky. (WKYT) - Daylight Saving Time ends on Nov. 1, so clocks will be set back an hour. While many will welcome an extra hour of sleep on Halloween night, changing the clocks twice a year carries health impacts. Fall back easier than spring forward Subhendu Rath is an assistant professor in the Department of Neurology and Internal Medicine at UK. As a Sleep Medicine Specialist, Dr. Rath deals extensively with sleep disorders. Rath says adjusting in the fall is easier on the body than springing forward in March, but issues remain. “People will still experience earlier waking, and that can be associated with fatigue or changes in their sleep routine,” Rath said. “So this can lead to temporary sleep disruption, daytime fatigue, with associated reduced concentration, irritability.” Circadian rhythm and morning light The disruption ties to the circadian rhythm. “That regulates sleep, alertness, and along with it also regulates our body temperature, several hormones,” explained Rath. “Sunlight, especially the early morning light, is one of the strongest signals that keeps it synchronized. Now, changing the clock does not instantly reset our internal biological rhythm. So these c

items.t: Widow searches for lost wedding ring when husband dies 3 days after getting married in Las Vegas
items.x: LAS VEGAS ( KVVU /Gray News) — A South Dakota woman is asking for help finding the wedding ring her husband lost in Las Vegas the night they married. Tammy Bishop and Will Mulroy were married Oct. 20 at the Viva Las Vegas Chapel. Bishop said they celebrated on a party bus and toured the Strip. At a bar, though, she says Mulroy looked down and realized his ring was gone. “We got to a bar. He looked down and his band was gone. He lost it. He started crying,” Bishop said. According to Bishop, he told her the ring was two sizes too big because he had lost weight. She said the ring may have slid off on the bus or while he moved into his wheelchair. It may also have come off while he rolled down the Strip. “We backtracked our steps. We told the bus driver. We had everyone looking. We couldn’t find it,” she said. The next day, she joked with him: “You didn’t even have your ring on for 24 hours and you lost it.” Everyone laughed, she said. “I said it’s not a big deal; we will buy you a new one, but now that he is gone it is a big deal to me,” Bishop said. items.t: Barr, Booker outline positions on costs, surveillance and child safety in Kentucky Senate race

items.t: ‘I miss her like crazy’: Loved ones remembering post office worker hit and killed by car
items.x: FORT THOMAS, Ky. ( WXIX /Gray News) - Loved ones and a Kentucky community are mourning a post office worker who was hit and killed by a car while walking earlier this month. Marchelle Bertram worked at the front desk of the Fort Thomas Post Office for years, helping people who came in. Sadly, she lost her life in a collision in Bellevue on Oct. 15. Her daughter, Whitney Bertram, said she is remembering her mother while seeing a large amount of support from the community following her death. “There are so many people I don’t know whose lives she’s touched and affected,” Whitney Bertram said. The crash occurred while Marchelle Bertram was walking on Memorial Parkway near her home. Her daughter said she rushed to the hospital after learning her mother had been hit by a vehicle. “Given the grave amount of injuries she sustained, there was no way she was going to survive,” she said. Marchelle Bertram died at the hospital. Whitney Bertram said the driver stayed at the scene and believes the crash was an accident. “I miss her like crazy; I try not to think about it too hard because I’ll break down,” she said. items.t: Wolfe Co. woman indicted for taking funds from animal shelter
items.x: FRANKFORT, Ky. (WYMT) - One Campton woman was indicted after she was accused of taking more than $110,000 from an animal shelter. In a news release from Attorney General Russell Coleman’s office, a grand jury indicted Pam Pilgrim, 74, on one count of Theft by Unlawful Taking - more than $10,000 but less than $1,000,000. The indictment states that the incident happened between January 2019 and July 2024. The theft was uncovered during a state audit, Attorney General Russell Coleman said. Pilgrim was the treasurer of the Wolfe Co. Animal Shelter during that period. She was charged with theft of $112,144.58. Following Pilgrim’s arraignment on Wednesday, the judge ordered her to not act as treasurer on any boards. She is scheduled to return to court on February 18, 2027.

items.t: Ernie Johnson announces this will be his final season on ‘Inside The NBA’
items.x: (Gray News) - Ernie Johnson announced he will be stepping down as host of “Inside the NBA” at the end of the season. The Sports Broadcasting Hall of Famer took to social media on Wednesday to explain his decision to step away, saying, “It’s just time.” Johnson, 70, stated that he would not be retiring, but cutting back. “This is by no means the end. It’s just a turning of the page,” Johnson said. “And I’ll forever cherish every chapter we have written with ‘Inside the NBA.’” Johnson said he plans to continue to work, including covering the NCAA men’s basketball tournament for CBS and Turner Sports. The six-time Sports Emmy Award winner acknowledged that he has dealt with heart issues in recent years, but that isn’t the reason he’s stepping away from the show. “I just want to slow down a bit,” he added in his social media post. Johnson joined Turner Sports in 1989 and has hosted “Inside the NBA” since 1990. He thanked his TNT Sports and ESPN crews for their support over the years, as well as the viewers. “I just want to say thanks to you. Thanks for your loyalty, for your love, for your support. And on this day, for your understanding,” Johnson said.

items.t: Police department closes its investigation into Hayden Panettiere’s death
items.x: GREENVILLE, S.C. ( WHNS /Gray News) - The Greenville Police Department said it has officially closed its investigation into the death of Hayden Panettiere. Police said Panettiere’s death has been ruled accidental based on the medical examiner’s determination and the findings of the investigation. Panettiere, 36, died from an accidental overdose involving multiple prescription medications and fentanyl, according to findings previously released by the Greenville County Coroner’s Office. Toxicology testing determined the cause of death to be the toxic effects of fentanyl, 4-ANPP, alprazolam, methocarbamol and quetiapine. An autopsy showed no signs of contributing trauma. On Aug. 16, Panettiere was found unresponsive inside an apartment in Greenville, where she had been temporarily staying. Dispatchers received a 911 call reporting a woman in cardiac arrest at approximately 1:51 p.m. She was pronounced dead at 2:32 p.m. Her on-and-off boyfriend Brian Hickerson and his brother Zach Hickerson were at the apartment where she died. items.t: Trump says US will beat China in AI as technology emerges
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Artificial intelligence has emerged as the critical sticking point between the U.S. and China. President Donald Trump, who has named it “super intelligence,” insists the U.S. will beat China in the AI competition. Trump said while campaigning for president that tariffs would form the crux of the bilateral relationship. The U.S. and China, the world’s two largest economies, have been engaged in a trade war during both of Trump’s terms. Speaking Sept. 13 in Ireland, Trump said the U.S. is leading China in AI. “We’re leading China in AI, we’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins,” Trump said. During a state visit to Beijing in May, Trump praised Chinese President Xi Jinping. “And it’s to me an honor. We’ve had a fantastic relationship. We’ve gotten along. When they were difficulties, we worked it out,” Trump said. Trump hosted Xi at the White House in September for a state visit. He touted what he called “the tremendous strides” he and Xi had already made on national security, trade and technology. ( KPHO /Gray News) - A man lost thousands of dollars after getting a call that appeared to come from his father’s phone number, with a stranger claiming his parents were being held at gunpoint. Curtis Indyke was asleep around 11:30 p.m. on Oct. 21 when he got a call that appeared to be from his dad, who lives in Virginia. Indyke lives in Arizona. “I answer the phone and it’s not my dad. It’s some other male saying he has my parents basically at gunpoint,” Indyke said. The caller told him to pay or his parents would be shot. While still on the phone, Indyke said he texted 911 to report his parents were being held hostage in Virginia. The person who claimed to be holding Indyke’s parents hostage continued making threats. In a panic, Indyke sent more than $4,000 through Apple Pay to two separate phone numbers. “And they also wanted $1,000 worth of crypto gift cards, which I’ve never even heard of. I’m in IT and I’ve never even heard of them,” Indyke said. Indyke said his bank blocked that purchase. items.t: 8-month-old dies after left alone in running bathtub, police say
items.x: STERLING, Va. (Gray News) - A Virginia woman was arrested after her 8-month-old died after being left unattended in a bathtub, according to authorities. Rosellena Pisani, 30, was arrested and charged with homicide, two counts of child abuse and three counts of child endangerment, a press release said. On Sept. 12, emergency medical personnel and sheriff’s deputies responded to the residence after receiving a call about an unresponsive infant. Investigators determined the baby had been left unsupervised in a bathtub with the water running. Three children, ranging in age from 8 months to 8 years old, were at home during the incident, according to police. Loudoun County Sheriff Mike Chapman called the baby’s death heartbreaking, saying caregivers have a fundamental duty to protect children. He added investigators remain committed to seeking justice in the case.

items.t: Missing 7-year-old, pregnant mother both found safe
items.x: OVERLAND, Mo. ( KMOV /Gray News) — Officials in Missouri said a missing 7-year-old boy and his pregnant mother were found safe Wednesday. The Missouri State Highway Patrol previously issued an Endangered Person Advisory for Dylan Fernando Zendejas-Gonzalez, 7. Dylan was last seen leaving his home in Overland, near St. Louis, with his mother, Maria Guadalupe Gonzalez-Sanchez, 28. The two were last seen around 1:30 p.m. Sunday. Officials were concerned after personal belongings were left behind at their home. On Wednesday, the Overland Police Department said in a Facebook post that the two were found safe.

( WDRB/WAVE /Gray News) — The sister of a man accused of threatening a girl with a gun to get in his car said that the whole thing was a “huge misunderstanding.” The incident happened on Friday in an Amish community in Salem, Indiana. Probable cause documents said 53-year-old Jeffrey Mauck went up to a girl outside her home and asked if her family sold any eggs. The girl told police that she said no and walked away. The Washington County Sheriff’s Department said Mauck then grabbed her and threatened her with a gun, telling her to get in his car. Officials said the girl’s family heard her screaming and came to the rescue. Court documents said that the girl’s father and his sons were able to restrain Mauck while waiting for the police to arrive. One of the responding officers said he found a pair of black handcuffs lying on the ground underneath Mauck and could smell what he believed to be the odor of alcohol coming from Mauck. Court documents said Mauck admitted to having been drinking. A chemical test determined that Mauck had a blood alcohol content of .292. items.t: Aging Untold: Fat-free doesn’t always mean healthy
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — On this episode of Aging Untold , we separate facts from fiction on “fat-free” foods to help you protect your heart and make healthier grocery choices. Then, National Alliance for Caregiving CEO Jason Resendez joins us to discuss the mounting pressures facing the sandwich generation and policy solutions offering caregiver relief. Plus, we meet the “Flower Buds,” an inspiring volunteer group in Kentucky that rescues discarded blooms to deliver hope and comfort across its community. Fat-free doesn’t always mean healthy: What to look for on food labels The “fat-free” option at the grocery store is not always the healthy option. Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said the label can be misleading. “So if they’re removing the fat, they had to replace it with something else. So you have to look at the ingredients and look at the packaging,” she said. Rogers said she used to find all the fat categories confusing, so she created a simple way to sort them. items.t: Man facing charges after being accused of speeding with infant inside vehicle
items.x: FLOYD COUNTY, Ky. (WYMT) - A Pike County man was arrested after deputies say he was driving more than 100 mph on U.S. 23 with an 8-month-old in the car. According to deputies with the Floyd County Sheriff’s Department, a deputy was stationary in the median of U.S. 23 in front of Tim Short Honda on Monday, Oct. 26, when he saw a black Toyota Camry weave between two vehicles. The deputy recorded the car at 104 mph in a 55 mph zone. After activating lights and sirens, the deputy says the car accelerated to about 105 mph before stopping near a bridge in the Tram community. The driver was identified as 20-year-old Zachary Crider, 20, of Coal Run. The deputy says Crider told him he did not realize how fast he was going, and said he had been arguing with his wife and texting her. During the stop, the deputy found an approximately 8-month-old infant in the back seat, properly restrained in a child safety seat, according to the citation. Crider was arrested and taken to the Floyd County Jail. He faces charges of speeding 26 mph or more over the limit, second-degree wanton endangerment, texting while driving and reckless driving.

items.t: Parents say students were forced to get off school bus and walk 3 miles home on dangerous roads

( WTVA /Gray News) — Parents in Mississippi are demanding answers after they said their 11-year-old daughter’s school bus driver told her to get off the bus and walk miles home. items.t: Estill Co. elementary PE teacher arrested on domestic violence charges
items.x: ESTILL COUNTY, Ky. (WKYT) -A physical education teacher at Estill Springs Elementary School has been placed on administrative leave following his arrest on domestic violence-related charges. The Estill County Board of Education confirmed Joseph Smith was arrested Tuesday evening by Kentucky State Police in Madison County. He is charged with fourth-degree assault - domestic violence, stalking and second-degree unlawful imprisonment. items.t: Crews battle overnight Hazard house fire that spread to 3 homes
items.x: HAZARD, Ky. (WYMT/WKYT) - Firefighters spent the overnight hours battling a house fire that spread to three homes, forcing one person to jump from a second story to escape. Crews were called to the scene around 1:20 a.m. Wednesday. Firefighters say it started in an abandoned home then spread to an unoccupied house on high street before spreading to an occupied home on Broadway behind it. One person was trapped upstairs and had to jump to get out, according to Chief Robert Keith with the Hazard Fire Department. Keith says the fire is burning deep in debris, so crews will stay on scene for a day or two to keep it under control. Nearby homes had minor heat damage and parts of the area are still without power because of damage to power lines.

items.t: Meet the volunteers who bring flowers from weddings and funerals to hospice patients
items.x: LOUISVILLE, Ky. ( Aging Untold ) — Inside Crescent Hill Baptist Church in Louisville, a group of volunteers gathers each week surrounded by color, creativity and collaboration. They call themselves the Flower Buds. From events to those in need The Flower Buds take donated flowers from weddings, funerals, wholesalers, supermarkets, florists, galas, banquets and other community events. They cut, clean and arrange the blooms into vases, then deliver them to nursing homes, the VA hospital, assisted living facilities and shelters. “Amazingly gifted with so many flowers from places like Kroger who have overbought and can’t sell them, and they allow us to pick them up and then bring them here, and then we cut them, clean them and vase them. Then we take them to nursing homes, the VA hospital, assisted living facilities,” Jodie Raible, a Flower Buds volunteer, said. The group sends out about 100 vases every week. “I take flowers to Up for Women and Children, it’s a day homeless shelter for women,” Stephanie Mullins, a Flower Buds volunteer, said. items.t: Illegal moonshine distillery explodes, catches fire in mountains, officials say
items.x: WILKES COUNTY, N.C. ( WBTV /Gray News) - An explosion at an illegal moonshine distillery sparked a fire in the North Carolina mountains on Monday, according to authorities. Special agents from North Carolina’s Alcohol Law Enforcement Division were called to investigate the explosion in Wilkes County, North Carolina. Agents found an active 200-gallon illegal distillery. They seized about 1,800 gallons of mash, which is used to make moonshine, and 161 gallons of illegal moonshine. North Carolina officials shared photos showing the charred inside of a metal building. Distilling equipment was also damaged. Billy Ray Anderson, 69, was arrested and charged with manufacturing a non-taxpaid alcoholic beverage, possession for sale of a non-taxpaid alcoholic beverage, possession of a non-taxpaid alcoholic beverage, possession of distillery equipment, possession of distillery ingredients and allowing property to be used for the manufacture of a non-taxpaid alcoholic beverage. Moonshine is believed to have originated in North Carolina and was once an important source of income, particularly for rural residents.

items.t: Some packaged salads recalled for undeclared allergens
items.x: (Gray News) - Packaged salads produced by Taylor Farms have been recalled due to an undeclared allergen. According to the Food and Drug Administration, Taylor Farms is recalling its H-E-B Backyard BBQ Chop Salad because it may contain undeclared soy and tree nuts, specifically almonds. “People who have sensitivity or allergy to soy and tree nuts (almonds) may be at risk of a serious adverse reaction if they consume this product,” an FDA press release said. So far there have not been any illnesses or “adverse reactions” reported in connection with the recall. The salads were sold in H-E-B stores across Texas. They can be identified by their UPC code, 041220300457, and their best-by date, Oct. 30, 2026. Customers are asked not to eat the recalled salads and to throw them away or return them to the store for a refund.

items.t: Laurel Co. officials announce burn ban
items.x: LAUREL COUNTY, Ky. (WKYT) - The Laurel County Fire Department announced a county-wide burn ban on Oct. 28. According to David Westerfield, the Laurel County Judge Executive, a fire hazard period exists, and an open burning ban will be in place until Laurel County receives enough rainfall to mitigate the hazard risk. This applies to all open burning in the county.

items.x: SEDONA, Ariz. ( Aging Untold ) — The crystal and gemstone industry is booming, fueled in part by social media, but experts warn buyers to be cautious of fake products flooding the market. Jamie Inglett, who owns a crystal shop in Sedona, said consumers can find fake crystals in stores and at gem shows. “As a consumer you really kind of have to do your own research,” Inglett said. Growing popularity drives demand The crystal craze has exploded online, with #crystals generating 20 billion views on TikTok. Inglett has built up 215,106 Instagram followers and opened a physical storefront in Sedona after finding success online. “You don’t have to believe in crystal healing or crystal energy to appreciate their beauty,” Inglett said. What to know about fake crystals Shannon Wimberly, a crystal collector for several years, said she has encountered fake crystals and now scrutinizes purchases more carefully. “I absolutely know I’ve run into getting fake ones, so I started scrutinizing other things more and more,” Wimberly said. items.t: Caregiver advocate shares 3 policies that could help family caregivers
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — More than 60 million Americans are family caregivers, balancing work, kids and care for an aging parent or loved one. Jason Resendez, president and CEO of the National Alliance for Caregiving, recently testified before the U.S. Senate Special Committee on Aging. He joined gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck to talk through the solutions he presented. The three policies he brought to lawmakers Resendez said the National Alliance for Caregiving is championing changes “to address so many of the pain points that family caregivers face every day.” 1) Older Americans Act funding He said one priority is reauthorization and funding of the Older Americans Act. Resendez said the law provides dollars for state Area Agencies on Aging to deliver services for older adults, such as Meals on Wheels and caregiver support. “One of the only federal line items for caregiving comes through the Older Americans Act, and it’s called the National Family Caregiver Support Program,” Resendez said. He said the program funds respite, which gives caregivers the chance to take breaks. It also funds training, education and outreach, so family caregivers have peer support and someone to turn to when na

items.t: Long-term care costs rose about 50% in five years, report finds
items.x: ( InvestigateTV ) — The cost of long-term care jumped nearly 50% in five years, while income for older households rose just 22%, according to a new AARP report . The report found long-term services and supports are becoming even less affordable for middle-class Americans. Alan Weil, senior vice president for public policy at AARP, said the gap is the most important finding. “Between 2019 and 2024, a five-year period, the cost of most long-term care services went up about 50%, but the incomes for older households only went up by about 22%,” Weil said. “So the gap between what people can afford and what it costs has grown.” The AARP also looked at what different types of care cost. Weil said the more skilled the service, the higher the price. “If you need someone to come in and help you prepare food, that’s less expensive than if you need someone to come in and provide nursing-level care,” Weil said. “Although I’ll also say that we’ve learned that a lot of caregivers are being forced to provide nursing care that they can’t afford to pay someone else to do, even though they’ve never been trained in nursing. So that’s where the burden falls back on the family.” The financial burden oft

items.t: Campton residents urged to conserve water
items.x: CAMPTON, Ky. (WKYT) - Officials in Campton are urging people to conserve water due to depleted levels. According to officials, the lack of rainfall over the past two months has “drastically depleted” water levels. Officials said they have been working closely with the Division of Water since January and monitoring water levels. “This has to be a community effort,” officials said. “Reduce shower times, do not leave water running when brushing teeth, only run dishwashers when they are filled to capacity, check for leaks around the home, limit hot tub fills, etc.” Officials said they have been approved for funding for a waterline from Wellington, but it will take time for funds to be released. “We continue to wait for upgrades to be completed on Lee Co Waterplant and pump stations in order to receive water from their side,” officials said. “In the meantime, we can continue to take conservation measures to slow our depletion.” Low water levels amid high tourism It comes at the tail end of tourist season in Eastern Kentucky. “I don’t think anyone thought that the Red River Gorge area would be as popular as it is,” said Cyndi Tapley, manager of the Red River Gorge Inn. “With all the Airb

items.t: Butter sold in 10 states recalled over possible yeast, mold and E. coli contamination
items.x: (Gray News) - Butter is being recalled because it might be contaminated with yeast, mold and E. coli, according to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration. More than 1,300 cases of Miyoko’s Creamery European Style Salted Plant Milk Butter have been recalled in Connecticut, Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Illinois, Indiana, Maryland, New Jersey, New Hampshire and Wisconsin. The recalled butter has lot code 07871 and a best-by date of Nov. 5, 2026. If you have the butter, you should not eat it, but the recall notice did not give further information about refunds.

items.t: She was born with eight fingers on one hand. Her family traveled to America for the surgery
items.x: ST. LOUIS, Mo. ( InvestigateTV ) - A family traveled from Turkey to St. Louis for their daughter’s surgery to treat a rare condition affecting fewer than 100 people worldwide. Elisa, an 18-month-old, was born with eight fingers on her left hand. She was diagnosed with Ulnar Dimelia, also known as Mirror Hand Syndrome. “Mirror Hand is incredibly uncommon, and even surgeons like myself who take care of a great deal of kids almost never see this in their career. So, it’s really uncommon. Numbers are hard to come by, but one in a million or less is probably about right,” said Dr. Charles Goldfarb, Chief of Orthopedic Surgery at St. Louis Children’s Hospital. The condition leaves patients without a radius bone. This means significant limitations in wrist and elbow motion and preserved shoulder movements. “From the very beginning, he was really warm, genuine, and gave us a lot of hope. Honestly, the trust and support he gave us played a huge role in our decision to come to St. Louis,” said Emircan Buga, Elisa’s father. items.t: Officials working to expand foster care for children in America, here’s how
items.x: NASHVILLE, Tenn. ( InvestigateTV ) - Kids sleeping in shelters, bussed between hotels, and overnights in office buildings. That’s the reality for many foster children in America. For every 100 children in foster care, federal data shows that only 57 licenses homes are available. In an effort to close that gap, the federal government launched a campaign in November 2025 called “A Home for Every Child.” “When we launched this, we offered states the choice: if they joined the Home for Every Child campaign, they would get administrative relief,” said Alex Adams, assistant secretary for the administration for children and families. “We would get them out of mountains of paperwork so that they could spend more time focused on things that actually improve child welfare outcomes. They would have more time working with kids, more time working with families. Since then, the idea to reinvent systems that recruit and retain foster families has gained nationwide momentum. Millions of dollars in cash rewards are available to the state, territory, or tribal agency with the greatest improvement of its ratio of children to foster homes. items.t: FIRST ALERT FORECAST: You guessed it... Another calm day
items.x: HAZARD, Ky. (WYMT) - We are stuck staying calm and mild as we round out the week, though rain chances will begin to rise as November arrives. Halloween plans are looking dry for now, with more showers expected to move in afterward. Today starts off cloudier, but skies will clear into a sunny afternoon. High temperatures will reach the mid 70s, running about 10 degrees above average for this time of year. Tonight will stay clear and calm, with lows dipping into the mid 40s. It will be another comfortable fall night across the region. Tomorrow will bring more mostly sunny conditions, with highs in the lower 70s. It will remain mild, dry, and great for any outdoor plans. The rest of the week stays fairly quiet, with Halloween trick-or-treating looking likely to stay rain-free. Showers are expected to increase once November arrives, so enjoy the calm stretch while it lasts.

items.t: Son indicted in mother’s death; medical staff say she had feces, insects in hair
items.x: TUSCALOOSA COUNTY, Ala. ( WBRC /Gray News) - A man has been indicted on charges related to the death of his mother in Alabama. Jonathan Chad Simmons faces one count of manslaughter and one count of second-degree elder abuse in the death of his mother, according to Tuscaloosa County court documents obtained by WBRC. The court documents referred to the victim as Jonathan Chad Simmons’ mother, Brenda Hallman Simmons. Deputies found woman unresponsive Tuscaloosa County deputies and medical personnel were called to the 13000 block of Alabama Highway 216 on May 16. Law enforcement found Brenda Hallman Simmons, 76, alive but unresponsive. Brenda Simmons died several days later while receiving medical care. The autopsy revealed she died from sepsis due to complications from multiple open bedsores. Joint investigation begins The Tuscaloosa Violent Crimes Unit and the state medical examiner’s office began a joint investigation after the family and health personnel suspected neglect. According to medical staff at the hospital, Simmons had multiple open wounds and sores on her body and showed signs of not being bathed. She had feces and insects in her hair. items.t: Canned fruit sold at Walmart recalled in several states
items.x: (Gray News) - A voluntary recall over lead concerns has been issued for cans of Walmart fruit cocktail distributed to stores in at least seven states. The Food and Drug Administration said the recall applies to 15-ounce containers of Great Value Fruit Cocktail in Fruit Juice from Concentrate. Where the product was distributed More than 1,830 cases, or approximately 44,000 individual cans, were distributed to Walmart locations in Alabama, Arizona, Louisiana, New Mexico, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wyoming, the FDA said. How to identify the product The product is marked with lot number “6FCB 04 C2263” and a best if used by date of Sept. 1, 2027. Recall details The FDA initiated the recall for “potential contamination with elevated levels of lead” on Oct. 1. It was reclassified as a Class II recall on Oct. 20. According to the FDA, Class II recalls are issued when a product can cause temporary health effects with a remote possibility of serious issues. What customers should do Customers should throw the item away or return it to Walmart.

items.t: Wayne County Board of Education updates Buffalo K-8 school project
items.x: WAYNE COUNTY, W.Va. (WSAZ) - Tuesday night, the Wayne County Board of Education got an update on the new Buffalo K-through-8 school, including a first look at construction photos showing the concrete base is now complete. The estimated overall project cost is around $24 million. “We were fortunate enough to be able to get funding from the state,” Superintendent Todd Alexander said. “They realized the worthiness of that project, and we got a significant amount of funding from the state to make this happen,” the superintendent Todd Alexander said. The project adds a 66,000-square-foot wing to the existing Buffalo Middle School, which was built in 1980. Once complete, the wing will include new amenities for the school including a new cafeteria. The board said the project remains on track, with more updates to come as construction moves forward.

items.t: 24-year-old deputy killed in crash with coal truck while on duty, sheriff’s office says
items.x: LOGAN COUNTY, W. Va ( WSAZ /Gray News) - A 24-year-old sheriff’s deputy was killed in a crash while responding to a call, authorities said. The Logan County Sheriff’s Department identified the deputy as 24-year-old Caden Mullins. Deputy Mullins’ fiancée was airlifted from the scene of the crash to a hospital. Deputies say Mullins and his fiancée were at a truck-or-treat event on Saturday in the Man area when he received an emergency call from the sheriff’s department. The sheriff’s department says Deputy Caden Mullins, 24, died in the crash. Mullins was on his way to drop his fiancée off and head to the call when the crash occurred around 5 p.m., deputies say. Deputies say the crash happened at the intersection of Rum Creek Road and Route 10 when a coal truck pulled off the road and hit Mullins’ vehicle. Mullins worked for the Charleston Police Department for about a year before joining the Logan County Sheriff’s Department to be closer to family, the department said.

items.t: How the One Big Beautiful Bill Act is impacting the midterms
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Throughout the 2026 midterm election season, candidates have been speaking out about the impacts of the GOP’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act. “With our Republican Congress, I signed a great, big, beautiful bill delivering the largest tax cuts in American history,” President Donald Trump said, at a midterm rally in Corpus Christi on Tuesday. The law, that was signed by the president in July 2025, implemented several tax breaks for Americans and cut some social service programs. Derrick Van Ordern, R-Wis, at the GOP’s midterm convention in September. But George Washington University Professor Dr. Todd Belt said that the law is not making much of a difference for voters right now because of affordability concerns that are plaguing many people. “That’s why affordability is the number one watchword,” he said. “Gasoline prices, grocery prices, health care, child care, all these things we’re hearing from voters who are saying that they just can’t make ends meet, whether they got a litt

items.t: WSAZ’s own honored in 2026 class of West Virginia Broadcasting Hall of Fame
items.x: HUNTINGTON, W.Va. (WSAZ) - The West Virginia Broadcasting Hall of Fame held its 2026 induction ceremony at the Museum of Radio and Technology on Tuesday. WSAZ’s Susan Nicholas was honored, along with six other inductees. Joining Nicholas in the class of 2026 are: Alan Dye Jim Damron Will Shumate Dave Allen Michele Crist Randy Yohe The hall’s chairman, Thomas Resler, said those honored offer so much to the communities around them. “It’s important in the fact that we recognize the people that have such an effect on our lives,” Resler said. “They entertain us, they bring us the news, it connects our community.” Congratulations to everyone inducted this year!

items.t: NASA leaders visit Morehead State space science center
items.x: LEXINGTON, Ky. (WKYT) - NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman, NASA astronaut Stephen Bowen and U.S. Rep. Hal Rogers visited Morehead State University to highlight the university’s Space Science Center and its partnership with NASA in preparing the next generation of scientists and engineers. Morehead State leaders welcomed the officials to campus. After speaking with faculty, staff and students, the three took a guided tour of the Space Science Center. Isaacman said the impact of Morehead State students on moon exploration begins now. “Students like right here at Morehead are going to be able to touch hardware that will make their way to the moon in the next couple of years, and it doesn’t have to be perfect. It’s not a human-rated mission at all. It’s an opportunity to learn what does and doesn’t work and roll into the next, so when they do graduate, they can put their hands on the hardware that might be taking astronauts to the moon or maybe even Mars,” Isaacman said. During the event, Rogers presented $7.5 million in federal funding for Morehead State’s space science program.

items.t: Couple charged after 4 children removed from ‘deplorable conditions’, police say

The home also had little to no edible food inside, officers said. According to the complaint, the floors were covered in dirty clothes, trash, animal feces, and debris. items.t: Son accused of stealing from dead mother for months while she decomposed in bed
items.x: PAINTSVILLE, Ky. (WYMT) - A man is in jail after Paintsville police said he failed to report his mother’s death for several months while benefiting from her bank account. Last week, Paintsville Police said they found the body of Patty Carroll in the bed of her Paintsville home. Her son, John Carroll, was her sole caregiver and was unaccounted for after a DUI crash days before, police said. “He let her lay there and decompose,” Preston said. Investigators said the Carrolls kept to themselves in the community. They said the last time anyone they interviewed saw Patty Carroll- who was elderly and diagnosed with dementia- was in June. They are still waiting on a medical examiner’s determination of when she died and how. Preston said investigators learned John Carroll had been taking money out of his mother’s bank account, which they believe was a motive for not telling anyone she was dead. “We’re also working with federal agencies, where she drew social security,” Preston said. John Carroll was arrested Monday at the bar of a Pikeville restaurant, according to Paintsville Public Safety Director Darrell Preston. items.t: Woman arrested after 4-year-old found dead in Atlanta townhome
items.x: WASHINGTON, Ga. ( WRDW /Gray News) - A woman was arrested Tuesday morning after a 4-year-old boy was found dead more than an hour away in an Atlanta townhome, authorities said. Wilkes County Sheriff Darrell Powers said Jasmaine Smoak was arrested and booked into the Wilkes County Detention Center. According to WRDW’s sister station, Atlanta News First , Atlanta police responded to a gated community in the 3500 block of Cardinal Drive SW on Monday night for a welfare check. Officers forced their way into the home “based on information received during the welfare check,” Atlanta police said. Once inside, officers found the child dead. Emergency personnel attempted lifesaving measures but were unsuccessful, police said. Powers said deputies worked closely with Atlanta homicide detectives to locate Smoak using license plate reader technology. Smoak is charged with second-degree cruelty to children and concealing the death of another. Atlanta police said Smoak is a friend of the child’s mother. The circumstances surrounding the boy’s death remain unclear.

items.t: Appalachian Arts Alliance raises more than $10,000 on Radio Day
items.x: HAZARD, Ky. (WYMT) - The Appalachian Arts Alliance held its annual Radio Day at WSGS on Tuesday to raise money for its projects. More than $10,000 was raised, according to WSGS. The Radio Day fundraiser at the downtown studios gave people a way to donate in person, over the phone or online. The Appalachian Arts Alliance is a nonprofit. Donations help cover costs that most people do not see. “That goes right into our operating fund. That helps us pay for our electricity, that helps us pay for our water, that helps us pay for salaries and benefits. You know, we got a lot of grant funding, but grant funding has to be distributed a specific way, and this is kind of money for operations,” said Luke Davis, director of operations for the Appalachian Arts Alliance. The alliance funds local art and music lessons, among countless other community initiatives. Contributions for Radio Day have ended, but the alliance accepts donations year-round to grow its reach.

items.t: 18-year-old charged in hate-motivated attack after luring victim through dating app, police say

items.t: Man enters plea in animal cruelty case
items.x: LETCHER COUNTY, Ky. (WYMT) - A Jenkins man pleaded guilty in connection to a shooting incident that occurred earlier this year. Johnny Tinnel was arrested in April when his neighbor accused him of shooting a dog on her property. The incident was caught on video. Tinnel was originally expected to begin a jury trial Monday, but officials with the Jenkins Police Department said he instead pleaded guilty to four counts of wanton endangerment and one count of torturing a dog or cat. Tinnel was arrested following the incident, which happened in April. If accepted at sentencing in December, he will lose his right to own firearms for life. The police department shared a statement Tuesday, saying, “Hopefully, this will go a long way towards restoring peace in that corner of Jenkins.”

items.t: FEMA awards $10.9 million for construction of new Robinson Elementary School
items.x: PERRY COUNTY, Ky. (WYMT) - FEMA has approved a $10.9 million grant to help rebuild a school in Perry County. Robinson Elementary School was destroyed after the July 2022 flood damaged it beyond repair. Jerry Stacy, Perry County Emergency Management Director, said the once in a lifetime disaster prompted a response never seen before. “It was the worst flash flooding event in the state’s history,” Stacy said. “And when you have the kind of disasters, local governments, local entities like our school system, there’s not enough funding to recover from those kinds of impacts.” For longtime staff members, the rebuilding goes beyond the building itself. “The school is the community. It’s such a small community, that’s really what they had. That’s really what held everybody together,” said Michelle Stacy, a 15-year teacher at Robinson Elementary. A site off of KY-80, near the Elk Run subdivision, will be the future campus of Robinson Elementary School. “It’s very important to us that our school still be located in an area that was close to where the old building was, so that it was still part of our community. items.t: Aging Untold: How to spot the early signs of Parkinson’s and when to talk to a doctor
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — On this episode of Aging Untold, we examine the subtle, easily overlooked early warning signs of Parkinson’s disease and discuss when to talk with a physician. Plus, we explore what to consider when starting antidepressants, emphasizing the importance of setting realistic expectations and building a comprehensive support plan. Then, we share how a grieving Michigan family turned heartbreak into hope by helping pair veterans and first responders with lifesaving service dogs. Parkinson’s doesn’t always start with a tremor — here’s what to watch for Parkinson’s disease can start long before a tremor and the subtle changes are easy to miss. Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said the loss of smell, constipation or changes in handwriting can be early signs. By the time tremors appear, Rogers said, significant damage has often already been done. Resources are available for people living with Parkinson’s. Read the full article here. items.t: ‘Amazed that she’s alive’: 18-year-old driver in ICU after hitting moose on icy road
items.x: ANCHORAGE, Alaska ( KTUU /Gray News) - A mother in Alaska said her 18-year-old daughter is lucky to be alive after hitting a moose Monday night while driving down an icy Anchorage road. “That’s what we’ve been hearing this entire ordeal, from the EMTs to the doctors; they are amazed that she’s alive,” Megan Stone said about her daughter’s crash. According to Stone, the collision occurred when her daughter Autumn was driving home and a moose appeared in the roadway. Stone said she does not believe her daughter had any time to brake. When firefighters arrived, they found a badly damaged vehicle with Autumn trapped inside. It took several crews to cut her out with the Jaws of Life hydraulic rescue tools. Anchorage firefighter Jason Dolph said moose are particularly dangerous when they are hit at highway speeds. “Typically when a car strikes a moose, that moose becomes suspended in the air,” Dolph said. “And when that moose then lands on the vehicle. In this case, it landed on the hood and kind of the windshield and roof area. items.t: Ukraine war continues despite Trump’s promise to end it
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - The war in Ukraine has lasted more than four-and-a-half years, and fighting continues despite repeated efforts by President Donald Trump to end the conflict. Trump made a pledge on the campaign trail dozens of times during the last presidential campaign. “Before I even arrive at the Oval Office shortly after I win the presidency, I will have the horrible war between Russia and Ukraine settled,” Trump said at a July 7, 2023, rally in Council Bluffs, Iowa. “Somebody said, are you on Russia’s side? Are you on Ukraine’s side? You know what? The side — I want people to stop dying. That’s the side I’m on.” That campaign promise has not been fulfilled. Trump has met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy twice at the White House. He met once with Russian President Vladimir Putin, in August 2025 in Anchorage, Alaska. “I will say that I believe we had a very productive meeting,” Trump said. “There were many, many points that we agreed on. Most of them, I would say. A couple of big ones that we haven’t quite got there, but we’ve made some headway. items.t: We Walk the Line: Turning loss into a lifeline
items.x: (Editor’s note: This story discusses suicide. If you or a loved one needs help, call or text the Suicide Prevention Hotline at 988.) LANSING, Mich. ( Aging Untold ) — Members of the military and first responders run toward crisis and the repeated trauma can take a serious toll on mental health. A growing number of veterans and first responders are dying by suicide, struggling with the invisible wounds of service. The U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs estimates an average of 22 veterans take their own lives each day, and hundreds of first responders die by suicide annually. Two Michigan nonprofits are working together to help, providing free therapy and service dogs to veterans and first responders. For Tonya and Scott Shea, the mission is personal. Their son, Army Specialist Connor Shea, was a quiet, old soul with a passion for fishing and Johnny Cash. “His peaceful part of him was fishing. And he would just go on the lakes with his buddies or by himself, put in some headphones, listen to some Johnny Cash, cast some reels, and he was just simple,” Tonya Shea said. items.t: ‘She just lit up the room’: Toddler dies after being hit by car at a pumpkin patch, family says
items.x: SEVIERVILLE, Tenn. ( WVLT /Gray News) - A Tennessee toddler died after being hit by a car at a pumpkin patch, according to her family. The family of 21-month-old Nyxailia Hinton said they want answers after she died Tuesday. The Sevier County Sheriff’s Office said she fell and was hit by a car driven by a family friend at a pumpkin patch. However, details have not been given about how or where she fell. “She just lit up the room,” said Peandra Hinton, the child’s mother. “If you were having a bad day, you see Zayla, she’s gonna turn it all around.” Hinton said her daughter was with a babysitter who took her to the pumpkin patch without permission. She said her daughter was with a group of people she did not know. Hinton rushed to the hospital, where her daughter died from her injuries Tuesday, according to the sheriff’s office. Hinton said the past 48 hours have been a whirlwind, adding the hardest part has been waking up without her daughter. “The fact that I couldn’t wake up this morning to my baby, it really tore me up,” Hinton said. items.t: ‘Breaking Away’ actress Barbara Barrie dies by medically assisted suicide, reports say
items.x: (Gray News) - Barbara Barrie, known for her 1979 role in “Breaking Away,” died Wednesday by medically assisted suicide, according to her daughter in a statement to The New York Times . Barrie was 95. Barrie had been diagnosed with terminal cancer and died in her New York City home, according to her daughter, Jane Harwick. Barrie’s agent, Gary Gersh, said her passing was “medically assisted in accordance with the New York State Medical Aid in Dying Law,” according to USA Today . In addition to “Breaking Away,” which earned her an Oscar nomination, Barrie also starred in several TV shows, including “Barney Miller” and “Suddenly Susan.” She also received a Tony nomination for her performance in the original production of “Company.”

items.t: Relocation offers on the rise as cities try big cash incentives to attract remote workers
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Remote work opportunities continue to thrive years after the COVID-19 pandemic made working from home mainstream. Now some communities across the U.S. are competing to attract new residents who are fully employed but can live anywhere, offering increasingly large cash incentives to lure remote workers. Cumberland, Maryland launched “Choose Cumberland,” a pilot program offering $20,000 to up to 10 people who agree to move to the city. The Appalachian Mountains community, located about 130 miles outside Washington D.C., saw its population decline from over 40,000 to less than 19,000 after several manufacturing companies and other large employers closed their doors starting in the 1970s. “At one time, the population of Cumberland was over 40,000 people,” said Mayor Ray Morriss. Program details and requirements The Cumberland incentive splits the money into two payments : $10,000 in relocation cash $10,000 for a down payment or approved home renovations Recipients must make Cumberland their primary residence for at least five years. “The people we are trying to entice are the people who are bringing their jobs with them,” Morriss said. items.t: Gen Z has more debt than Millennials did at the same age
items.x: ( InvestigateTV ) — Gen Z carries more debt than Millennials did at the same age, even after adjusting for inflation, according to TransUnion data cited by a credit counseling expert. Ted Rossman, with nonprofit credit counseling agency Money Management International , said the agency has seen a 35% increase in demand from Gen Z clients in the past year. Their debt loads are about 12% higher than they were a year ago. Student loans, high rents and buy now, pay later plans are adding up and leaving many young adults living paycheck to paycheck with little savings. “That’s really showcasing a lot of these early career pressures,” Rossman said. “You have student loans, you have high housing costs. Those household formation years are very expensive, so GenZer’s actually have more debt than Millennials did at the same age, even adjusted for inflation according to TransUnion.” For Gen Z, Rossman said the starting point is the basics: knowing your budget and watching buy now, pay later spending. “It’s very popular among people in their 20’s, but it’s still debt,” Rossman said. “It can work in your favor.
