(Atlanta News First) — The national Democratic Party’s most popular figure was in metro Atlanta on Wednesday to rally supporters ahead of next week’s nationally watched midterms. The rally was held at Morrow’s Arena at Southlake. REWATCH CAMPAIGN RALLY: Ossoff’s seat is seen as crucial by national Democrats to maintaining a narrow margin with Republicans in the U.S. Senate. items.t: Hilton Head man gets 20 years after shooting woman in head over argument
items.x: BEAUFORT COUNTY, S.C. (WTOC) - A Hilton Head Island man will spend 20 years in prison for shooting a woman in the head after a brief argument in an apartment parking lot. A Beaufort County jury found Bernard Garvin Jr., 35, guilty Wednesday of attempted murder and possession of a weapon during a violent crime in the June 9, 2023, shooting at Hilton Head Gardens on Southwood Park Drive. Prosecutors said Garvin shot the victim after she confronted him for fighting with another woman over a liquor bottle. He fired at least four shots from a 9mm handgun, grazing her in the head. She was treated in intensive care for possible bleeding on the brain. Circuit Court Judge Robert Bonds sentenced Garvin to 20 years, followed by five years’ probation. Garvin, known as “Berney,” was arrested Sept. 26, 2023, in Stockbridge, Ga., and extradited to Beaufort County. His record dates to 2011.

items.t: College professor among 2 found dead in home; suspect in custody, police say
items.x: LORAIN COUNTY, Ohio. ( WOIO /Gray News) - An Ohio college professor and a woman were found shot to death in a home, and a suspect is in custody, according to authorities. Herbert Kimble was sentenced to 20 years’ imprisonment with three years of court-ordered supervision. He was also ordered to pay more than $199 million in restitution to Medicare and forfeit more than $195 million in what prosecutors described as “ill-gotten gains.” Kimble pleaded guilty in 2019 to conspiring to commit health care fraud, violate the anti-kickback statute, and defraud the United States in connection with a telemedicine and durable medical equipment scheme involving back, shoulder, wrist, and knee braces. Prosecutors say Kimble ran offshore call centers that recruited elderly Medicare beneficiaries, paid kickbacks to telemedicine companies for signed prescriptions, then sold those orders to medical equipment companies that billed Medicare. items.t: Veteran firefighter starts over at Savannah Fire Station 5 after 11 years with Columbus Fire
items.x: SAVANNAH, Ga. (WTOC) - An advanced firefighter who spent 11 years with Columbus Fire started over two months ago at Savannah Fire Department Fire Station 5. Oct. 28 is National First Responders Day. The day honors the service and sacrifice of those who work in public safety. Starting over at Station 5 John Hammock spent 11 years with Columbus Fire before moving to the Coastal Empire. He is now learning a new crew and new ways of operating at Station 5. He is trusting new colleagues with his life while hoping they become family. Hammock said every day is different, including structure fires and medical calls. Brotherhood and advice for rookies Hammock said the constant is the brotherhood he came looking for and found at Savannah Fire. He told WTOC that being at the station is second to none. His advice for incoming rookies is the same advice he would give himself 11 years ago. “But I would say just keep your head up. Keep moving forward. Keep doing what you’re doing. Just do the next right thing. You’ll be alright,” Hammock said. Hammock said he hopes to pass on the same brotherhood that welcomed him to the next generation of firefighters.

items.x: SAVANNAH, Ga. (WTOC) - Savannah Police Department Patrol Officer Keziah Green has patrolled the south side on her own for the past three weeks. She was born and raised in Savannah and worked as a 911 dispatcher before becoming an officer. WTOC highlighted first responder rookies in the community on National First Responder Day. WTOC’s Alex Rivero spent the day with them. Training on the job Green told WTOC the academy built the foundation and set her up for success. In three weeks, she has used her training on calls ranging from a 6:30 a.m. call to tense negotiations. She hopes to continue her training, including with the hostage negotiation team, and to move up the ranks. Advice for her younger self WTOC asked Green what she would tell her younger self about the job. “Even though things can get scary, everything you want is on the other side of fear. Sometimes we just have to be willing to walk through that door and see what’s there... And doing what scares you. I learned that being in an academy. Do what scares you and you’ll get the best outcome,” Green said. Green said the work is not just a regular job. It is a bigger mission that she hopes to serve each day.

items.t: For politics, what is an October surprise?
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - An October surprise is an event that could shake up an election, but does it often make the difference? Matt Dallek, a professor of political management at George Washington University, described it as “an event that, at least in theory, has the potential to shake up an election, something that people did not foresee coming that upends the debate.” He said the term dates back to around the 1980 election, when President Jimmy Carter failed to secure the release of American hostages being held in Iran before November 4, 1980, election day. Carter lost to Republican rival Ronald Reagan. Several surprises have occurred in the years since. Surprises can be driven by a campaign or by news events. Examples include Iran-Contra-related indictments in 1992 and the global financial collapse in 2008. Dallek said those surprises likely did not change the outcome of the election that November. “There’s no evidence that they flip a dynamic that was already in place,” Dallek said. “What’s more typical is that an event occurs, it dominates the news cycle and the trend line starts to move further toward the candidate who was already doing well, who was already likely to prevai

items.t: Library says person threw box of cockroaches at a staff member, prompting closure
items.x: TOLEDO, Ohio ( WTVG /Gray News) - A cockroach attack forced the closure of a library in Ohio this week. Surveillance footage apparently shows someone throwing a box of cockroaches at a library employee in Ohio. The library was said to have gone into restricted access before closing for the rest of the day for cleanup and remediation. The Kent Branch Library reopened Wednesday. Officials did not say whether anyone would be facing any charges.

items.x: SAVANNAH, Ga. (WTOC) - River Street Sweets is celebrating 10 years of giving back to Savannah families with a major donation to America’s Second Harvest of Coastal Georgia. The candy company presented more than $21,000 on Wednesday to support the Kids Cafe program, which provides after-school meals, tutoring and a safe place for at-risk children. The money was raised during the store’s annual Pralines Day campaign held each June. “One of our biggest things is we really want to thank the community. We’re Savannah’s original candy store, we’ve been here since 1973 and the community has always supported us,” said Kelley Cale, vice president of marketing at River Street Sweets. “And so one of the best ways to be able to give back to that community is to help kids that might be in need.” Cale said the partnership started when the company learned about the Kids Cafe program around the same time as National Pralines Day. “What better fit than to give back to kids that might need some meals,” she said. Over the past decade, River Street Sweets says it has helped provide more than 500,000 meals for local children.

items.t: Grandmother not indicted in baby’s death after police say she left her in hot car for 8 hours while she worked
items.x: MADISONVILLE, Ky. ( WFIE /Gray News) — A Kentucky doctor who accidentally left her grandchild unattended in a hot car for about eight hours will not be indicted for the baby’s death. Madisonville police said 10-month-old Scottie Crowell died in August . On Tuesday, a grand jury found there was insufficient probable cause for an indictment. Police said Scottie’s grandmother picked her up in the morning of Aug. 13 and was supposed to take her to daycare. She forgot the child was in the car and went to work, police said. She arrived at Owensboro Health Multi-Care, where she works as a doctor, around 8 a.m. The baby’s father called his wife after trying to pick up Scottie from daycare, but the child was not there. The baby’s mother called the grandmother at work, and the grandmother ran outside and saw Scottie was still in the vehicle around 4 p.m., police said. After 911 was called, first responders tried to administer lifesaving measures, but the baby died. “I would ask that you keep the infant’s parents and family in your thoughts and prayers as they continue to grieve and process this unimaginable loss,” said Commonwealth’s Attorney Hannah Kington-Jarvis.

items.t: Widow searches for lost wedding ring when husband dies 3 days after getting married in Las Vegas
items.x: LAS VEGAS ( KVVU /Gray News) — A South Dakota woman is asking for help finding the wedding ring her husband lost in Las Vegas the night they married. Tammy Bishop and Will Mulroy were married Oct. 20 at the Viva Las Vegas Chapel. Bishop said they celebrated on a party bus and toured the Strip. At a bar, though, she says Mulroy looked down and realized his ring was gone. “We got to a bar. He looked down and his band was gone. He lost it. He started crying,” Bishop said. According to Bishop, he told her the ring was two sizes too big because he had lost weight. She said the ring may have slid off on the bus or while he moved into his wheelchair. It may also have come off while he rolled down the Strip. “We backtracked our steps. We told the bus driver. We had everyone looking. We couldn’t find it,” she said. The next day, she joked with him: “You didn’t even have your ring on for 24 hours and you lost it.” Everyone laughed, she said. “I said it’s not a big deal; we will buy you a new one, but now that he is gone it is a big deal to me,” Bishop said. items.t: Ernie Johnson announces this will be his final season on ‘Inside The NBA’
items.x: (Gray News) - Ernie Johnson announced he will be stepping down as host of “Inside the NBA” at the end of the season. The Sports Broadcasting Hall of Famer took to social media on Wednesday to explain his decision to step away, saying, “It’s just time.” Johnson, 70, stated that he would not be retiring, but cutting back. “This is by no means the end. It’s just a turning of the page,” Johnson said. “And I’ll forever cherish every chapter we have written with ‘Inside the NBA.’” Johnson said he plans to continue to work, including covering the NCAA men’s basketball tournament for CBS and Turner Sports. The six-time Sports Emmy Award winner acknowledged that he has dealt with heart issues in recent years, but that isn’t the reason he’s stepping away from the show. “I just want to slow down a bit,” he added in his social media post. Johnson joined Turner Sports in 1989 and has hosted “Inside the NBA” since 1990. He thanked his TNT Sports and ESPN crews for their support over the years, as well as the viewers. “I just want to say thanks to you. Thanks for your loyalty, for your love, for your support. And on this day, for your understanding,” Johnson said.

items.t: Police department closes its investigation into Hayden Panettiere’s death

Police said Panettiere’s death has been ruled accidental based on the medical examiner’s determination and the findings of the investigation. Panettiere, 36, died from an accidental overdose involving multiple prescription medications and fentanyl, according to findings previously released by the Greenville County Coroner’s Office. items.t: 8-month-old dies after left alone in running bathtub, police say
items.x: STERLING, Va. (Gray News) - A Virginia woman was arrested after her 8-month-old died after being left unattended in a bathtub, according to authorities. Rosellena Pisani, 30, was arrested and charged with homicide, two counts of child abuse and three counts of child endangerment, a press release said. On Sept. 12, emergency medical personnel and sheriff’s deputies responded to the residence after receiving a call about an unresponsive infant. items.t: Illegal moonshine distillery explodes, catches fire in mountains, officials say
items.x: WILKES COUNTY, N.C. ( WBTV /Gray News) - An explosion at an illegal moonshine distillery sparked a fire in the North Carolina mountains on Monday, according to authorities. Special agents from North Carolina’s Alcohol Law Enforcement Division were called to investigate the explosion in Wilkes County, North Carolina. Agents found an active 200-gallon illegal distillery. They seized about 1,800 gallons of mash, which is used to make moonshine, and 161 gallons of illegal moonshine. North Carolina officials shared photos showing the charred inside of a metal building. Distilling equipment was also damaged. Billy Ray Anderson, 69, was arrested and charged with manufacturing a non-taxpaid alcoholic beverage, possession for sale of a non-taxpaid alcoholic beverage, possession of a non-taxpaid alcoholic beverage, possession of distillery equipment, possession of distillery ingredients and allowing property to be used for the manufacture of a non-taxpaid alcoholic beverage. Moonshine is believed to have originated in North Carolina and was once an important source of income, particularly for rural residents.

items.t: Some packaged salads recalled for undeclared allergens
items.x: (Gray News) - Packaged salads produced by Taylor Farms have been recalled due to an undeclared allergen. According to the Food and Drug Administration, Taylor Farms is recalling its H-E-B Backyard BBQ Chop Salad because it may contain undeclared soy and tree nuts, specifically almonds. “People who have sensitivity or allergy to soy and tree nuts (almonds) may be at risk of a serious adverse reaction if they consume this product,” an FDA press release said. So far there have not been any illnesses or “adverse reactions” reported in connection with the recall. The salads were sold in H-E-B stores across Texas. They can be identified by their UPC code, 041220300457, and their best-by date, Oct. 30, 2026. Customers are asked not to eat the recalled salads and to throw them away or return them to the store for a refund.

items.t: Caregiver advocate shares 3 policies that could help family caregivers
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — More than 60 million Americans are family caregivers, balancing work, kids and care for an aging parent or loved one. Jason Resendez, president and CEO of the National Alliance for Caregiving, recently testified before the U.S. Senate Special Committee on Aging. Trump made a pledge on the campaign trail dozens of times during the last presidential campaign. “Before I even arrive at the Oval Office shortly after I win the presidency, I will have the horrible war between Russia and Ukraine settled,” Trump said at a July 7, 2023, rally in Council Bluffs, Iowa. “Somebody said, are you on Russia’s side? Are you on Ukraine’s side? You know what? The side — I want people to stop dying. That’s the side I’m on.” That campaign promise has not been fulfilled. Trump has met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy twice at the White House. He met once with Russian President Vladimir Putin, in August 2025 in Anchorage, Alaska. “I will say that I believe we had a very productive meeting,” Trump said. “There were many, many points that we agreed on. items.t: ‘Breaking Away’ actress Barbara Barrie dies by medically assisted suicide, reports say
items.x: (Gray News) - Barbara Barrie, known for her 1979 role in “Breaking Away,” died Wednesday by medically assisted suicide, according to her daughter in a statement to The New York Times . Barrie was 95. Barrie had been diagnosed with terminal cancer and died in her New York City home, according to her daughter, Jane Harwick. Barrie’s agent, Gary Gersh, said her passing was “medically assisted in accordance with the New York State Medical Aid in Dying Law,” according to USA Today . In addition to “Breaking Away,” which earned her an Oscar nomination, Barrie also starred in several TV shows, including “Barney Miller” and “Suddenly Susan.” She also received a Tony nomination for her performance in the original production of “Company.”

items.t: Relocation offers on the rise as cities try big cash incentives to attract remote workers
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Remote work opportunities continue to thrive years after the COVID-19 pandemic made working from home mainstream. Now some communities across the U.S. are competing to attract new residents who are fully employed but can live anywhere, offering increasingly large cash incentives to lure remote workers. Cumberland, Maryland launched “Choose Cumberland,” a pilot program offering $20,000 to up to 10 people who agree to move to the city. The Appalachian Mountains community, located about 130 miles outside Washington D.C., saw its population decline from over 40,000 to less than 19,000 after several manufacturing companies and other large employers closed their doors starting in the 1970s. “At one time, the population of Cumberland was over 40,000 people,” said Mayor Ray Morriss. Program details and requirements The Cumberland incentive splits the money into two payments : $10,000 in relocation cash $10,000 for a down payment or approved home renovations Recipients must make Cumberland their primary residence for at least five years. “The people we are trying to entice are the people who are bringing their jobs with them,” Morriss said. items.t: Gen Z has more debt than Millennials did at the same age

Their debt loads are about 12% higher than they were a year ago. Student loans, high rents and buy now, pay later plans are adding up and leaving many young adults living paycheck to paycheck with little savings. “That’s really showcasing a lot of these early career pressures,” Rossman said. “You have student loans, you have high housing costs. items.t: Antidepressants: What to know before you decide
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Feeling low, disconnected or not like yourself for weeks or months is different from a bad day. When it starts to affect sleep, energy or everyday life, it’s time to talk about support and treatment options. For some people, that could include an antidepressant. Start with a conversation with your provider Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said the decision looks different for everyone. “Everybody is individualized so you can just talk with your provider,” Rogers said. Rogers said to recognize whether you’re feeling depressed and to look at signs such as loss of sleep, loss of energy or loss of motivation. Some people might also experience a triggering event that starts a downward spiral, which they can’t pull themself out of, she said. “When your quality of life is being affected, then you might want to look into antidepressant therapy,” Rogers said. Antidepressants are not “happy pills” Rogers cautioned that antidepressants do not take away sadness. “They’re not happy pills. items.t: The barbershop quartet tradition is alive in New Orleans
items.x: NEW ORLEANS ( InvestigateTV ) - On a Mid City evening, a four-part harmony rang out just off Canal Street. The group, Southern Tradition, has been around since 1999. The quartet is a place where a traditional American art form forges a friendship. “The main attribute to be a barbershop quartet singer is to not be embarrassed, just keep going,” said Karl Hansen. Four men with four different careers create one sound. Hansen is a doctor who sings bass. Hansen Eschette is a med tech singing tenor. Joe Jacquat is a civil engineer who sings baritone. Johnnie Oufnac is the only actual barber in this barbershop quartet, singing lead. “Being together for a long time helps us harmonize and understand where the other person is going,” Hansen said. Barbershop quartets have been around for more than a century. Though they can be found all over the world, ties to New Orleans are strong. “It really is the nexus of American music at its most basic level and a lot of it comes from New Orleans,” said Zachary Matherne. items.t: Nearly 11 million people in the U.S. could be living with undiagnosed diabetes
items.x: CHARLOTTE, N.C. ( InvestigateTV ) - Diabetes is the seventh leading cause of death in the United States, the No. 1 cause of kidney disease, and an estimated 40 million people are living with it nationwide. Despite decades of prevention education and major breakthroughs in treatment, doctors say diabetes continues to hit the South especially hard — including North Carolina. It can create serious long-term complications, including coronary artery disease, heart attacks, never damage, and amputations. But many people who have the disease may not know it. The CDC estimates around 11 million live with undiagnosed diabetes. “Every day, almost every hour” battle Andrew Tucker has lived with Type 2 diabetes for nearly two decades. He’s made major lifestyle changes but said managing the disease is still a daily fight. Tucker was diagnosed about 15 years ago, when he was 35. “Yes, for me, it is truly an everyday, almost every hour watching what I do,” Tucker said. Type 2 diabetes develops when the body doesn’t make enough insulin or doesn’t use insulin properly. Doctors say obesity is a major risk factor. items.t: This veteran is using his service dog to regain independence
items.x: ST. LOUIS, Mo. ( InvestigateTV ) - Veteran James Poggi served in the Marine Corps working in aviation. His time in the military led to a lifelong strain on his body, including five back surgeries and a below-the-knee amputation. “You go from being six foot three, 250 pounds and able to travel halfway across the world and do whatever they ask you to do, to being relying on wheelchairs, walkers, mobility devices, things like that, you become a vulnerable person that you never thought you’d be,” Poggi said. Poggi said he was in multiple accidents, hard landings, PT accidents and a car crash. He also developed spinal meningitis. “And that was all while I was active,” he said. To help ease some of the emotional toll, Poggi’s wife, who is also his caregiver, suggested he get a service dog. Service dog provides daily support Poggi got Teddy, a Goldendoodle, who serves as his service dog and daily lifeline. “You never went anywhere without your battle buddy. And he always, always better have your back. And that’s how it is. He’s always got my back,” Poggi said. items.t: Gulf County to test St. Joseph Bay water as red tide presence grows
items.x: GULF COUNTY, Fla. (WJHG/WECP) -Dead fish are showing up again in St. Joseph Bay, and Gulf County officials are looking for answers. Residents say they are concerned about the bay and how red tide will affect the local economy. The Board of County Commissioners approved a proposal Tuesday from the St. Andrew and St. Joseph Bays Estuary Program to test the water. Crews will collect samples from six sites Thursday to look for possible sources of the problem. Katie Shealy, Gulf County public information officer, said the commission is treating the issue as a priority. “The commission is taking this very seriously because we know that the bay is the lifeline of our community and our economy, so we are taking it very seriously for those charters, fishermen and everyone else in our community, as well as our visitors,” Shealy said. items.t: Economist explains how the ‘K-shaped economy’ is impacting the midterms
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - As voters prepare to head to the polls for the midterm elections, a conflicting economic sentiment is once again emerging on the campaign trail. “Voters reflect the perception of the cost of living as they experienced, as opposed to what is in the data,” said Alessandro Rebucci, an economics professor at Johns Hopkins Carey Business School. “In the data, you have an economy that is very strong as a whole. How that pie is distributed affects how a large segment of the population and the voters are feeling about the economy right now.” The contradiction has been described by many economists recently, as the “k-shaped” economy, using a graph to depict how high-income earners and asset owners are doing compared to middle and lower-income earners. “To be concrete, the wealthiest households are presumed to spend much more than the lowest ones, not only in absolute terms, which is obvious, but also as a share of their income and in their wealth,” Rebucci said. items.t: For politics, what is an October surprise?
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - An October surprise is an event that could shake up an election, but does it often make the difference? Matt Dallek, a professor of political management at George Washington University, described it as “an event that, at least in theory, has the potential to shake up an election, something that people did not foresee coming that upends the debate.” He said the term dates back to around the 1980 election, when President Jimmy Carter failed to secure the release of American hostages being held in Iran before November 4, 1980, election day. Carter lost to Republican rival Ronald Reagan. Several surprises have occurred in the years since. Surprises can be driven by a campaign or by news events. Examples include Iran-Contra-related indictments in 1992 and the global financial collapse in 2008. Dallek said those surprises likely did not change the outcome of the election that November. “There’s no evidence that they flip a dynamic that was already in place,” Dallek said. “What’s more typical is that an event occurs, it dominates the news cycle and the trend line starts to move further toward the candidate who was already doing well, who was already likely to prevai

items.t: Health alert issued for red tide near Mexico Beach
items.x: PANAMA CITY, Fla. (WJHG/WECP) - Health officials have issued a red tide health alert for waters near Mexico Beach following water samples collected earlier this week. The Florida Department of Health in Bay County (DOH-Bay) announced the alert Wednesday based on test results from water samples gathered on Monday, Oct. 26. Officials are urging beachgoers, residents, and visitors to exercise caution in and around the area. Red tide is caused by high concentrations of Karenia brevis ( K. brevis ), a naturally occurring microscopic algae native to the Gulf of Mexico. When winds and currents carry blooms toward shore, the algae can discolor the water with a red or brown hue and release neurotoxins called brevetoxins into the air and surf. Exposure can trigger skin rashes, burning eyes, and respiratory problems. Those with chronic respiratory conditions, young children, the elderly, and immunocompromised individuals face a greater risk of severe symptoms. Recommended precautions Health officials advise residents and visitors near Mexico Beach to take the following safety measures: Avoid the water: Do not swim or wade in or near red tide blooms. items.t: Grandmother not indicted in baby’s death after police say she left her in hot car for 8 hours while she worked
items.x: MADISONVILLE, Ky. ( WFIE /Gray News) — A Kentucky doctor who accidentally left her grandchild unattended in a hot car for about eight hours will not be indicted for the baby’s death. Madisonville police said 10-month-old Scottie Crowell died in August . On Tuesday, a grand jury found there was insufficient probable cause for an indictment. Police said Scottie’s grandmother picked her up in the morning of Aug. 13 and was supposed to take her to daycare. She forgot the child was in the car and went to work, police said. She arrived at Owensboro Health Multi-Care, where she works as a doctor, around 8 a.m. The baby’s father called his wife after trying to pick up Scottie from daycare, but the child was not there. The baby’s mother called the grandmother at work, and the grandmother ran outside and saw Scottie was still in the vehicle around 4 p.m., police said. After 911 was called, first responders tried to administer lifesaving measures, but the baby died. “I would ask that you keep the infant’s parents and family in your thoughts and prayers as they continue to grieve and process this unimaginable loss,” said Commonwealth’s Attorney Hannah Kington-Jarvis.

items.t: Florida surgeon performs robotic surgery on patient 35 miles away
items.x: ORLANDO, Fla. ( WWSB ) - A Florida surgeon operated on a patient Sunday while more than 30 miles away, using robotic surgical instruments. The 66-year-old patient walked into Advent Health Mineola outside of Orlando. His surgeon, Dr. Vipul Patel, was at Advent Health Celebration in Kissimmee and performed the surgery remotely. The patient needed surgery to have his prostate removed. Patel controlled the robotic surgical instruments from 35 miles away. Sarasota Memorial surgeon combines two new heart devices in single procedure The surgery was part of an FDA-authorized research study and is the first reported robotic tele-surgery in the United States. The same medical team previously performed this surgery from Central Florida on a patient in Africa. The technology would theoretically allow a surgeon to operate from anywhere in the world. Advent Health said more research is necessary before larger conclusions can be made regarding the technology.

items.t: Ernie Johnson announces this will be his final season on ‘Inside The NBA’
items.x: (Gray News) - Ernie Johnson announced he will be stepping down as host of “Inside the NBA” at the end of the season. The Sports Broadcasting Hall of Famer took to social media on Wednesday to explain his decision to step away, saying, “It’s just time.” Johnson, 70, stated that he would not be retiring, but cutting back. “This is by no means the end. It’s just a turning of the page,” Johnson said. “And I’ll forever cherish every chapter we have written with ‘Inside the NBA.’” Johnson said he plans to continue to work, including covering the NCAA men’s basketball tournament for CBS and Turner Sports. The six-time Sports Emmy Award winner acknowledged that he has dealt with heart issues in recent years, but that isn’t the reason he’s stepping away from the show. “I just want to slow down a bit,” he added in his social media post. Johnson joined Turner Sports in 1989 and has hosted “Inside the NBA” since 1990. He thanked his TNT Sports and ESPN crews for their support over the years, as well as the viewers. “I just want to say thanks to you. Thanks for your loyalty, for your love, for your support. And on this day, for your understanding,” Johnson said.

items.t: Police department closes its investigation into Hayden Panettiere’s death
items.x: GREENVILLE, S.C. ( WHNS /Gray News) - The Greenville Police Department said it has officially closed its investigation into the death of Hayden Panettiere. Police said Panettiere’s death has been ruled accidental based on the medical examiner’s determination and the findings of the investigation. Panettiere, 36, died from an accidental overdose involving multiple prescription medications and fentanyl, according to findings previously released by the Greenville County Coroner’s Office. Toxicology testing determined the cause of death to be the toxic effects of fentanyl, 4-ANPP, alprazolam, methocarbamol and quetiapine. An autopsy showed no signs of contributing trauma. On Aug. 16, Panettiere was found unresponsive inside an apartment in Greenville, where she had been temporarily staying. Dispatchers received a 911 call reporting a woman in cardiac arrest at approximately 1:51 p.m. She was pronounced dead at 2:32 p.m. Her on-and-off boyfriend Brian Hickerson and his brother Zach Hickerson were at the apartment where she died. President Donald Trump, who has named it “super intelligence,” insists the U.S. will beat China in the AI competition. items.t: DeSantis announces $100 million for 45 water quality, springs and water supply projects
items.x: CRYSTAL RIVER, Fla. ( WWSB ) - Florida will spend $100 million on 45 projects aimed at improving water quality, protecting springs and expanding water supplies, Gov. Ron DeSantis announced Wednesday. “Today in Crystal River, I was proud to announce $100 million for springs restoration and alternative water supply projects throughout Florida,” DeSantis said in a statement. Half of the money, or $50 million, will support 23 projects intended to improve Florida’s springs, according to the Florida Department of Environmental Protection. The work includes upgrading wastewater systems, helping homeowners replace or improve septic systems, and expanding sewer service. State officials said those projects are expected to cut nitrogen pollution by more than 55,000 pounds a year. Nitrogen is a nutrient that can harm water quality when too much of it enters waterways. Awards include $3 million for Citrus County to convert some properties from septic systems to sewer service and improve remaining systems. items.t: 8-month-old dies after left alone in running bathtub, police say
items.x: STERLING, Va. (Gray News) - A Virginia woman was arrested after her 8-month-old died after being left unattended in a bathtub, according to authorities. Rosellena Pisani, 30, was arrested and charged with homicide, two counts of child abuse and three counts of child endangerment, a press release said. On Sept. 12, emergency medical personnel and sheriff’s deputies responded to the residence after receiving a call about an unresponsive infant. Investigators determined the baby had been left unsupervised in a bathtub with the water running. Three children, ranging in age from 8 months to 8 years old, were at home during the incident, according to police. Loudoun County Sheriff Mike Chapman called the baby’s death heartbreaking, saying caregivers have a fundamental duty to protect children. He added investigators remain committed to seeking justice in the case.

items.x: OVERLAND, Mo. ( KMOV /Gray News) — Officials in Missouri said a missing 7-year-old boy and his pregnant mother were found safe Wednesday. The Missouri State Highway Patrol previously issued an Endangered Person Advisory for Dylan Fernando Zendejas-Gonzalez, 7. Dylan was last seen leaving his home in Overland, near St. Louis, with his mother, Maria Guadalupe Gonzalez-Sanchez, 28. The two were last seen around 1:30 p.m. Sunday. The Panama City Fire Department responded around 5:50 p.m. on Oct. 27 to a house fire on Loyola Ln. items.t: Beachfront home heavily damaged in late-night South Walton fire
items.x: SOUTH WALTON, Fla. (WJHG/WECP) - A beachfront home on stilts was significantly damaged in a house fire late Tuesday evening, according to the South Walton Fire District. Fire officials say crews were dispatched around 9:20 p.m. to Beach Drive East, arriving to find heavy fire and smoke showing from the front right corner of the home. Firefighters went to work immediately, spending the following hour bringing the flames under control and overhauling hot spots, releasing most crews by midnight. Residents were inside the home when the blaze broke out but escaped without injuries. No firefighter injuries were reported. The fire left the residents displaced. Firefighters contacted the American Red Cross for help. Crews report they stopped the blaze from spreading to nearby houses, though intense heat shattered the windows of a neighboring home. South Walton Fire District fire investigators and the Florida State Fire Marshal’s Office are conducting a joint investigation into the cause. They cut, clean and arrange the blooms into vases, then deliver them to nursing homes, the VA hospital, assisted living facilities and shelters. “Amazingly gifted with so many flowers from places like Kroger who have overbought and can’t sell them, and they allow us to pick them up and then bring them here, and then we cut them, clean them and vase them. Then we take them to nursing homes, the VA hospital, assisted living facilities,” Jodie Raible, a Flower Buds volunteer, said. The group sends out about 100 vases every week. “I take flowers to Up for Women and Children, it’s a day homeless shelter for women,” Stephanie Mullins, a Flower Buds volunteer, said. items.t: Illegal moonshine distillery explodes, catches fire in mountains, officials say
items.x: WILKES COUNTY, N.C. ( WBTV /Gray News) - An explosion at an illegal moonshine distillery sparked a fire in the North Carolina mountains on Monday, according to authorities. Special agents from North Carolina’s Alcohol Law Enforcement Division were called to investigate the explosion in Wilkes County, North Carolina. Agents found an active 200-gallon illegal distillery. They seized about 1,800 gallons of mash, which is used to make moonshine, and 161 gallons of illegal moonshine. North Carolina officials shared photos showing the charred inside of a metal building. Distilling equipment was also damaged. Billy Ray Anderson, 69, was arrested and charged with manufacturing a non-taxpaid alcoholic beverage, possession for sale of a non-taxpaid alcoholic beverage, possession of a non-taxpaid alcoholic beverage, possession of distillery equipment, possession of distillery ingredients and allowing property to be used for the manufacture of a non-taxpaid alcoholic beverage. Moonshine is believed to have originated in North Carolina and was once an important source of income, particularly for rural residents.

items.t: Some packaged salads recalled for undeclared allergens
items.x: (Gray News) - Packaged salads produced by Taylor Farms have been recalled due to an undeclared allergen. According to the Food and Drug Administration, Taylor Farms is recalling its H-E-B Backyard BBQ Chop Salad because it may contain undeclared soy and tree nuts, specifically almonds. “People who have sensitivity or allergy to soy and tree nuts (almonds) may be at risk of a serious adverse reaction if they consume this product,” an FDA press release said. So far there have not been any illnesses or “adverse reactions” reported in connection with the recall. The salads were sold in H-E-B stores across Texas. They can be identified by their UPC code, 041220300457, and their best-by date, Oct. 30, 2026. Customers are asked not to eat the recalled salads and to throw them away or return them to the store for a refund.

items.t: Caregiver advocate shares 3 policies that could help family caregivers
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — More than 60 million Americans are family caregivers, balancing work, kids and care for an aging parent or loved one. Jason Resendez, president and CEO of the National Alliance for Caregiving, recently testified before the U.S. Senate Special Committee on Aging. He joined gerontologist “Sam” Cradduck to talk through the solutions he presented. The three policies he brought to lawmakers Resendez said the National Alliance for Caregiving is championing changes “to address so many of the pain points that family caregivers face every day.” 1) Older Americans Act funding He said one priority is reauthorization and funding of the Older Americans Act. Resendez said the law provides dollars for state Area Agencies on Aging to deliver services for older adults, such as Meals on Wheels and caregiver support. “One of the only federal line items for caregiving comes through the Older Americans Act, and it’s called the National Family Caregiver Support Program,” Resendez said. He said the program funds respite, which gives caregivers the chance to take breaks. items.t: Long-term care costs rose about 50% in five years, report finds
items.x: ( InvestigateTV ) — The cost of long-term care jumped nearly 50% in five years, while income for older households rose just 22%, according to a new AARP report . The report found long-term services and supports are becoming even less affordable for middle-class Americans. Alan Weil, senior vice president for public policy at AARP, said the gap is the most important finding. “Between 2019 and 2024, a five-year period, the cost of most long-term care services went up about 50%, but the incomes for older households only went up by about 22%,” Weil said. “So the gap between what people can afford and what it costs has grown.” The AARP also looked at what different types of care cost. Weil said the more skilled the service, the higher the price. “If you need someone to come in and help you prepare food, that’s less expensive than if you need someone to come in and provide nursing-level care,” Weil said. “Although I’ll also say that we’ve learned that a lot of caregivers are being forced to provide nursing care that they can’t afford to pay someone else to do, even though they’ve never been trained in nursing. So that’s where the burden falls back on the family.” The financial burden oft

items.x: ST. LOUIS, Mo. ( InvestigateTV ) - A family traveled from Turkey to St. Louis for their daughter’s surgery to treat a rare condition affecting fewer than 100 people worldwide. Elisa, an 18-month-old, was born with eight fingers on her left hand. She was diagnosed with Ulnar Dimelia, also known as Mirror Hand Syndrome. “Mirror Hand is incredibly uncommon, and even surgeons like myself who take care of a great deal of kids almost never see this in their career. So, it’s really uncommon. Numbers are hard to come by, but one in a million or less is probably about right,” said Dr. Charles Goldfarb, Chief of Orthopedic Surgery at St. Louis Children’s Hospital. The condition leaves patients without a radius bone. This means significant limitations in wrist and elbow motion and preserved shoulder movements. “From the very beginning, he was really warm, genuine, and gave us a lot of hope. items.t: Canned fruit sold at Walmart recalled in several states
items.x: (Gray News) - A voluntary recall over lead concerns has been issued for cans of Walmart fruit cocktail distributed to stores in at least seven states. The Food and Drug Administration said the recall applies to 15-ounce containers of Great Value Fruit Cocktail in Fruit Juice from Concentrate. Where the product was distributed More than 1,830 cases, or approximately 44,000 individual cans, were distributed to Walmart locations in Alabama, Arizona, Louisiana, New Mexico, Pennsylvania, Washington and Wyoming, the FDA said. How to identify the product The product is marked with lot number “6FCB 04 C2263” and a best if used by date of Sept. 1, 2027. Recall details The FDA initiated the recall for “potential contamination with elevated levels of lead” on Oct. 1. It was reclassified as a Class II recall on Oct. 20. According to the FDA, Class II recalls are issued when a product can cause temporary health effects with a remote possibility of serious issues. What customers should do Customers should throw the item away or return it to Walmart.

items.t: 24-year-old deputy killed in crash with coal truck while on duty, sheriff’s office says
items.x: LOGAN COUNTY, W. Va ( WSAZ /Gray News) - A 24-year-old sheriff’s deputy was killed in a crash while responding to a call, authorities said. The Logan County Sheriff’s Department identified the deputy as 24-year-old Caden Mullins. Deputy Mullins’ fiancée was airlifted from the scene of the crash to a hospital. Deputies say Mullins and his fiancée were at a truck-or-treat event on Saturday in the Man area when he received an emergency call from the sheriff’s department. The sheriff’s department says Deputy Caden Mullins, 24, died in the crash. Mullins was on his way to drop his fiancée off and head to the call when the crash occurred around 5 p.m., deputies say. Deputies say the crash happened at the intersection of Rum Creek Road and Route 10 when a coal truck pulled off the road and hit Mullins’ vehicle. Mullins worked for the Charleston Police Department for about a year before joining the Logan County Sheriff’s Department to be closer to family, the department said.

items.t: Biloxi Farmers Market hosts Halloween event with candy, costumes and food vendors

Then, we share how a grieving Michigan family turned heartbreak into hope by helping pair veterans and first responders with lifesaving service dogs. Parkinson’s doesn’t always start with a tremor — here’s what to watch for Parkinson’s disease can start long before a tremor and the subtle changes are easy to miss. Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said the loss of smell, constipation or changes in handwriting can be early signs. According to Stone, the collision occurred when her daughter Autumn was driving home and a moose appeared in the roadway. Stone said she does not believe her daughter had any time to brake. When firefighters arrived, they found a badly damaged vehicle with Autumn trapped inside. It took several crews to cut her out with the Jaws of Life hydraulic rescue tools. Anchorage firefighter Jason Dolph said moose are particularly dangerous when they are hit at highway speeds. “Typically when a car strikes a moose, that moose becomes suspended in the air,” Dolph said. “And when that moose then lands on the vehicle. items.t: ‘Breaking Away’ actress Barbara Barrie dies by medically assisted suicide, reports say
items.x: (Gray News) - Barbara Barrie, known for her 1979 role in “Breaking Away,” died Wednesday by medically assisted suicide, according to her daughter in a statement to The New York Times . Barrie was 95. Barrie had been diagnosed with terminal cancer and died in her New York City home, according to her daughter, Jane Harwick. Barrie’s agent, Gary Gersh, said her passing was “medically assisted in accordance with the New York State Medical Aid in Dying Law,” according to USA Today . In addition to “Breaking Away,” which earned her an Oscar nomination, Barrie also starred in several TV shows, including “Barney Miller” and “Suddenly Susan.” She also received a Tony nomination for her performance in the original production of “Company.”

items.t: Relocation offers on the rise as cities try big cash incentives to attract remote workers
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Remote work opportunities continue to thrive years after the COVID-19 pandemic made working from home mainstream. Now some communities across the U.S. are competing to attract new residents who are fully employed but can live anywhere, offering increasingly large cash incentives to lure remote workers. Cumberland, Maryland launched “Choose Cumberland,” a pilot program offering $20,000 to up to 10 people who agree to move to the city. The Appalachian Mountains community, located about 130 miles outside Washington D.C., saw its population decline from over 40,000 to less than 19,000 after several manufacturing companies and other large employers closed their doors starting in the 1970s. “At one time, the population of Cumberland was over 40,000 people,” said Mayor Ray Morriss. Program details and requirements The Cumberland incentive splits the money into two payments : $10,000 in relocation cash $10,000 for a down payment or approved home renovations Recipients must make Cumberland their primary residence for at least five years. “The people we are trying to entice are the people who are bringing their jobs with them,” Morriss said. items.t: Gen Z has more debt than Millennials did at the same age
items.x: ( InvestigateTV ) — Gen Z carries more debt than Millennials did at the same age, even after adjusting for inflation, according to TransUnion data cited by a credit counseling expert. Ted Rossman, with nonprofit credit counseling agency Money Management International , said the agency has seen a 35% increase in demand from Gen Z clients in the past year. Their debt loads are about 12% higher than they were a year ago. Student loans, high rents and buy now, pay later plans are adding up and leaving many young adults living paycheck to paycheck with little savings. “That’s really showcasing a lot of these early career pressures,” Rossman said. “You have student loans, you have high housing costs. Those household formation years are very expensive, so GenZer’s actually have more debt than Millennials did at the same age, even adjusted for inflation according to TransUnion.” For Gen Z, Rossman said the starting point is the basics: knowing your budget and watching buy now, pay later spending. “It’s very popular among people in their 20’s, but it’s still debt,” Rossman said. “It can work in your favor. items.t: ‘He’s a monster’: Convicted Tennessee murderer still on the run as authorities investigate Wisconsin bank robbery
items.x: LAKE COUNTY, Tenn. ( WMC /Gray News) - The manhunt for escaped Tennessee inmate Jacob Allen Morley continues and authorities are investigating a possible link in Wisconsin after a man robbed a bank at gunpoint there on Tuesday. Dane County authorities said the Bank of Deerfield was robbed just before it closed. A gunman walked in, demanded money, restrained two employees and left with cash. Nobody was hurt during the robbery. The gunman stole a Lincoln MKZ from the parking lot to get away. The car was later found unoccupied. The Tennessee Bureau of Investigation said it is aware of the robbery in Wisconsin, but has not confirmed it is linked to Morley. Morley escaped from the Northwest Correctional Complex Monday. He stole a white 2008 Ford F-150 marked with Lindamood Planting Company. The truck was found abandoned early Tuesday in Marion, Illinois. Police said there is no evidence Morley is still in that area. Morley was serving a life sentence for the 2022 murder of Cody Birchfield. Tyreece Miller, the U.S. marshal for the Western District of Tennessee, is asking for help in the search for Morley. items.t: Antidepressants: What to know before you decide
items.x: ( Aging Untold ) — Feeling low, disconnected or not like yourself for weeks or months is different from a bad day. When it starts to affect sleep, energy or everyday life, it’s time to talk about support and treatment options. For some people, that could include an antidepressant. Start with a conversation with your provider Dr. Rhea Rogers, a board-certified physician, said the decision looks different for everyone. “Everybody is individualized so you can just talk with your provider,” Rogers said. Rogers said to recognize whether you’re feeling depressed and to look at signs such as loss of sleep, loss of energy or loss of motivation. Some people might also experience a triggering event that starts a downward spiral, which they can’t pull themself out of, she said. “When your quality of life is being affected, then you might want to look into antidepressant therapy,” Rogers said. Antidepressants are not “happy pills” Rogers cautioned that antidepressants do not take away sadness. “They’re not happy pills. They don’t take away the sadness, but they will be a way for you to work on how you got there or what else is going on,” Rogers said. She listed chronic stress, a thyroid imbala

items.t: InvestigateTV+: Tracking the trackers
items.x: ( InvestigateTV ) — As the number of cameras capturing vehicle information multiplies, so do concerns of privacy for everyday people. InvestigateTV+ explores what can happen when the tool is misused and meet one man on a mission to track every police camera in the country. Plus, four-legged companions jump into action to help heal our heroes. We share the recent gift bringing military members support in the form of service animals. Tracking the trackers Flock Safety says its cameras don’t track people. But the company’s own training videos show police using the system to track suspects “from location to location to location.” And some of its cameras are designed to follow people as they walk. “And they quite literally use AI to zoom in and follow you around whether you’re a person of interest or not,” said Benn Jordan , a security researcher who found dozens of Flock cameras streaming openly online. items.t: The barbershop quartet tradition is alive in New Orleans
items.x: NEW ORLEANS ( InvestigateTV ) - On a Mid City evening, a four-part harmony rang out just off Canal Street. The group, Southern Tradition, has been around since 1999. The quartet is a place where a traditional American art form forges a friendship. “The main attribute to be a barbershop quartet singer is to not be embarrassed, just keep going,” said Karl Hansen. Four men with four different careers create one sound. Hansen is a doctor who sings bass. Hansen Eschette is a med tech singing tenor. Joe Jacquat is a civil engineer who sings baritone. Johnnie Oufnac is the only actual barber in this barbershop quartet, singing lead. “Being together for a long time helps us harmonize and understand where the other person is going,” Hansen said. Barbershop quartets have been around for more than a century. Though they can be found all over the world, ties to New Orleans are strong. “It really is the nexus of American music at its most basic level and a lot of it comes from New Orleans,” said Zachary Matherne. One of the city’s most famous native sons sang before he played. “Louis Armstrong was in a vocal quartet before he ever started playing a horn,” Matherne said. Matherne is an award-win

items.t: Nearly 11 million people in the U.S. could be living with undiagnosed diabetes
items.x: CHARLOTTE, N.C. ( InvestigateTV ) - Diabetes is the seventh leading cause of death in the United States, the No. 1 cause of kidney disease, and an estimated 40 million people are living with it nationwide. Despite decades of prevention education and major breakthroughs in treatment, doctors say diabetes continues to hit the South especially hard — including North Carolina. It can create serious long-term complications, including coronary artery disease, heart attacks, never damage, and amputations. But many people who have the disease may not know it. The CDC estimates around 11 million live with undiagnosed diabetes. “Every day, almost every hour” battle Andrew Tucker has lived with Type 2 diabetes for nearly two decades. He’s made major lifestyle changes but said managing the disease is still a daily fight. Tucker was diagnosed about 15 years ago, when he was 35. “Yes, for me, it is truly an everyday, almost every hour watching what I do,” Tucker said. Type 2 diabetes develops when the body doesn’t make enough insulin or doesn’t use insulin properly. Doctors say obesity is a major risk factor. items.t: This veteran is using his service dog to regain independence
items.x: ST. LOUIS, Mo. ( InvestigateTV ) - Veteran James Poggi served in the Marine Corps working in aviation. His time in the military led to a lifelong strain on his body, including five back surgeries and a below-the-knee amputation. “You go from being six foot three, 250 pounds and able to travel halfway across the world and do whatever they ask you to do, to being relying on wheelchairs, walkers, mobility devices, things like that, you become a vulnerable person that you never thought you’d be,” Poggi said. Poggi said he was in multiple accidents, hard landings, PT accidents and a car crash. He also developed spinal meningitis. “And that was all while I was active,” he said. To help ease some of the emotional toll, Poggi’s wife, who is also his caregiver, suggested he get a service dog. Service dog provides daily support Poggi got Teddy, a Goldendoodle, who serves as his service dog and daily lifeline. “You never went anywhere without your battle buddy. And he always, always better have your back. And that’s how it is. He’s always got my back,” Poggi said. items.x: NASHVILLE, Tenn. ( WSMV /Gray News) — Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee said he suspects Christa Pike’s sentence will remain the same following her failed execution last month, unless the courts determine otherwise. Lee’s comments on Pike Lee was asked Wednesday whether the state will try to execute Pike again or if he will commute her sentence to life in prison. “As it related to a particular individual like Christa Pike and her crime, she’s still incarcerated under the laws of the state of Tennessee,” Lee said. “I suspect her sentence will be the same as before unless determined otherwise by the courts.” Pike’s condition Pike was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer. In September, Pike survived two doses of the lethal injection drug. The execution attempt failed. Pike is back in prison after spending days in the hospital. She is now able to speak in full sentences and walk on her own. items.t: Jackson museum seeks names of unidentified people in civil rights photographs
items.x: JACKSON, Miss. (WLBT) - Photographers who followed the civil rights movement through Mississippi shot thousands of frames. A handful of famous images made the history books. For 60 years, many of the people in the rest of those frames have gone unnamed. A new exhibit at the Smith Robertson Museum in Jackson is asking the public to help change that. “Proof Positive” opened Tuesday. It features 51 contact sheets, the full sets of frames photographers shot, not just the one picture that ran in a newspaper or magazine. Visitors are invited to look closely at the faces and say so if they recognize someone. “You could have been standing in a mass meeting or protest and the person next to you is the person that was featured,” said Theresa King, the museum’s manager. Visitors can identify someone at a kiosk in the gallery or on a paper card. They can explain who the person is or share the person’s story. When someone is identified, the museum sends a print of the photo to that person’s family as a gift. Jokic needs 10 more regular season triple-doubles to supplant Russell Westbrook, who retired after last season, as the NBA leader. items.t: Sleep specialist shares tips for adjusting to end of daylight saving time
items.x: GULFPORT, Miss. (WLOX) — Daylight saving time ends Sunday, Nov. 1, and clocks go back one hour this weekend. Some people see “falling back” as adding an hour of sleep. Memorial Hospital sleep specialist Dr. John Douglas said the extra hour could still affect sleep quality. Light affects circadian rhythm Douglas said light affects a person’s circadian rhythm the most. “I tell all my patients that it’s kind of like caveman days, you know, cave women days. You wake up with the sunrise, and you go to sleep when the sun goes down,” Douglas said. He said people should turn on every light, open the drapes and look at the reflected sunlight as soon as it comes up after waking at the new time. “So, that’ll set the clock in your brain as sunrise,” Douglas said. Douglas said it takes approximately three days for someone to adjust to the one-hour difference. Coast residents share opinions Coast residents gave mixed opinions on the time change. Some said the extra sleep is good. Others said it is too confusing to keep changing. “I think time change is a mess. It should stay the same all year long. It should never go back and forth back and forth. It’s too confusing,” Don Sweat said. Glenn Marie

items.t: Economist explains how the ‘K-shaped economy’ is impacting the midterms
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - As voters prepare to head to the polls for the midterm elections, a conflicting economic sentiment is once again emerging on the campaign trail. “Voters reflect the perception of the cost of living as they experienced, as opposed to what is in the data,” said Alessandro Rebucci, an economics professor at Johns Hopkins Carey Business School. “In the data, you have an economy that is very strong as a whole. How that pie is distributed affects how a large segment of the population and the voters are feeling about the economy right now.” The contradiction has been described by many economists recently, as the “k-shaped” economy, using a graph to depict how high-income earners and asset owners are doing compared to middle and lower-income earners. “To be concrete, the wealthiest households are presumed to spend much more than the lowest ones, not only in absolute terms, which is obvious, but also as a share of their income and in their wealth,” Rebucci said. items.t: Members of 1961 Freedom Ride welcomed to New Orleans 65 years later
items.x: NEW ORLEANS (WVUE) - With a brass band and dancing Zulu members, a handful of civil rights icons from the 1961 Freedom Ridge were welcomed onto Xavier University of Louisiana’s campus 65 years after the initial trip. Back then, the group of young students took a bus from Washington D.C. through the Deep South as a way to test discriminations laws and Jim Crow policies. But the ride stopped in Alabama after violent, racial protests, instead of making it to New Orleans, the final destination. Wednesday evening, five riders got the homecoming they were hoping for 65 years ago after a two-week bus ride down the same routes and through the same towns as 1961. “It’s been quiet an expansive trip. I really enjoyed it,” Freedom Rider Kredelle Petway-Philips said. “It feels very gratifying... It’s about time,” Freedom Rider Stephen Thomas said. The five freedom riders took the 2026 trip with a total of 67 people; some were relatives of the original Freedom Riders, while others were community and faith leaders. The sheriff’s office and FBI conducted a joint investigation on Friday at the teen’s home after investigators learned he was having online conversations with members and supporters of the Islamic State group, also known as ISIS. Authorities spoke with the 15-year-old’s parents, who allowed them to search the boy’s phone. On Monday, investigators searched the teen’s home with his parents’ consent after they revealed the information found on the phone. Inside, they found two jars in his bedroom. items.t: College professor among 2 found dead in home; suspect in custody, police say
items.x: LORAIN COUNTY, Ohio. ( WOIO /Gray News) - An Ohio college professor and a woman were found shot to death in a home, and a suspect is in custody, according to authorities. Wednesday morning, police responded to the Oberlin College Conservatory lot at 77 E. College St. to assist firefighters with a vehicle smoking and possibly on fire. When crews arrived, they tried to find the registered vehicle owner, identified as Daniel Jones, 31, to conduct a welfare check. When officers arrived at Jones’ home to check on his family, they found the victims dead inside the home. Pipo Nguyen-Duy, a professor of studio art and photography at Oberlin College, was found dead on the first floor with an apparent gunshot wound. A woman found dead on the second floor was not immediately identified. She also had an apparent gunshot wound. Jones was located aat bout 10:20 a.m. and taken into custody. Charges are pending. The investigation is ongoing.

items.t: International fugitive sentenced for one of the largest health care fraud schemes in U.S. history
items.x: COLUMBIA, S.C. ( WIS /Gray News) - A man whom federal prosecutors called the architect of one of the largest health care fraud schemes in U.S. history was sentenced Monday. Herbert Kimble was sentenced to 20 years’ imprisonment with three years of court-ordered supervision. He was also ordered to pay more than $199 million in restitution to Medicare and forfeit more than $195 million in what prosecutors described as “ill-gotten gains.” Kimble pleaded guilty in 2019 to conspiring to commit health care fraud, violate the anti-kickback statute, and defraud the United States in connection with a telemedicine and durable medical equipment scheme involving back, shoulder, wrist, and knee braces. Prosecutors say Kimble ran offshore call centers that recruited elderly Medicare beneficiaries, paid kickbacks to telemedicine companies for signed prescriptions, then sold those orders to medical equipment companies that billed Medicare. Court filings put the intended loss at more than $400 million, with Kimble personally gaining more than $195 million. X2X is an AI governance company. Darline Graham (R-S.C.) as she faces Democrat Annie Andrews. The latest stop on Trump’s “midterm blitz,” will be at the Rock Hill Sports and Event Center. items.t: 98-year-old YMCA member gives tips on how to stay fit as you age
items.x: HATTIESBURG, Miss. (WDAM) - Samuel Rosso is a 98-year-old man from Centreville, Mississippi, and the oldest member of the Family YMCA in Hattiesburg. Despite his age and two knee replacements, Rosso keeps himself busy with constant exercise. “Don’t talk age,” Rosso said. “I’ve known people who become 50 or 60 and they worry about being old. Forget being old. Just try to be yourself and do enough exercise to be comfortable.” Rosso has been a member of the YMCA for around 13 years. He said he may have done more treadmill exercises in those days, but now, he focuses more on workouts that keep his arms and legs limber. “I perhaps don’t do a typical workout,” he said. “I just come out, I use a bicycle, and on the bicycle they have a TV, and while I’m pedaling, I watch a western show.” Rosso tries to keep his meals light: black coffee, toast and oatmeal for breakfast, and a meat and vegetable for lunch. The connections he’s made over the years help him stay motivated, and he loves to meet new people, learn their stories and bond through hobbies and interests. “He reads, he talks, he loves to just meet with people, and he’s that constant person that’s just willing to engage with people,”

items.t: Jackson County emergency operations center could open in January 2027
items.x: JACKSON COUNTY, Miss. (WLOX) — Jackson County’s new Emergency Operations Center could open in January 2027, Emergency Services Director Earl Etheridge said. Crews are finishing work on the center, which Etheridge said is the final major project of his career before he retires. “If you’ve gotta go out on a high note, this is a high note. This is gonna be a major factor for the safety of the citizens of Jackson County,” Etheridge said. Center to replace flood-prone facility Etheridge said the $7.2 million center along Highway 57 will replace the county’s older, flood-prone emergency operations facility in downtown Pascagoula. An open room will become the operations floor, where county leaders and emergency responders will make decisions during storms, evacuations and other emergencies. Building features “This building is built to federal standards. It will stand up to 200-mile-an-hour winds. The systems in the building are redundant, so we’re not dependent on any one thing,” Etheridge said. The 10,000-square-foot facility will also include conference and training rooms, bunk rooms for overnight stays and a full commercial kitchen. Etheridge said he is looking forward most to his new

items.t: Gulfport church distributes food three days a week
items.x: GULFPORT, Miss. (WLOX) — Rescue Mission Baptist Church in Gulfport distributes food to community members three days a week. Volunteers hand out fresh produce, meat, dairy and bread every Monday, Wednesday and Friday starting at 11:30 until supplies run out. Residents of Gulfport are not the only people who can receive food. Jantail Thomas, the church’s food minister, said the church receives a variety of items. “We get something for everything. We get meat, dairy, bread, sweet snacks, salads, you name it. Whatever I get it, I give back,” Thomas said. Thomas said people do not have to live in the community to receive food. “You ain’t got to live in this community. You can be from any community, any city, state. If you need food, pull up at Rescue Mission Baptist Church, and Big Mama is going to give you something to eat,” Thomas said. Food distributions take place at the church on Indiana Avenue. Organizers said anyone in need is welcome, no questions asked. See a spelling or grammar error in this story? Report it to our team HERE .

items.t: Harrison County schools awarded nearly $700,000 for daily student snacks
items.x: HARRISON COUNTY, Miss. (WLOX) — The Harrison County School District has been awarded nearly $700,000 in grant funding for the 2026-27 Fresh Fruit & Vegetable Program, according to a district news release. The grant ensures all elementary and middle school students in the district receive a healthy snack each day. The snack is in addition to the district’s breakfast and lunch meals. The snack changes each day. Students receive vegetables two days a week and fruit three days a week. The district said the snacks will introduce students to a variety of fresh produce, including seasonal and locally grown options. The snacks also include fruits and vegetables that may be less common than those typically offered at breakfast and lunch, the district said. Brad Barlow, Harrison County Schools director of child nutrition programs, said the district keeps serving new foods even if students do not like them at first. “They’re all about trying new things, and they may not like it the first time, but we keep going and serving it over and over again, and eventually we hope that what we’re offering will instill lifelong healthy eating habits,” Barlow said. items.t: For politics, what is an October surprise?
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - An October surprise is an event that could shake up an election, but does it often make the difference? Matt Dallek, a professor of political management at George Washington University, described it as “an event that, at least in theory, has the potential to shake up an election, something that people did not foresee coming that upends the debate.” He said the term dates back to around the 1980 election, when President Jimmy Carter failed to secure the release of American hostages being held in Iran before November 4, 1980, election day. Carter lost to Republican rival Ronald Reagan. Several surprises have occurred in the years since. Surprises can be driven by a campaign or by news events. Examples include Iran-Contra-related indictments in 1992 and the global financial collapse in 2008. Dallek said those surprises likely did not change the outcome of the election that November. “There’s no evidence that they flip a dynamic that was already in place,” Dallek said. “What’s more typical is that an event occurs, it dominates the news cycle and the trend line starts to move further toward the candidate who was already doing well, who was already likely to prevai

items.t: Library says person threw box of cockroaches at a staff member, prompting closure
items.x: TOLEDO, Ohio ( WTVG /Gray News) - A cockroach attack forced the closure of a library in Ohio this week. Surveillance footage was released by the Toledo Lucas County Public Library, appearing to show a person throwing a box of cockroaches at a staff member on Tuesday at the Kent Branch Library. Surveillance footage apparently shows someone throwing a box of cockroaches at a library employee in Ohio. (Source: Toledo Lucas County Public Library) A library spokesperson confirmed the throwing of the box of cockroaches at the library worker on Collingwood Blvd. But it wasn’t immediately shared what led up to the cockroach attack. The library was said to have gone into restricted access before closing for the rest of the day for cleanup and remediation. The Kent Branch Library reopened Wednesday. Officials did not say whether anyone would be facing any charges.

items.t: Grandmother not indicted in baby’s death after police say she left her in hot car for 8 hours while she worked
items.x: MADISONVILLE, Ky. ( WFIE /Gray News) — A Kentucky doctor who accidentally left her grandchild unattended in a hot car for about eight hours will not be indicted for the baby’s death. Madisonville police said 10-month-old Scottie Crowell died in August . On Tuesday, a grand jury found there was insufficient probable cause for an indictment. Police said Scottie’s grandmother picked her up in the morning of Aug. 13 and was supposed to take her to daycare. She forgot the child was in the car and went to work, police said. She arrived at Owensboro Health Multi-Care, where she works as a doctor, around 8 a.m. The baby’s father called his wife after trying to pick up Scottie from daycare, but the child was not there. The baby’s mother called the grandmother at work, and the grandmother ran outside and saw Scottie was still in the vehicle around 4 p.m., police said. After 911 was called, first responders tried to administer lifesaving measures, but the baby died. “I would ask that you keep the infant’s parents and family in your thoughts and prayers as they continue to grieve and process this unimaginable loss,” said Commonwealth’s Attorney Hannah Kington-Jarvis.

items.t: Widow searches for lost wedding ring when husband dies 3 days after getting married in Las Vegas
items.x: LAS VEGAS ( KVVU /Gray News) — A South Dakota woman is asking for help finding the wedding ring her husband lost in Las Vegas the night they married. Tammy Bishop and Will Mulroy were married Oct. 20 at the Viva Las Vegas Chapel. Bishop said they celebrated on a party bus and toured the Strip. At a bar, though, she says Mulroy looked down and realized his ring was gone. “We got to a bar. He looked down and his band was gone. He lost it. He started crying,” Bishop said. According to Bishop, he told her the ring was two sizes too big because he had lost weight. She said the ring may have slid off on the bus or while he moved into his wheelchair. It may also have come off while he rolled down the Strip. “We backtracked our steps. We told the bus driver. We had everyone looking. We couldn’t find it,” she said. The next day, she joked with him: “You didn’t even have your ring on for 24 hours and you lost it.” Everyone laughed, she said. “I said it’s not a big deal; we will buy you a new one, but now that he is gone it is a big deal to me,” Bishop said. items.t: ‘I miss her like crazy’: Loved ones remembering post office worker hit and killed by car
items.x: FORT THOMAS, Ky. ( WXIX /Gray News) - Loved ones and a Kentucky community are mourning a post office worker who was hit and killed by a car while walking earlier this month. Marchelle Bertram worked at the front desk of the Fort Thomas Post Office for years, helping people who came in. Sadly, she lost her life in a collision in Bellevue on Oct. 15. Her daughter, Whitney Bertram, said she is remembering her mother while seeing a large amount of support from the community following her death. “There are so many people I don’t know whose lives she’s touched and affected,” Whitney Bertram said. The crash occurred while Marchelle Bertram was walking on Memorial Parkway near her home. Her daughter said she rushed to the hospital after learning her mother had been hit by a vehicle. “Given the grave amount of injuries she sustained, there was no way she was going to survive,” she said. Marchelle Bertram died at the hospital. Whitney Bertram said the driver stayed at the scene and believes the crash was an accident. “I miss her like crazy; I try not to think about it too hard because I’ll break down,” she said. items.t: Ernie Johnson announces this will be his final season on ‘Inside The NBA’
items.x: (Gray News) - Ernie Johnson announced he will be stepping down as host of “Inside the NBA” at the end of the season. The Sports Broadcasting Hall of Famer took to social media on Wednesday to explain his decision to step away, saying, “It’s just time.” Johnson, 70, stated that he would not be retiring, but cutting back. “This is by no means the end. It’s just a turning of the page,” Johnson said. “And I’ll forever cherish every chapter we have written with ‘Inside the NBA.’” Johnson said he plans to continue to work, including covering the NCAA men’s basketball tournament for CBS and Turner Sports. The six-time Sports Emmy Award winner acknowledged that he has dealt with heart issues in recent years, but that isn’t the reason he’s stepping away from the show. “I just want to slow down a bit,” he added in his social media post. Johnson joined Turner Sports in 1989 and has hosted “Inside the NBA” since 1990. He thanked his TNT Sports and ESPN crews for their support over the years, as well as the viewers. “I just want to say thanks to you. Thanks for your loyalty, for your love, for your support. And on this day, for your understanding,” Johnson said.

items.t: Police department closes its investigation into Hayden Panettiere’s death
items.x: GREENVILLE, S.C. ( WHNS /Gray News) - The Greenville Police Department said it has officially closed its investigation into the death of Hayden Panettiere. Police said Panettiere’s death has been ruled accidental based on the medical examiner’s determination and the findings of the investigation. Panettiere, 36, died from an accidental overdose involving multiple prescription medications and fentanyl, according to findings previously released by the Greenville County Coroner’s Office. Toxicology testing determined the cause of death to be the toxic effects of fentanyl, 4-ANPP, alprazolam, methocarbamol and quetiapine. An autopsy showed no signs of contributing trauma. On Aug. 16, Panettiere was found unresponsive inside an apartment in Greenville, where she had been temporarily staying. Dispatchers received a 911 call reporting a woman in cardiac arrest at approximately 1:51 p.m. She was pronounced dead at 2:32 p.m. Her on-and-off boyfriend Brian Hickerson and his brother Zach Hickerson were at the apartment where she died. items.t: Trump says US will beat China in AI as technology emerges
items.x: WASHINGTON (Gray DC) - Artificial intelligence has emerged as the critical sticking point between the U.S. and China. President Donald Trump, who has named it “super intelligence,” insists the U.S. will beat China in the AI competition. Trump said while campaigning for president that tariffs would form the crux of the bilateral relationship. The U.S. and China, the world’s two largest economies, have been engaged in a trade war during both of Trump’s terms. Speaking Sept. 13 in Ireland, Trump said the U.S. is leading China in AI. “We’re leading China in AI, we’re the most sophisticated country in the world, and frankly, I want to keep it that way because whoever wins AI, wins,” Trump said. During a state visit to Beijing in May, Trump praised Chinese President Xi Jinping. “And it’s to me an honor. We’ve had a fantastic relationship. We’ve gotten along. When they were difficulties, we worked it out,” Trump said. Trump hosted Xi at the White House in September for a state visit. He touted what he called “the tremendous strides” he and Xi had already made on national security, trade and technology. ( KPHO /Gray News) - A man lost thousands of dollars after getting a call that appeared to come from his father’s phone number, with a stranger claiming his parents were being held at gunpoint. Curtis Indyke was asleep around 11:30 p.m. on Oct. 21 when he got a call that appeared to be from his dad, who lives in Virginia. Indyke lives in Arizona. “I answer the phone and it’s not my dad. It’s some other male saying he has my parents basically at gunpoint,” Indyke said. The caller told him to pay or his parents would be shot. While still on the phone, Indyke said he texted 911 to report his parents were being held hostage in Virginia. The person who claimed to be holding Indyke’s parents hostage continued making threats. In a panic, Indyke sent more than $4,000 through Apple Pay to two separate phone numbers. “And they also wanted $1,000 worth of crypto gift cards, which I’ve never even heard of. I’m in IT and I’ve never even heard of them,” Indyke said. Indyke said his bank blocked that purchase.
